text:
Welcome back to The State of AI, a new collaboration between the Financial Times and MIT Technology Review. Every Monday, writers from both publications debate one aspect of the generative AI revolution reshaping global power. You can read the rest of the series here.

In this conversation, Helen Warrell, FT investigations reporter and former defense and security editor, and James O’Donnell, MIT Technology Review’s senior AI reporter, consider the ethical quandaries and financial incentives around AI’s use by the military.

Helen Warrell, FT investigations reporter 

It is July 2027, and China is on the brink of invading Taiwan. Autonomous drones with AI targeting capabilities are primed to overpower the island’s air defenses as a series of crippling AI-generated cyberattacks cut off energy supplies and key communications. In the meantime, a vast disinformation campaign enacted by an AI-powered pro-Chinese meme farm spreads across global social media, deadening the outcry at Beijing’s act of aggression.

Scenarios such as this have brought dystopian horror to the debate about the use of AI in warfare. Military commanders hope for a digitally enhanced force that is faster and more accurate than human-directed combat. But there are fears that as AI assumes an increasingly central role, these same commanders will lose control of a conflict that escalates too quickly and lacks ethical or legal oversight. Henry Kissinger, the former US secretary of state, spent his final years warning about the coming catastrophe of AI-driven warfare.

Grasping and mitigating these risks is the military priority—some would say the “Oppenheimer moment”—of our age. One emerging consensus in the West is that decisions around the deployment of nuclear weapons should not be outsourced to AI. UN secretary-general António Guterres has gone further, calling for an outright ban on fully autonomous lethal weapons systems. It is essential that regulation keep pace with evolving technology. But in the sci-fi-fueled excitement, it is easy to lose track of what is actually possible. As researchers at Harvard’s Belfer Center point out, AI optimists often underestimate the challenges of fielding fully autonomous weapon systems. It is entirely possible that the capabilities of AI in combat are being overhyped.

Anthony King, Director of the Strategy and Security Institute at the University of Exeter and a key proponent of this argument, suggests that rather than replacing humans, AI will be used to improve military insight. Even if the character of war is changing and remote technology is refining weapon systems, he insists, “the complete automation of war itself is simply an illusion.”

Of the three current military use cases of AI, none involves full autonomy. It is being developed for planning and logistics, cyber warfare (in sabotage, espionage, hacking, and information operations; and—most controversially—for weapons targeting, an application already in use on the battlefields of Ukraine and Gaza. Kyiv’s troops use AI software to direct drones able to evade Russian jammers as they close in on sensitive sites. The Israel Defense Forces have developed an AI-assisted decision support system known as Lavender, which has helped identify around 37,000 potential human targets within Gaza. 

There is clearly a danger that the Lavender database replicates the biases of the data it is trained on. But military personnel carry biases too. One Israeli intelligence officer who used Lavender claimed to have more faith in the fairness of a “statistical mechanism” than that of a grieving soldier.

Tech optimists designing AI weapons even deny that specific new controls are needed to control their capabilities. Keith Dear, a former UK military officer who now runs the strategic forecasting company Cassi AI, says existing laws are more than sufficient: “You make sure there’s nothing in the training data that might cause the system to go rogue … when you are confident you deploy it—and you, the human commander, are responsible for anything they might do that goes wrong.”

It is an intriguing thought that some of the fear and shock about use of AI in war may come from those who are unfamiliar with brutal but realistic military norms. What do you think, James? Is some opposition to AI in warfare less about the use of autonomous systems and really an argument against war itself? 

James O’Donnell replies:

Hi Helen, 

One thing I’ve noticed is that there’s been a drastic shift in attitudes of AI companies regarding military applications of their products. In the beginning of 2024, OpenAI unambiguously forbade the use of its tools for warfare, but by the end of the year, it had signed an agreement with Anduril to help it take down drones on the battlefield. 

This step—not a fully autonomous weapon, to be sure, but very much a battlefield application of AI—marked a drastic change in how much tech companies could publicly link themselves with defense. 

What happened along the way? For one thing, it’s the hype. We’re told AI will not just bring superintelligence and scientific discovery but also make warfare sharper, more accurate and calculated, less prone to human fallibility. I spoke with US Marines, for example, who tested a type of AI while patrolling the South Pacific that was advertised to analyze foreign intelligence faster than a human could. 

Location

A location I care about is

Generating your personalized response…

Secondly, money talks. OpenAI and others need to start recouping some of the unimaginable amounts of cash they’re spending on training and running these models. And few have deeper pockets than the Pentagon. And Europe’s defense heads seem keen to splash the cash too. Meanwhile, the amount of venture capital funding for defense tech this year has already doubled the total for all of 2024, as VCs hope to cash in on militaries’ newfound willingness to buy from startups. 

I do think the opposition to AI warfare falls into a few camps, one of which simply rejects the idea that more precise targeting (if it’s actually more precise at all) will mean fewer casualties rather than just more war. Consider the first era of drone warfare in Afghanistan. As drone strikes became cheaper to implement, can we really say it reduced carnage? Instead, did it merely enable more destruction per dollar?

But the second camp of criticism (and now I’m finally getting to your question) comes from people who are well versed in the realities of war but have very specific complaints about the technology’s fundamental limitations. Missy Cummings, for example, is a former fighter pilot for the US Navy who is now a professor of engineering and computer science at George Mason University. She has been outspoken in her belief that large language models, specifically, are prone to make huge mistakes in military settings.

The typical response to this complaint is that AI’s outputs are human-checked. But if an AI model relies on thousands of inputs for its conclusion, can that conclusion really be checked by one person?

Tech companies are making extraordinarily big promises about what AI can do in these high-stakes applications, all while pressure to implement them is sky high. For me, this means it’s time for more skepticism, not less. 

Helen responds:

Hi James, 

We should definitely continue to question the safety of AI warfare systems and the oversight to which they’re subjected—and hold political leaders to account in this area. I am suggesting that we also apply some skepticism to what you rightly describe as the “extraordinarily big promises” made by some companies about what AI might be able to achieve on the battlefield. 

There will be both opportunities and hazards in what the military is being offered by a relatively nascent (though booming) defense tech scene. The danger is that in the speed and secrecy of an arms race in AI weapons, these emerging capabilities may not receive the scrutiny and debate they desperately need.

Further reading:

Michael C. Horowitz, director of Perry World House at the University of Pennsylvania, explains the need for responsibility in the development of military AI systems in this FT op-ed.

The FT’s tech podcast asks what Israel’s defense tech ecosystem can tell us about the future of warfare 

This MIT Technology Review story analyzes how OpenAI completed its pivot to allowing its technology on the battlefield.

MIT Technology Review also uncovered how US soldiers are using generative AI to help scour thousands of pieces of open-source intelligence.

text:
AI superintelligence may not be what you think. And it may be closer than you imagine.

Humanity has achieved many things beyond the capability of any one human: particle accelerators, advanced CPUs, fusion reactors, fighter jets, novel cures, reusable rockets, the list goes on and on.

How? By assembling some of the brightest minds on the planet, experts in many fields, and having them work together as teams to achieve goals that were previously impossible for an individual.

AI will be like that, at least for a while.

When you're dealing with a superintelligent AI, behind the scenes it will spin up thousands or millions of AI agents. Each one is an expert, capable of autonomous thought. (Whether it's thinking as we know it or not is a hair not worth splitting here.) You may be aware of this happening, or blissfully oblivious. Either way, the result will be the same.

Alone, any one agent could not achieve the astonishing breakthroughs that AI will offer us. But together, the hive or swarm of AI agents will combine to achieve things greater than any feats of history.

Later, perhaps much later, all that will be condensed into a single opaque super AI agent sitting on your desktop. It will have all the knowledge and skills it needs to solve any problem buried within its quadrillions of weights.

But for the longest time, we don't even need individual AI to approach genius human level thinking for an AI collective to handily surpass it.

6. What this means for your phone bill  the pricing disruption.

SpaceX hasn’t announced Starlink Mobile pricing. But the structural economics point toward disruption:

Current carrier pricing (2026):

AT&T, T-Mobile, Verizon unlimited plans: $65-90/month per line. Family plans: $35-55/month per line. Prepaid/value (Boost, Cricket, Metro): $25-50/month.

SpaceX’s cost advantages:

No legacy network to maintain (starting fresh). Satellites already in orbit (sunk cost). Rockets already operational (sunk cost). Spectrum acquired at scale (fixed cost). Qualcomm base stations are commodity hardware (declining cost).

The analyst view:

Madden expects SpaceX to build its network more efficiently than incumbents  partly because it won’t support legacy equipment and can take advantage of nationwide spectrum holdings from day one.

The competitive pressure  even before launch:

The mere announcement of SpaceX entering the carrier market forces AT&T, T-Mobile, and Verizon to compete on coverage claims. If SpaceX can credibly promise “zero dead zones”  the incumbents must match or explain why they can’t.

This is the SpaceX playbook applied to telecom: enter an industry dominated by legacy players. Build from scratch with modern technology. Offer a fundamentally different value proposition (zero dead zones). Use vertical integration to undercut on cost. Force incumbents to either compete or watch customers leave.

It worked with rockets (SpaceX vs ULA). It worked with satellite internet (Starlink vs HughesNet). The question is whether it works with mobile carriers  an industry with $400+ billion in annual US revenue and three entrenched players with 100+ million subscribers each.

THE PRICE MAP

The strangest part is how far the same plan can swing from one address to the next.

Higher:
• Starlink’s site lists prices 20% higher for addresses in Portland, Oregon; Spokane, Washington; Murphy, North Carolina; El Dorado, Arkansas; and Lafayette, Louisiana.
• Toronto shows a 10% increase.
• Rolla, Missouri defaults to the Max plan at $156. Warsaw, Missouri lists it at $143.

Lower:
• New Residential customers in New York City, San Francisco and Boston are being offered 30% off, and in some cases 50%.
• Kansas City, Missouri lists Max at $117, with the 100 Mbps and 200 Mbps tiers at $49.50 and $76.50.
• Marysville, Kansas lists Max at $104, the bottom of the band.

Put Rolla next to Marysville and you get the cleanest example. Same Max plan. $156 in one town, $104 in the other. That’s $52 a month, or $624 a year.

Two details make this different from an ordinary price hike:

1. The price follows the address, not the account. If you move, you get a new price.
2. Where new-customer discounts exist, existing subscribers are asking why they pay more than someone who signs up today. Those discounts are a separate offer from the dynamic pricing.

Some customers are seeing 10% to 20% increases. Others are seeing cuts. Which one you get depends on a map you can’t see.

Today, we have a Prabhat Pheri (प्रभात फेरी) at home! 🙏

But have you ever wondered why people wake up before sunrise, walk through neighbourhoods, and sing the Divine’s name, especially during Kartik Maas?

There’s a beautiful meaning behind this tradition.

Prabhat means dawn, and Pheri means a procession or round.

During Kartik Maas, devotees gather early in the morning for bhajans, prayers, and naam-sankirtan.

But why is the morning so significant?

The hours before sunrise, particularly Brahma Muhurta, are considered especially conducive to spiritual practices. In the yogic tradition, this is a time to turn inward and consciously shape ourselves.

Kartik mas is a significant period for spiritual growth, symbolising the transition from sadhana towards reaping its inner fruits.

Devotion is about what devotion can transform within us.

When we sing, pray, or offer ourselves wholeheartedly, the practice becomes an opportunity to cultivate love, awareness, and inner stillness.

Perhaps that’s the deeper beauty of Prabhat Pheri.

A simple morning procession becomes an occasion to step away from our daily distractions, experience devotion together, and begin the day more consciously.

As I welcome this tradition into my home today, I feel grateful that such practices are still alive in our families and communities.

Because the most meaningful part of welcoming the Divine into our homes may be the opportunity to awaken something beautiful within ourselves. ❤️🙏

Have you ever experienced a Prabhat Pheri during Kartik Maas?

text:
A bird this small has no business being awake at this hour. And yet.

Look at the time. Look at the dark. Every rule that keeps a tiny songbird alive says the same thing at night: be still, be hidden, be nobody. Stay quiet. Stay out of sight. Hope the hours pass without anything noticing you exist.

So what happens when something does notice?

I have watched a lot of animal videos. Most of them are about the moment of drama. This one is about a moment that almost never gets filmed: the thin, fragile gap between a wild creature's sleep and the world finding it.

That gap is where this story lives.

Here is what most people never think about. A small wild bird does not sleep the way you do. You lie down in a locked room, under a roof, with a phone charging beside you and a hundred small guarantees that nothing will happen before morning. A bird gets none of that. Its bedroom has no walls. Its alarm system is its own nervous system. Its entire security plan is to be somewhere nobody thinks to look.

Think about how strange that is. Every night, billions of birds close their eyes in places that offer almost no protection, and trust that the night will leave them alone. Not one of them has ever been told it would.

Now add one thing.

A person. In the dark. Close enough to touch.

That is the situation behind this video, and I am deliberately telling you very little about it, because the part worth seeing is not something I can hand you in a paragraph. What I can tell you is why it matters more than it looks like it should.

Start with the numbers that make a small bird's night so hard.

A songbird of this size burns through its energy at a rate that would be alarming in any larger animal. Its heart runs many times faster than yours. Its body is tiny, which means it loses heat quickly, which means it has to eat constantly just to stay warm. For many small species, a single cold night can cost a meaningful share of their body weight. They go to sleep with a full tank and wake up with an almost empty one, and the first hour of daylight is a race to refuel before the next night comes.

That means two things.

First, every night is a small survival test, even when nothing goes wrong. Second, sleep is not a luxury for these animals. It is an operation. Fluffed feathers trap warmth. A tucked body loses less heat. A chosen spot shelters from wind. Every detail of how a small bird settles down has been refined over an unimaginable number of generations, and it all depends on one assumption: nobody interrupts.

So when a small bird is found in the dark, the question is never just "is it cute?"

The question is: what does it cost to be woken up?

Here is another thing that does not get said enough. Most songbirds are built for daylight. Their eyes are tuned for it. Their flight is tuned for it. When a day bird is startled out of sleep, it is not like a night owl switching on. It is closer to you being thrown out of bed in a strange building with the power out. The instincts are fast. The sight is not. Many species that are perfectly graceful at noon become hesitant, disoriented, and clumsy in the dark.

That is why a startled bird at night is a different kind of problem than a startled bird at noon.

And that is why I keep coming back to this clip.

Because somewhere in the space between "a bird asleep" and "a bird awake" there is a decision. Several, actually. The kind that nobody notices when they are made quickly, and everybody notices when they go wrong.

I will not tell you how this one went. That is the point of the video, and I would rather you see it yourself than take my word for it.

But I will tell you what I noticed.

I noticed how quiet it was.

Not silent. Quiet in the way a place is quiet when something very small is trying not to be seen. The kind of quiet where every second feels louder than it should. The kind that makes you lean toward the screen without realizing you are doing it.

There is a particular kind of attention that only wild animals can pull out of us. It is not the attention we give to a pet, which comes with familiarity and affection and a thousand shared mornings. It is something rawer. It is the attention you give to a stranger who did not choose you and does not owe you anything. A creature that could vanish in a heartbeat and would not look back.

That is a very different kind of tension.

A pet can forgive you. A wild bird cannot afford to.

Let that sit for a second.

When we talk about "rescuing" or "helping" wild animals, we usually picture a clear villain and a clear ending. A cliff. A net. A storm. A cruel person. A happy escape. It makes the story easy to tell and easy to feel.

But some of the most interesting moments in wildlife never have a villain at all. They have only a fragile creature, a human with an unknowable intention, and the question of whether the two of them can get through the next few seconds without making things worse.

That is a quieter kind of drama. And in my experience, it is the kind that stays with people.

I have a theory about why.

We spend almost our entire lives surrounded by animals we have already decided about. The dog is a friend. The mosquito is an enemy. The pigeon is background. Wild songbirds slot into a gentle category in the mind, somewhere between decoration and soundtrack. We hear them, we do not meet them.

Then, once in a while, a video makes one of them individual.

Not a species. Not "a bird." One bird, on one night, with one small body and one very large unknown ahead of it.

And suddenly the category collapses.

Suddenly you are not watching "wildlife." You are watching someone.

I think that is what happens in this clip. I think that is why it works on people who have never cared about birds in their lives.

Let me slow down and give you the bigger picture, because it changes how you will watch.

Birds have been sleeping in the open for longer than humans have existed. Over that time they developed some of the most unusual sleep habits in the animal kingdom. Several bird species have been shown to sleep with one half of the brain at a time, keeping one eye open and one side of the brain alert, as if part of them refuses to fully leave. Birds at the end of a roosting line, the ones most exposed to the edge, tend to keep that watchful eye turned outward. The sleeper in the middle gets the deeper rest.

Read that again. Even in sleep, a bird is still doing a form of guard duty.

Some small birds go further. In cold conditions, certain species can lower their body temperature and slow their metabolism overnight, a state called torpor, to survive the hours until sunrise. It is a calculated shutdown. A bet that the saved energy is worth the risk of being slower to react.

A bird in that state is not simply resting. It is operating on borrowed time, with the body running at a lower setting and the reflexes dialed down to match.

So here is the tension I want you to feel before you press play.

The most vulnerable moment of a wild animal's day is the moment it is most deeply asleep. And the safest-looking hiding place is only safe as long as nobody finds it.

Both of those things can be true at once, and the video lives in the space where they collide.

Now let me ask you something uncomfortable.

If you came across a small wild creature in the dark, completely still, apparently unaware, what would you do?

Most people answer fast. Some say they would leave it alone. Some say they would help. Some say they would take a photo first. Almost nobody says they would think about it for long.

But what makes this interesting is that every one of those answers can be right or wrong depending on details you cannot see from a distance. Is the animal hurt, or just resting? Is it stuck, or simply sheltered? Does your presence reduce its risk, or add to it? Would a gentle hand change the outcome, or would the gentlest hand in the world still be a catastrophe in the eyes of something that weighs less than a handful of coins?

Wildlife rehabilitators often say the same thing: good intentions are the starting point, not the finish line. Plenty of the animals that end up in care arrived there because someone wanted to do something kind and did not yet know what the kind thing was.

That is not an argument against compassion. It is an argument for paying attention.

And attention is exactly what this video is made of.

I want to be careful here, because I know how posts like this usually go. They promise something enormous and then deliver a sunset and a moral. I will not do that to you. I am not going to tell you this story ends one way or another. I am not going to claim anyone was a hero or anyone was in danger. I do not know what was in anyone's mind that night, and neither do you.

What I know is smaller and, I think, more honest.

I know that a very small wild animal was in a very exposed place in the middle of the night.

I know that a person was close enough to change what happened next.

And I know that the video shows what the two of them did with that closeness.

That is it. That is the whole contract.

So why does a story with so few facts feel so large?

Because of scale. Our brains are wired to read size as significance. A mountain feels important. A war feels important. A bird the size of your thumb feels like a footnote.

But think about what a footnote actually is. It is a small piece of text carrying something the main story could not hold. And a tiny animal at night often carries exactly that: the thing the larger world forgot to include.

We built entire economies around speed. Around volume. Around never being still. And here is a creature whose whole survival strategy is the opposite. Stillness as armor. Silence as defense. Smallness as a method.

It makes you wonder what we lose when we only notice the loud things.

Let me put this another way.

Most of what happens on this planet happens at night, out of sight, with no audience. Animals feeding, hiding, migrating, resting, being found, being missed. A staggering amount of life takes place in hours when the human world is asleep and the lights are off. We know this the way we know the ocean is deep. As a fact. Not as an experience.

Then a clip like this shows up, shot in a single vertical frame by someone standing in the dark with a phone, and for a few seconds the fact becomes an experience.

That is what I think the best nature videos do. They do not teach you anything. They briefly remove the glass.

There is a name for the feeling that follows, and I do not think English has a good word for it. It is not pity. It is not excitement. It is closer to responsibility without instructions. The sense that you have been handed something fragile and nobody told you what you are supposed to do with it.

I have felt it watching this.

Let me tell you what I did not expect.

I did not expect to care about the sound.

Or rather, the absence of it. When I first pressed play I assumed the interesting part would be whatever happened on screen. I was wrong. The interesting part was how much the clip made me aware of the space around it. The darkness at the edges. The things that could not be seen. The sense that the frame was a small lit window into a very large, very quiet night.

Maybe that is why it works. A bright clip about a bird would be a nature video. A dark clip about a bird becomes a question.

Who is out there? What are they carrying? How many nights like this go by with nobody watching?

I do not have answers. I just think the questions are better than the answers I would make up.

Let me say something about trust, because it is the word that kept coming into my head.

Trust is usually framed as a feeling. In the animal world, it is a measurement. How close will something let you come before it leaves? How long will it hold still? How much of its guard will it lower, and for how long?

Wild animals do not give trust. They tolerate proximity, and only up to a line. That line is not arbitrary. It is the output of an incredibly sensitive calculation, run again and again, every second you are near: is this thing a threat, yes or no, and what does it cost me to find out?

Which means that watching a human and a wild bird share a few feet of space is, in a strange way, watching a negotiation. One side does not speak the other's language. Neither can explain its intentions. And both are reading each other anyway, in the only way available: through movement, through stillness, through what they choose not to do.

I find that moving. Not sentimental. Moving in the plain sense of the word: it moves something in you.

Here is where I will plant a flag.

I do not think the question is "should humans interfere with wildlife." That framing is too clean. Sometimes the answer is yes, sometimes no, and the people who know best are the ones most willing to say "it depends."

I think the better question is: what kind of attention do we bring when we are close to something that cannot ask us for anything?

Is it curiosity? Care? Impatience? Possession? The urge to capture rather than to understand?

Because the same hand can do any of those things. The same lens too. Same night, same bird, same few seconds, and the meaning changes completely depending on what the person behind it is actually after.

That is why I keep telling you I am not going to spoil it. Not because there is a twist. There may not be one. But because the way you read it will say something about you. About what you expect from people when nobody is watching. About what you expect from yourself.

And I would rather you discover that on your own.

Let me widen the lens for a moment, because there is a pattern here that goes beyond one bird.

Ecologists have a phrase for the things most people never see: the unobserved majority. Most animal lives are not documented. Most deaths are not witnessed. Most close calls are never recorded by anyone, human or otherwise. The wild runs on a ledger that nobody audits.

So whenever a camera does happen to be present at one of these moments, it is working against enormous odds. The right person. The right night. The right few seconds. A phone already out. A steady enough hand to keep filming.

I find myself wondering how many nearly identical scenes have happened without a single witness.

Probably more than we could count. Probably every night.

That should change how we hold a clip like this. It is not an exception to the rule of the wild. It is a rare glimpse of the rule itself, a window into what is going on constantly, just beyond the edge of the porch light.

And there is a second layer.

People often assume that wild animals live dramatic lives, full of chases and fights. Biologists will tell you the opposite. Most of an animal's life is spent on the least cinematic activities imaginable: waiting, conserving energy, staying put, avoiding notice. The drama is the exception. The patience is the norm.

For a small bird, a successful night is one where nothing happens at all. The best possible outcome of a night is that it is boring. Nobody will ever make a video about the thousands of dull nights that kept it alive.

Which makes the one night that gets recorded strange by definition. Out of every night a bird has lived, this is the one we got to see. We can only guess what made this one different, and I will not pretend to know.

There is something humbling about that. We are always watching the exception and mistaking it for the typical.

Let me give you one more thing to carry into the video.

Think about the vocabulary we have for the care of wild animals. Rescue. Release. Rehabilitate. Rewild. Every one of those words has an ending built into it. An arc. A direction. We love stories that go somewhere.

But some moments with wildlife do not go anywhere. They are brief, ambiguous, and incomplete. A person and an animal meet, something is decided in a few seconds, and then the animal is gone and the person is left holding nothing but the memory and, if they were quick, a file on their phone.

I think those are the moments that deserve the most careful watching, precisely because they do not resolve into a lesson. They just are what they are, and you have to decide for yourself what you make of them.

So many viral videos tell you exactly how to feel. A swelling song. A caption in capital letters. A narrator who explains the emotion before you have had it.

This is not that kind of video. And I would argue that is its strength.

It trusts you.

Let me try to name what I think is at stake without giving anything away.

It is not life and death, necessarily. I will not claim that, because I cannot confirm it, and you should be suspicious of anyone who would.

It is something more ordinary and more universal: the experience of being very small in the presence of something much larger, and having no control over what the larger thing does.

Every one of us knows that feeling. A child in a hospital hallway. A new employee in a meeting where decisions are being made about them. A passenger in a car on an icy road. A person waiting for a phone call. Being small is not an animal condition. It is a human one, only usually better hidden.

When we watch a very small animal in that position, we are borrowing a feeling we already know.

And maybe that is the real reason it hits.

Not because the animal is cute. Plenty of things are cute, and we scroll past them in half a second.

It hits because, for a moment, we recognize ourselves in the one who has no say.

Then comes the second recognition, the sharper one. We are also, sometimes, the larger thing. The hand. The decision. The weather in someone else's night.

Which one are you in this story?

Honestly, I changed my answer while I was watching.

Here is a smaller point that I think is worth making, and it is about the setting.

Night changes what we can know. In daylight, we assume we see everything. At night, we see only what a light happens to reach. A flashlight does not illuminate a scene. It carves out a tiny circle and declares everything else irrelevant.

Footage shot like that has a strange intimacy. You are not given the whole picture. You are given a narrow beam of attention, and what lies beyond is left to your imagination.

It reminds me of how most of our moral lives actually work. We rarely get the full context. We see a small circle of the situation, act on it, and live with the result.

The best wildlife footage is honest about that. It does not pretend to be omniscient. It says: this is what was visible, from here, at this time.

That honesty is rarer than it should be.

Let me turn to the question that I suspect many of you are already forming.

"Is the bird okay?"

I understand the instinct. It is the first thing I wanted to know too. But notice what that question does. It turns the video into a checklist item. A verdict to be collected. Once you have the answer, the experience is over.

I would invite you to try something different. Watch it without hunting for the verdict. Watch what the clip is actually showing you about attention, about restraint, about the physical reality of sharing a tiny space with a wild animal. Let the question stay open while you look.

Then decide whether the ending you were hunting for was the thing that mattered.

I suspect it will not be.

Or maybe it will. I do not know. I will not pretend to.

What I do know is that the version of you that watches it with the question held open will see more than the version that races to the last second.

And now a word on why I think this clip is worth sending to someone.

There is a particular kind of friend you think of when a video like this finishes. Not the one who would like it. The one who would sit with it. The one who would text back a single sentence, and the sentence would be exactly right.

Send it to that person.

Send it to the one who still stops to look at a bird on a windowsill. The one who has stood in a field at night just to hear what was out there. The one who pulls over for turtles and does not apologize for it.

And send it to the one who thinks none of this matters. Not as an argument. Just as an offering. Sometimes a few seconds of quiet attention does more than a hundred reasons.

One more angle, because it surprised me when I read about it.

Light changes everything for a night bird that is not built for night. Researchers have documented that artificial light after dark can disturb the rhythms of wild birds, shifting when they wake, when they sing, and how well they rest. A bright beam that feels harmless to us can register to a small sleeper as something else entirely: a sudden, enormous change in its world, arriving without any warning at all.

Think about what that means for a moment where a person and a bird are close in the dark. Every choice is amplified. Where the light points. How long it stays. Whether a voice is used or withheld. Even breathing becomes part of the conversation.

We are used to thinking of ourselves as bystanders in nature. Up close, there is no such thing. The moment you are near, you are a participant, whether you meant to be or not.

That is an uncomfortable idea and also a clarifying one. It means that paying attention is not optional, and that the quality of our attention is the only real tool we have.

And then there is the morning, which is the part of the story nobody ever films.

Dawn is when a small bird's whole night is finally paid off or lost. The first light brings the first meal, and the first meal is what the body has been waiting for since dusk. Every hour of stillness was a loan, and sunrise is when the debt comes due.

So when I think about any bird that gets through a night like this one, I do not picture the dramatic moment. I picture the ordinary one that comes after it: a body shaking out cold feathers, a small voice testing the air, a day beginning as if nothing had ever interrupted it. That quiet resumption is the real miracle of the wild, and it happens so often that we stopped calling it one. Nobody ever applauds one solitary quiet morning. Maybe someone should, now and then.

Before you go, a few last thoughts I could not leave out.

First: be wary of the urge to turn every encounter with wildlife into content. I say that as someone writing a very long post about a video. The tension is real. A camera can protect a moment by preserving it, or damage it by changing what the people in it choose to do. The honest creators know that line exists. They feel it every time they raise a phone toward something that did not agree to be seen.

What I respect most about this clip is that it does not feel staged for the lens. It feels like something that happened, and a camera happened to be there. That distinction is subtle, and it is the difference between a video you remember and a video you merely watch.

Second: the next time you hear a bird at dusk, listen to how the sound thins out. The chorus does not end abruptly. It fades, voice by voice, as each small body settles into whatever it has decided is safe enough. That fading is the sound of thousands of tiny decisions about trust.

Somewhere in that quiet, one of them might be sleeping closer to you than you would ever guess.

Third, and this is the one I care about most.

We tend to think kindness needs to be big to count. A rescue. A donation. A grand gesture with a before and an after. But the more I look at how animals actually live, the more I think the most important kindness is often the smallest: the decision not to make someone's worst moment worse. To move slowly. To lower your voice. To ask what the situation needs rather than what you need from it.

That is a hard skill. It is harder than being brave. Bravery is loud, and everyone can see it. Gentleness in the dark is invisible by design.

If this video is about anything, I think it is about that.

I am not going to tell you what happens. I have said all I can say without taking something from you that you deserve to meet on your own.

I will only say this.

Go in expecting nothing grand. Go in expecting a small bird, a quiet night, and a few seconds of attention that most of the world will never witness.

Then notice what it does to you.

Notice whether you lean in. Notice whether you hold your breath. Notice the moment, if there is one, where you realize you have been rooting for a stranger who does not know you exist and could not thank you if it did.

That feeling has no practical use. It will not fix anything. It will not pay a bill or win an argument.

But it is one of the clearest signs we have that something in us is still working the way it was meant to.

A creature small enough to disappear into the dark.

A night that could have gone any number of ways.

And a few seconds that someone thought were worth keeping.

Press play, and decide for yourself what the night was whispering.

Black Friday...

You can see it as being about LACK...

❤️ Or, you could view it as an ABUNDANT opportunity.  

- that’s the way I choose to see it - and coach my clients to approach it.  

It’s the ONE DAY in the YEAR when a high % of people wake up in the morning, wondering what ‘deals’ will be available for them to buy. 

Advertisers have spent BILLIONS over many years, ‘training’ consumers to buy on Black Friday!

The question is whether you want your audience to buy from YOU - or someone else?!

Let’s talk about the word ‘deal’ for a minute. 

A ‘good deal’ does NOT automatically mean DISCOUNT!

That feeling IMO does NOT come from PENALISING people who recently paid full price for the thing you’re discounting. 

❤️🔥 An ABUNDANT Black Friday offer is one that REWARDS your audience for their attention, trust and loyalty. 

✅ NEW
💡 Maybe a new thing that you make available for the BF weekend. 

✅ ADDED
💡 perhaps an additional bonus that is added to an existing offer for those who buy over the BF weekend.

💡 for example, beat a pending price increase when you buy over the BF weekend.

text:
You keep exchanging your soul for a decaying world.

You wake up every day with an existential crisis, doing all you can to make sense of your own world, trying to find meaning in your experiences, your ambitions, your relationships and the realities that shape your existence. You wrap your ideologies around your own realities, interpreting life through the limitations of your experiences and the conclusions you have drawn from the little you have been able to understand about the world around you.

You have never lived another person's life in its entirety, you have never experienced existence through another person's consciousness, and you have never had the privilege of seeing the world through every possible lens. Yet, somehow, you acclaim to believe that this world is all there is, and proceed to do everything within your means, sometimes even at the expense of your own soul, to attain, accumulate and possess everything this world has to offer.

You pursue the things that promise you a sense of permanence in a world whose very nature is characterised by decay, building your confidence around things that are constantly subject to change, and investing the entirety of your existence in realities that are themselves awaiting an eventual end. Somehow, in the midst of all this, the question of eternity becomes an inconvenient thought, something you would rather leave unexplored while you continue to make sense of the immediate world around you.

Then suddenly, you find yourself on your deathbed, and in those final moments, you are gripped by the fear of an unfamiliar realisation: the moment you close your eyes here in this world, you are going to open them somewhere else, in another realm, with the full awareness that death was simply a door ushering you into a reality beyond the one you have spent your entire lifetime trying to understand. It suddenly dawns on you that eternity is real, that your existence extends beyond the boundaries of your physical body, and that there is an eternal consequence to the choices you have made with your soul.

Sadly, you have spent years deliberately exchanging your soul for the decay of this world, continually refusing to acknowledge the knowledge of God that has been so profoundly displayed before you, over and over again, through the design, order and intricacies of creation. You have had countless opportunities to consider the intelligence behind existence, to allow the curiosity of your own observations to lead you towards the Creator, and to recognise that the existence of a created thing necessarily points to the existence of a Creator.

You would rather choose what your physical eyes can see, what your hands can touch, what your intellect can process and what your limited understanding of existence can accommodate. You would rather find peace in what appears logical to you, in what you can explain, predict and control, because the possibility of having to confront the vastness of existence beyond your comprehension seems far too unsettling. Far be it from you to venture into the questions of existence and eternity with the possibility of having to reconsider everything you have ever assumed about life, its origin and its ultimate destination.

And in all of creation, it is particularly fascinating that mankind, the very creature endowed with the capacity to observe, reason, question, explore and exercise dominion, appears to have the least regard for the One from whom all things derive their existence. The rest of creation, in its own appointed order, eagerly awaits its own deliverance from the bondage of corruption, groaning together as it awaits the manifestation of the sons of God.

text:
I Asked My Wife for Sex Every Morning Before Work. By Thursday, She Was Avoiding Me.

I thought I had discovered the secret to a perfect marriage.

Whenever my wife and I made love before she left for work, I felt happier, more relaxed, and unusually confident throughout the day. Even the worst meetings seemed easier to handle.

So I decided to make it a daily routine.

I didn't realise that what started as a playful request would soon make my wife dread hearing the alarm.

One night, while we were lying in bed after dinner, I turned toward her.

Me: “I've noticed something.”

Wife: “What now?”

Me: “Whenever we have sex in the morning, my whole day feels lighter. I get to work in a better mood, I'm less stressed, and even traffic doesn't annoy me as much.”

She laughed.

Wife: “So?”

Me: “So I want us to do it every morning.”

She lifted her head from the pillow.

Wife: “Every morning?”

Me: “Every single morning.”

Wife: “You're joking.”

I kissed her shoulder.

Me: “I'm serious. Why are you looking at me like I've just asked you to run a marathon?”

She shook her head, smiling.

Wife: “Baby, do you understand what you're asking? I have to wake up early, shower, get dressed, prepare breakfast, and deal with traffic. You want to add another activity to my morning routine?”

Me: “You're my wife. Who else am I supposed to ask?”

She laughed again.

Wife: “I thought marriage was supposed to give me some peace.”

Me: “This is peace. You'll leave the house happier, and I'll have a good day.”

She gave me a suspicious look.

Wife: “And what happens when I'm tired?”

I grinned.

Me: “Then I'll have to be very convincing.”

She hit my arm with a pillow.

Wife: “You better learn to take no for an answer.”

We eventually negotiated like two people settling a workplace agreement. I wanted five mornings a week. She offered two. After plenty of teasing, we settled on four, with weekends off so she could “recover.”

At the time, I thought I'd struck an excellent deal.

Monday morning was wonderful. We woke up a little earlier, shared some intimacy, showered, and had breakfast together. She left for work smiling, and I spent the entire morning feeling like the luckiest husband alive.
Tuesday was just as good.

By Wednesday, however, I began noticing small changes.

She started setting her alarm earlier. Sometimes she'd remain under the shower longer than usual. One morning, she said her back was hurting. Another morning, she simply rolled over and pulled the blanket over her head.

I tried to joke about our agreement.

Me: “Madam, I believe we have a commitment.”

She opened one eye.

Wife: “And I believe I need another hour of sleep.”

I laughed, but I could tell she wasn't enjoying the routine as much as I was.

Black Friday is roughly 3 weeks away, and Fable 5.2 is about to do 80% of your prep for you...

Here’s every prompt you need to crush Q4 Google Ads:

(Bookmark this)

First things first: feed it everything

Create a Claude Project for your brand and upload:

- Your AOV, product costs, shipping and fees per order
- Last year's Q4 exports from Google Ads and Shopify
- Last year's auction insights graph (Oct to Dec)
- Your BFCM offer, stock levels and Christmas shipping cut-offs
- 20 to 50 real customer reviews
- Your top 3 to 5 competitor URLs

Fable 5.1 can read a massive amount in one go (1,000,000 tokens), so ALL of it fits, and every prompt after can use it.

Prompt 1: The Q4 brief

"You are a senior Google Ads strategist preparing my brand for Black Friday (27 Nov), Cyber Monday (30 Nov) and Christmas 2026. Using everything uploaded, build a Q4 Brief: break-even ROAS at full price AND at my sale price, max CPA during the sale, last year's Q4 lessons from auction insights, a competitor table, a keyword map including brand + sale terms and gift-intent terms, a negative list, 8 to 10 ad angles from my customers' exact words, and a tracking and feed fix list. Flag every assumption. Change nothing in my account."

The sale price break-even is the number that saves you.

An $80 product with $30 of costs breaks even at 1.6x.

Sell it at 25% off and break-even jumps to 2x.

A 1.8x ROAS looks healthy at full price. At 25% off, you're losing money on every order.

Prompt 2: The BFCM build

"Using the Q4 Brief, plan my BFCM campaigns: daily budgets from 15 Nov to 6 Dec weighted to 27 to 30 Nov, a branded search refresh with brand + sale terms and a countdown customizer headline, custom labels splitting sale products, sale prices with effective dates, a Merchant Center promotion ready to submit by 13 Nov, gift-intent search ad groups, a PMax Black Friday asset group, a competitor campaign on Max Clicks, and ad copy scheduled for early access, main sale and last chance. Give me a build sheet, then STOP and ask me to approve. Build everything PAUSED. Never enable anything yourself."

Connect Claude to Google Ads with an MCP, a plug-in that lets it work inside your account. We like Pipeboard, which builds everything paused, so nothing goes live until you approve it.

Prompt 3: The daily war room

"It's BFCM week. Pull yesterday and the last 7 days. Give me a scorecard per campaign marked green, amber or red against my SALE PRICE break-even. List every budget-limited campaign beating target on NEW customer traffic, wasted search terms, competitors showing on my brand terms, feed disapprovals, and the gap between Google Ads and Shopify revenue. Rank the top 5 actions by profit impact. Change nothing until I approve."

Save it as a scheduled task at 7am every morning from 26 Nov to 1 Dec.

You wake up to a ranked to-do list instead of a dashboard.

Prompt 4: The demand machine

"Using the ad angles from the Q4 Brief, build 3 phases of Demand Gen and YouTube: early access list building (6 to 20 Nov), offer-first retargeting during the sale, and Christmas gifting (2 to 18 Dec). For each angle give a creative brief, 5 headlines, 3 image prompts in 1:1, 4:5 and 1.91:1, a 15 to 30 second 16:9 script with a 3-second hook, audiences, and exclude anyone who bought in the last 14 days from prospecting."

Connect the Higgsfield MCP and it generates the first image per angle without leaving the chat.

Three rules to keep your BFCM profitable while Claude does the work:

- Fix tracking before you run any of this. If Google Ads and Shopify revenue are more than 10 to 15% apart, Claude will happily tell you to scale a campaign that's losing you money
- If ROAS drops below your sale-price break-even, pull back immediately. Until then, BFCM lets you scale budgets faster than the usual 15 to 20% every 2 to 3 days
- Claude drafts, YOU approve. BFCM traffic is the most expensive traffic you'll buy all year

The brands that run this will spend Black Friday watching budgets scale.

The ones that don't will spend it rebuilding campaigns at midnight while Amazon eats their search terms.

ICYMI O/N - November 12th, 2026

NVIDIA -6%:

US futures fell as Nvidia’s leadership crisis hit the AI trade: Nasdaq 100 contracts lost 1% and S&P 500 futures fell 0.5%. MSCI Asia Pacific down 0.8%, the Hang Seng down 1.3% and Shanghai down 0.8%, while Euro Stoxx 50 futures rose 0.2%. (BBG)

Alibaba fell as much as 7.1% in Hong Kong as the Nvidia scandal renewed concerns about Chinese firms’ access to advanced chips. https://t.co/giNUCibwEV and MiniMax each fell at least 7%. (BBG)

Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom each gained more than 3% after hours on expectations they could win business from Nvidia’s turmoil. Alphabet rose 0.3% as investors considered alternatives to Nvidia’s AI accelerators. (BBG)

Nvidia directors were preparing to remove Jensen Huang, WSJ reported, following reports of affairs with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset and healthcare VP Kimberly Powell. No completed removal decision has yet been confirmed. (WSJ, FT)

Nvidia engaged an outside firm to find successors, Bloomberg reported. Some directors favour CFO Colette Kress as interim CEO and have discussed adding a COO, while Apple hardware chief Johny Srouji is being considered for the permanent role, Semafor reported. (BBG, Semafor)

US Commerce department is finalising Chinese remote-access curbs for Blackwell and newer chips, possibly this month, The Information reported. Proposed licensing would extend to Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, Norway and South Africa. (The Information)

US-operated data centres in those markets would avoid chip-import licensing if they bar access by arms-embargoed countries and report customers and capacity. Commerce also plans formal repeal of the AI Diffusion Rule. (The Information)

Chinese AI companies are approaching overseas data-centre operators to reserve Nvidia computing capacity, fearing tighter US remote-access controls, Reuters reports. Grey-market buyers inside China are also stockpiling restricted processors amid concerns about tougher enforcement. (RTRS)

The suspected Chinese spy at the center of the scandal (Alice Huang) has returned to Beijing, according to Bloomberg sources. It wasn’t immediately clear when or why she traveled to the capital, nor what she may be engaged in.  (BBG)

Elon Musk said it would be an “honor” to hire Jensen Huang if he is removed from Nvidia. (Musk)

'Nvidia’s Disappearing Singapore Sales Deepen Mystery Around Megaspeed' WSJ article notes Nvidia switched its geographic revenue reporting from billing addresses to customer headquarters after blocking Megaspeed in June 2025. Singapore, previously 22% of sales, disappeared as a separate category. (WSJ)

Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons asked Lutnick, Rubio and White House chief of staff Stephen Miller to preserve records covering Nvidia’s China exports and Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese intelligence asset. They requested confirmation by Tuesday that staff had been instructed to retain the material. (WSJ)

Some Trump administration officials had privately warned that Huang’s lobbying for China chip sales undermined national security, WSJ reported. Officials opposing his approach were sidelined or left, while David Sacks and Howard Lutnick helped sustain Huang’s influence with Trump, people familiar said. (WSJ)

Alibaba was an anchor customer behind Megaspeed’s successful push for priority access as an Nvidia cloud partner in November 2023, people familiar told WSJ. Megaspeed supplied Alibaba with computing power from Nvidia servers housed in Malaysia. (WSJ)

Nvidia customer Megaspeed shipped some restricted chips into China, including to Shanghai cloud provider Century Litong, WSJ reported, citing people familiar with the matter. Megaspeed says it complies with applicable export controls. (WSJ)

'Megaspeed's links to rural Australian store raise fresh questions in Nvidia scandal' Reuters article notes Megaspeed registered overseas affiliates using a director whose listed address is a rural Victorian newsagency. Australian and Delaware filings identify Kai Kang as the sole officer; Reuters could not establish whether Australian authorities are investigating the company. (RTRS)

Beijing said Washington should stop using the Huang allegations as a pretext for technology restrictions. Foreign Ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said China remains in contact with US counterparts ahead of next week’s leaders’ meeting. (BBG)

MACRO:

Bloomberg reports OpenAI’s downsized fundraising deal, combined with rival Anthropic PBC’s decision to pursue an IPO at a lower-than-expected valuation, has sent shockwaves throughout the venture landscape. Suddenly, an industry already rattled by a weeks-long public market AI selloff is worrying more about whether private companies are on the cusp of a correction. (BBG)

Following the election results, both Meta and OpenAI executives said that they believe it will be more difficult to build data centers in the future, according to public comments and remarks OpenAI CEO Sam Altman made at a company Q&A. (WSJ)

Congressional Democrats are planning an initial push for bipartisan healthcare, tariff and Iran-war legislation next year, with reconciliation expected to move up the agenda if Republicans block their bills. (Burgess Everett, Laura Weiss)

Sovereign wealth fund assets are set to surge nearly 50% to $22.4 trillion by 2030 as state-backed investors deepen their involvement in artificial intelligence and infrastructure, according to a PwC report released on Thursday. (RTRS)

Japan’s producer inflation accelerated to 7.1% y/y in October from 6.8%, defying expectations for a slowdown. Prices rose 0.7% m/m, the fastest increase since May, reinforcing the case for another BOJ hike. (BBG)

BOJ’s Toichiro Asada urged caution on further tightening, seeking evidence that higher wages are generating demand-driven inflation. He said he was neither advocating a cut nor categorically opposed to hikes. (WSJ, BBG)

Japan’s FX chief Atsushi Mimura warned recent currency moves were “too fast” and said it was too early to forget this summer’s intervention. Government spokesperson Minoru Kihara later called yen undervaluation a problem and pledged continued coordination with the US Treasury. (BBG)

State Street’s Masahiko Loo warned that a yen move into the mid-160s per dollar could trigger a stronger policy response than investors anticipate. (WSJ)

New Zealand’s April 2037 bond auction drew bids for 7.46 times the amount offered, the strongest demand for any tenor since February 2013. The benchmark 10-year yield extended its decline, falling 4bp to 4.64%. (BBG)

UK GDP grew 0.7% q/q and 1.9% y/y in Q3, with quarterly growth matching forecasts and accelerating from 0.5% in Q2. Services and manufacturing each grew 0.9%, while construction fell 0.7%; September output rose 0.2% m/m versus flat expected, and August was revised to flat from 0.1%. (ONS, BBG)

Britain's economy grew at the fastest rate in two-and-a-half years in the third quarter of 2026, helped by investment in artificial intelligence, extending a strong first half and defying predictions of a slowdown made after the Iran war began. (RTRS)

UK estate agents’ expectations for sales and house prices fell to three-year lows in October. Rics’ year-ahead sales balance dropped to -17 from +1, while price expectations fell to -17 from zero. (FT)

France has signaled it may support Spain's nominee Pablo Hernandez de Cos to succeed Christine Lagarde as European Central Bank president next year, the Financial Times reported on Thursday, citing sources. (FT)

Sentiment among European companies has picked up across industry and services since June, but there are growing concerns about rising inflation and sovereign debt, according to a survey published by BusinessEurope on Thursday. (RTRS)

The EU and UK are set to postpone the 10% tariff due to hit most electric vehicles traded between them from January. Brussels is consulting on a one-year delay or a two-year arrangement allowing manufacturers to offset non-compliant exports against compliant domestic sales, people familiar said. (FT)

Jefferies’ Mohit Kumar said the bank would be inclined to short French debt against Germany if the ten-year spread fell below 140bp. The spread was 147bp in early European trading. (WSJ)

Chatter on the online discussion site Reddit can tell policymakers how retail investors are feeling sooner than traditional surveys, particularly when markets are under stress, two European Central Bank economists concluded. (RTRS)

Norwegian oil and gas companies have cut their projected investments for 2026 while raising the outlook for 2027 compared with estimates made three months ago, an industry survey by the statistics office (SSB) showed on Thursday. (RTRS)

Bank Indonesia confirmed intervention in spot, offshore and domestic forwards, alongside secondary-market government-bond purchases, after the rupiah hit a record low. The currency weakened as much as 0.5% to 18,241/$, while the 10-year yield rose 4bp to 7.66%. (BBG)

Vietnam put its planned international bond sale on hold because borrowing costs were too high, Finance Minister Ngo Van Tuan told parliament. Mexico wants to buy more US steel as it seeks better tariff treatment from Washington, Deputy Economy Minister Luis Rosendo Gutiérrez told Bloomberg. China and Turkey have signed a preliminary agreement for China to invest some $15 billion to build solar and wind power plants with a total capacity of 7,000 MW in Turkey, the Turkish energy minister said on Thursday. (RTRS)

Turkey's central bank raised its end-2027 inflation forecast to 21% and its end-2028 forecast to 13.5% on Thursday, with Governor Fatih Karahan saying the bank would maintain a tight policy stance until prices stabilise. (BBG)

US and allied military officials told WSJ that the ballistic-missile threat requires a rethink of America’s military posture as interceptor shortages persist. India’s crude imports through Hormuz rose to 2.1 million b/d so far in November, overtaking Russian supplies of 1.8 million b/d for the first time since the Iran war began, according to Kpler. Shuttle tankers and ship-to-ship transfers are helping restore Gulf flows. (BBG)

Strategy will leave MSCI’s global benchmarks at the November 30 close under its non-operating-company rules. The confirmed deletion could prompt selling by index-tracking funds. (WSJ)

Rolls-Royce announced a £1.5bn interim buyback running to February, within its existing programme of up to £9bn through 2028. Power-systems orders rose 62% in the first nine months, taking the backlog to £8.6bn, with defence and civil-aerospace demand remaining strong. (WSJ)

BAE Systems raised its 2026 free-cash-flow forecast to about £3bn from more than £2bn, partly reflecting customer advances. Orders reached £33bn year to date, versus more than £27bn a year earlier; sales and earnings growth guidance was maintained. (WSJ)

Wizz Air’s first-half net income fell 67% to €108.1 million from €323.5 million as higher jet-fuel costs hit earnings. Fuel remains a major headwind heading into winter. (BBG)

HSBC has discussed giving its Singapore business greater independence to diversify its reliance on Greater China, according to people familiar with “Project Sirena.” HSBC confirmed plans to combine its Singapore units but said it had no plans to change the ownership or management of its Asia-Pacific banking entities. (BBG)

Siemens’ Q4 orders jumped 58% to a record €34.77bn and net profit rose to €2.16bn from €1.62bn. It raised its medium-term growth ceiling to 11% from 9%; FY2027 targets are 9–11% comparable growth and €10.20–10.80 EPS, with a proposed €5.50 dividend versus €5.35. (WSJ, BBG)

Merck KGaA raised annual sales guidance to €21.5–21.9bn from €21.0–21.8bn and adjusted EBITDA to €6.2–6.4bn from €5.9–6.3bn, its third upgrade this year. Q3 sales of €5.63bn beat €5.46bn expected; adjusted EBITDA of €1.68bn exceeded €1.61bn. (WSJ)

Hapag-Lloyd reported Q3 revenue of €5.97bn versus €6.13bn expected and EBITDA of €1.49bn versus €1.63bn expected. CEO Rolf Habben Jansen said unit costs remained under pressure from geopolitical tensions and operational disruption. (WSJ)

Munich Re’s Q3 major reinsurance losses were €646mn, or 14.9% of net reinsurance revenue versus 18% anticipated. Insurance revenue rose 14% to €16.63bn; its profit-guidance increase was announced last month. (WSJ)

Telefonica cut its revenue-growth forecast to 1%–1.5% from 1.5%–2.5%, citing weaker handset sales. It nevertheless raised its adjusted EBITDA-growth outlook to slightly above 2.5%, after Q3 adjusted EBITDA increased 6.2% to €3.08 billion. (BBG)

bitcoin-cash:native. $4.6B market cap. ~96% of supply already mined.

NO.1 WHAT IS

Bitcoin Cash is a proof-of-work network that split from Bitcoin in 2017. It prioritizes low-cost onchain payments through larger blocks. BCH is the asset users send and the currency they use to pay transaction fees.

NO.2 WHY PEOPLE CARE

The May 2026 network upgrade added Pay to Script, bounded loops, and reusable functions. Those changes give developers more flexibility to build payment and escrow applications. The next test is whether people use those applications regularly.

NO.3 NARRATIVE

The thesis is peer-to-peer cash with a fixed supply. BCH aims to make direct onchain payments practical. Its adoption case depends on people choosing to hold and spend it when stablecoins offer a dollar-denominated alternative.

NO.4 EDGE

BCH combines a familiar Bitcoin-style transaction model with more room for transactions in each block. That helps keep fees low when demand fits available capacity. For a payments network, merchant acceptance and repeat usage matter more than unused capacity.

Reported 24h trading volume — ~$98.3M
Block subsidy — 3.125 BCH

Exchange trading volume measures turnover in BCH. It gives limited visibility into merchant payments.
NO.6 TOKENOMICS
Users pay network fees in BCH, and miners receive those fees plus newly issued BCH. At the 10-minute block target, the current subsidy implies about 164K BCH in annual issuance, or roughly 0.8% of circulating supply. That’s a predictable supply schedule. Demand still depends on people choosing to hold or spend BCH.
NO.7 UNLOCKS & RISKS
New supply comes from mining. The next halving is expected in 2028 and will cut the subsidy to 1.5625 BCH per block. As subsidies decline, fees matter more to miner economics. BCH shares its mining algorithm with Bitcoin, so miners can shift hash power as relative profitability changes.

NO.8 BULL vs BEAR

BULL — Merchant integrations lead to repeat payments, apps make practical use of the upgraded scripting features, and demand grows as issuance falls.

BEAR — Users choose stablecoins for everyday payments, BCH usage stays modest, and miner economics remain sensitive to the block subsidy.

NO.9 VERDICT

Project Design — B+
Adoption & Ecosystem — C+
Narrative — B
Competitive Edge — B−
Market & Onchain Metrics — B−
Tokenomics & Value Capture — B−
Issuance & Supply Risk — B+
Bull vs Bear Setup — C+

Overall Grade — B−

BCH’s strongest point is its predictable supply. The weaker part is evidence of repeat payment demand at a ~$4.6B valuation. I’d give more weight to sustained merchant usage than to another spike in exchange volume.

What would move your bitcoin-cash:native grade higher, more merchants accepting it or proof customers are using it every week?

In our #WMGVenueGuide series, we showcase competition venues alongside nearby tourist attractions!

For vol. 12, we would like to introduce Shiga Prefecture, where the rowing competition is going to be held. 🚣

The competition venue is in the city of Otsu in Shiga Prefecture at Kansai Mirai Rowing Centre (Shiga Prefectural Biwako Rowing Centre).

The Centre, which was renovated in April 2021, is located on the edge of Lake Biwa and Seta River and is one of the premier courses dedicated to rowing and canoeing in the Kansai region.

And there are tons of sightseeing destinations nearby.
If you head north from the venue, you’ll find the Lake Biwa Museum.
This museum offers an enjoyable and educational look at the origins of Lake Biwa, its surrounding natural environment, and the relationship between people and wildlife. Its freshwater aquarium exhibits are among the largest of their kind in Japan.
Visitors of all ages, from children to adults, can enjoy fascinating discoveries and inspiring experiences that spark their curiosity. 🐟

If you head south from the venue to Shigaraki, you’ll find Ogama, where you can experience the art of pottery-making.
Ogama is a shop directly operated by Meizangama, a Shigaraki pottery studio.
Exhibitions are held in the traditional climbing kiln and the main building at the back, while pottery-making classes are offered in the atelier (reservations required).
Take your time and enjoy the experience while admiring Shigaraki’s cultural heritage, which played an important role in supporting Japan’s modernization.

In addition to rowing, Shiga Prefecture will also host a wide variety of sporting events, including: Athletics (10 km Road Race), Baseball (Rubber Baseball), Canoe (Dragon Boat), Hockey, and Softball!

Plan a trip where you can enjoy both the sporting events and the local sightseeing attractions!
