MARKET UPDATE — THURSDAY, 12 NOVEMBER 2026

On Wednesday, Wall Street almost erased its post-election losses. The S&P 500 rose 1.3%, and Nvidia gained 2.9%.

Then, after the closing bell, the Wall Street Journal reported that Nvidia's board was preparing to remove Jensen Huang, the man who co-founded the company 33 years ago and steered it to the centre of the AI boom. The shares fell more than 8% within minutes.

The AI trade isn't collapsing. Money is shifting from Nvidia to its rivals and customers. Meanwhile, the price of money keeps climbing.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 NVIDIA: THE BOARDROOM THAT COULD MOVE THE MARKET

💠 Reuters, CNBC and CNN confirmed that Nvidia's directors met on Wednesday evening to decide Huang's future. As of this morning, no decision has been announced.

🔸 The trigger was a New York Times report that Huang had a relationship with an Nvidia executive who reports to him.

🔸 That is separate from the affair Huang admitted on Sunday, with Alice Huang (no relation). She is a former executive at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based Nvidia customer, and US officials suspect her of passing information to China's government.

🔸 The Irish Times reports that Nvidia is working with an outside firm to find possible replacements. According to CNN, Huang has no clear No. 2. He has said in the past that he doesn't believe in succession planning.

💠 The shares closed Wednesday up 2.87% at $173.73, then fell as much as 8.6% to $158.76 in after-hours trading.

🔸 Pre-market, they are down 6.60% at $162.27 (4:25 am ET), so some of the overnight losses have been recovered.

🔸 Wednesday's volume was 339m shares, more than double the 30-day average of 144m. That shows how heavily the stock is being traded.

💡 Pre-market trading is thin, with few buyers and sellers, so prices can swing sharply once the full market opens at 9:30 am ET.

🔸 Nvidia had already fallen 9.5% across Monday and Tuesday. If the after-hours losses hold, reports estimate that about $600bn of market value has gone since the board opened its investigation on Sunday.

💠 Wall Street analysts are backing away:

🔸 Baird: downgraded to Neutral, with its price target cut to $200 from $500

🔸 Bernstein: downgraded to Market Perform, with its target cut to $200 from $400

🔸 Morgan Stanley: removed Nvidia from its Top Pick list but still rates it Overweight

Baird's Tristan Gerra:

"We contend a new CEO is needed to establish internal safeguards to align with existing and upcoming U.S. policies enforcing restrictions to China's access to U.S.-made AI technologies, and to re-establish trust both externally and internally."

💠 Washington is turning up the heat. 

Republican Senator Kevin Cramer has said Huang should step down. House China Committee chair John Moolenaar warned that Huang could face subpoenas if he didn't respond to a request to appear before three House committees. Democratic Senators Elizabeth Warren and Chris Coons have asked the administration to preserve its records on chip exports to China.

💡 Why one CEO matters this much: 
Nvidia makes the chips behind most of the AI boom, and it also helps fund that boom by investing in AI companies. MarketWatch notes it has been called the "central bank of artificial intelligence". Huang is also a leading AI adviser to President Trump. Investors fear losing the pilot and his influence in Washington at the same time.

💠 The case for buying: Barron's calculates that Nvidia now trades at less than 11 times expected earnings, compared with a five-year average of 33.7 times.

💡 A price-to-earnings (P/E) ratio is what you pay for each $1 of a company's yearly profit. At 11 times, buyers are paying about a third of what they typically paid over the past five years.

The counterargument: a low multiple only helps if the profits actually arrive. Democrats swept last week's midterms partly on promises of data-centre moratoriums, and turmoil at the top could slow big deals. If profit forecasts fall, today's "cheap" price may not be cheap at all.

Jake Dollarhide of Longbow Asset Management thinks the board won't rush:

"I believe the board won't oust him until they have an all-star, a known entity in the tech sector, to replace him."

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 MARKETS: THE RALLY HITS A WALL

💠 Wednesday's close:

🔸 Dow: +254.60 (+0.49%) to 52,486.49

🔸 S&P 500: +98.45 (+1.31%) to 7,619.38

🔸 Nasdaq: +400.31 (+1.60%) to 25,466.19

🔸 The S&P 500 tech sector rose 2.7%, and CoreWeave jumped 24.7%.

🔸 Europe's STOXX 600 rose 0.7%, and MSCI's world index rose 1.1%.

💠 Futures this morning (around 4:15 am ET):

🔸 Nasdaq 100: −0.82% to 28,241

🔸 S&P 500: −0.38% to 7,611.50

🔸 Dow: +0.04% to 52,601

🔸 Euro Stoxx 50: +0.18% to 6,416.30

🔸 VIX: +5% to 18.36

Nasdaq futures were down about 1% earlier, so the selling has eased.

💡 Futures are bets on where an index will open. The VIX is Wall Street's "fear gauge": when it rises, investors are paying more to protect themselves against a fall.

💡 Nvidia makes up about 7% of the Nasdaq 100. According to Swissquote, a 10% fall in Nvidia alone takes roughly 0.7 percentage points off the index. The Dow is weighted by share price rather than company size, so Nvidia counts for far less there. That explains why the Dow is flat.

Ipek Ozkardeskaya of Swissquote:

"Nvidia's troubles are reinforcing the rotation towards non-tech stocks this morning."

💠 Asia shrugged it off. 
Japan's Nikkei and Taiwan both rose 0.5%, and South Korea's Kospi rose 0.2%. Losses in Hong Kong left the wider Asia-Pacific index down 0.1%. Asian chipmakers held firm.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 AI: ROTATION, NOT RETREAT

💠 Nvidia's rivals are rising before the US open. 
AMD, its closest competitor in data-centre chips, is up about 3.5%. Broadcom, which designs custom AI chips, is up more than 2%, on top of an 18% gain over the past three days.

💡 When customers worry about the stability of their main supplier, they spread their orders around. AMD's chips and Broadcom's custom designs are the obvious alternatives.

💠 Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon are flat to slightly higher. Some investors think a slower AI build-out would let these giants spend less and charge more, and all three design their own chips.

💠 Westpac said Wednesday's rally was driven by positive news around CoreWeave and Anthropic. CoreWeave expects to turn profitable in 2028 and is lining up cheaper funding, which eased fears about debt-fuelled AI growth.

The connecting thread: investors aren't pulling money out of AI. They are moving it away from a single dominant supplier and towards its rivals and customers.

💠 Tesla: Elon Musk said Cybertruck production will continue until the end of summer 2027 to work through its order backlog. Tesla had planned to stop making it to free up capacity for its Cybercab robotaxi.

"This is not the smartest move from a profit-maximizing standpoint. But there must be some room in this world for sentimentality, or what's the point?"

🔸 The bigger news for investors: Finland has approved Tesla's supervised self-driving software, marketed there as "Tesla Assisted Driving". Tesla is aiming for EU-wide approval by 2027. Its shares were up 3.6% at midday on Wednesday.

💡 This software is the foundation of Tesla's robotaxi plans. More than a million drivers have already paid for it, so each new approval opens a new market for it.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 BONDS, THE FED & THE DOLLAR: THE PRICE OF MONEY

💠 The US government bond market reopens today after the Veterans Day holiday:

🔸 2-year yield: 4.763% (+1.7 basis points)

🔸 10-year yield: 4.992% (−0.8 basis points)

🔸 30-year yield: 5.335% (−2.3 basis points)

💡 A basis point is one-hundredth of a percentage point. The 2-year yield tracks what investors expect the Fed to do. The 10-year helps set mortgage rates and is the yardstick for valuing shares.

🔸 The gap between the 2-year and 10-year yields has narrowed to about 23 basis points, from about 32 before Tuesday's inflation report.

💡 When short-term yields rise faster than long-term ones, markets are expecting tighter policy now and slower growth later.

💠 As MarketWatch puts it, falling oil prices are no longer enough to pull down borrowing costs. The Fed's worry has moved on from fuel to stubborn prices for services and labour.

💠 The Fed decides on 8–9 December. 
According to CME FedWatch, markets see an 87.3% chance of a quarter-point rise and a 12.7% chance of a half-point rise. Reuters reports that another rise by March is also fully priced in.

🔸 Four Fed officials speak today: 
Cleveland's Beth Hammack, Governor Michael Barr, San Francisco's Mary Daly and New York's John Williams. Williams is vice-chair of the committee that sets rates, so any hint from him in favour of a half-point move would carry the most weight.

🔸 At 1:00 pm ET, the government sells new 30-year bonds. This week's 10-year sale drew softer demand. Another weak sale would tell you buyers want even higher yields to lend to Washington for 30 years.

💡 In an auction, the government borrows by selling new bonds. When demand is weak, it has to offer higher interest, and that pushes up borrowing costs across the economy.

💠 The dollar index is at 102.87, its highest since 9 April 2025, just after the "Liberation Day" tariffs. It rose about 0.7% on Wednesday as traders priced in Fed rate rises.

🔸 The euro is at $1.1087, and the dollar buys ¥159.83.

💡 Higher US interest rates draw money from around the world into dollars. ¥160 is close to the level where Japan stepped in to support its currency in 2024, so watch for warnings from Tokyo.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 GLOBAL: INFLATION ISN'T ONLY AMERICAN

💠 Japan's wholesale prices rose 7.1% in the year to October, faster than the 6.5% expected and up from 6.8% in September.

🔸 Petroleum and coal products rose 15.9%, and chemicals 15.5%. Strong AI demand pushed up chip prices.

🔸 A weak yen pushed import prices, measured in yen, up 24.8%.

💡 Wholesale prices are what companies charge each other. Those costs usually reach shoppers later.

🔸 Many analysts expect the Bank of Japan to raise rates to 1.5% from 1.25% at its 17–18 December meeting. That would be its third rise this year, after June and September.

💡 This matters beyond Japan. Japanese investors are among the world's biggest buyers of foreign bonds, and higher rates at home can pull some of that money back.

💠 The UK economy grew 0.7% in the third quarter, as forecast and its strongest pace in well over a year. Growth over the past year accelerated to 1.9% from 1.4%.

🔸 Services led the way with growth of 0.9%. Information and communication rose 2.1%, and businesses invested in IT, data centres and defence.

🔸 Construction fell 0.7%, dragged down by a 4.7% drop in private house-building.

🔸 September grew 0.2%, against expectations of no growth. August was revised down to flat.

🔸 The Bank of England expects 1.6% growth this year, more optimistic than the Office for Budget Responsibility's 1.2%.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 GOLD: THE SHINE FADES

💠 Gold futures are down 1.3% at $3,947.30 an ounce, back below $4,000. The spot price touched its lowest since 4 November.

💡 Gold pays no interest. When the dollar strengthens and bonds pay more, holding gold costs you more in lost income.

🔸 OCBC says the backdrop has become less favourable for gold, but it is not turning bearish on the medium-term outlook.

🔸 Friday's producer-price figures are the next test.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 OIL & ENERGY: PAIN AT THE PUMP, AND SOON IN THE BOILER

💠 On Wednesday, Brent crude rose 1.4% to $92.76 a barrel and US crude (WTI) rose 0.6% to $86.53. The trigger was Iran's top security official saying that not a single particle of enriched nuclear material would leave the country. Washington says nuclear issues must be part of any initial talks.

🔸 WTI is up another 0.5% this morning, at $86.94.

💠 US diesel costs $6.13 a gallon, according to AAA. That is down from $6.33 when Trump waived some sanctions on Russian fuel in October, but still up 63% from $3.76 before the Iran war began in late February.

🔸 The first tanker carrying Russian diesel to the US is idling off the East Coast with no confirmed destination. Banks, ports and importers are wary of legal risk and of congressional investigations.

🔸 Dozens of senators, six of them Republicans, have urged Trump to scrap the plan.

💡 Importing sanctioned Russian fuel was meant to bring diesel prices down. If no US company will touch it, that relief may never reach American drivers and truckers.

💠 Home heating: the National Energy Assistance Directors Association expects the average US household to spend $1,002 heating its home this winter, up 7.1%. Homes that rely on heating oil, common in the Northeast, face $2,977, up 70.2%.

💡 Higher heating bills hit family budgets and feed into inflation over the winter. That is one more reason the Fed can't relax.

💠 Watch at 12:00 pm ET: the government's weekly oil inventory figures, delayed by the holiday. Forecasters expect crude stocks to fall by 1.48m barrels. The industry group API estimated a rise of almost 9m barrels. A big build would weigh on prices.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 GEOPOLITICS: TALKS ABOUT TALKS, WHILE THE MISSILES FLY

💠 The WSJ reports that Vice President JD Vance is considering face-to-face talks with Mohsen Rezaei, the hard-line secretary of Iran's top security body. Trump has authorised Vance to negotiate, though officials stress that the discussions remain preliminary. Doha is a possible venue.

🔸 Iran wants the US to lift its naval blockade, release frozen assets and ease oil sanctions before any talks.

🔸 Mediators have proposed a trade: the US pulls its aircraft carriers back and eases the blockade, and in return Iran lets 25 tankers through the Strait of Hormuz.

🔸 Secretary of State Marco Rubio:

"The Iranian demands are totally unrealistic. We expect that could change, and if it does, we'll be prepared for diplomacy."

🔸 Trump said the US is moving another aircraft carrier into the region and is "loaded up to the gills".

🔸 According to Al Jazeera English, Israel has ordered its military to step up preparations for a possible attack on Iran. Tehran has rejected a US proposal to move its stockpile of highly enriched uranium to a third country.

💠 In the Strait of Hormuz, Iran attacked ship-navigation systems on Oman's Didamar island, Reuters reports, citing three sources. Shipping sources expect limited impact because backup systems exist.

🔸 Gulf oil exports had recovered to over 80% of pre-war levels in September and October. US military escorts helped, as did Saudi exports through Yanbu, its Red Sea port.

💠 In the Red Sea, the Houthis claimed attacks on Riyadh's main airport, an oil pumping station in Yanbu and a Saudi military command centre in Aden. These claims are unverified. Saudi Arabia said debris from intercepted missiles fell in the Mecca region.

💡 This is the connection that matters: Yanbu is Saudi Arabia's escape route around Hormuz. When both routes are under threat at once, oil prices find a floor, even on days when diplomacy makes headlines.

🔸 The UN Security Council meets today to discuss the Middle East.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CRYPTO: STRATEGY SHOWN THE INDEX DOOR

💠 Bitcoin is down 0.75% at $73,358, and Ether is down 0.61% at $2,041.

💠 MSCI will remove Strategy, the largest corporate holder of bitcoin, from its main global indexes at the close on 30 November. That includes the MSCI USA index, which means Strategy also drops out of the MSCI World and ACWI indexes. The move comes under MSCI's new rule excluding "non-operating" companies.

💡 Index funds must hold exactly what is in the index. When a stock is removed, they are forced to sell it. This is not a delisting, and Strategy does not have to sell any bitcoin.

🔸 Strategy held 850,364 bitcoin as of 8 November, after buying 1,036 last week.

🔸 Strategy says index-tracking funds hold about 13m of its shares. That is 3.1% of its shares outstanding and less than a day's normal trading.

🔸 Last year, JPMorgan estimated forced selling of about $2.8bn, with up to $8.8bn more if other index providers follow MSCI. At today's lower share price, one estimate puts the value of the MSCI-held shares nearer $1.6bn.

🔸 Japan's Metaplanet and uranium holder Yellow Cake were also removed from MSCI indexes, so the rule isn't aimed only at crypto.

🔸 Strategy slipped just 0.85% after hours, as the move was widely expected. By this morning, though, it is down 4.6% pre-market.

💡 Traders rarely wait for the deadline. Hedge funds often sell, or bet against, a stock before index funds are forced to sell it, and then buy it back from those funds on the day. That means the pressure can arrive well before 30 November.

The counterargument: part of today's fall reflects bitcoin's dip and a weaker Nasdaq, both of which Strategy tends to amplify. History also shows that stocks removed from indexes often fall when the news is announced and then partly recover once the forced selling is over.

💡 Why it matters: Strategy pays for its bitcoin purchases largely by selling new shares. Losing a reliable group of buyers could make that harder over time. Strategy disagrees and says the move won't meaningfully affect its business.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 CALENDAR

Today (ET):

🔸 8:30 am: weekly jobless claims (forecast 195,000, previous 189,000), and continuing claims (forecast 1.71m, previous 1.718m)

🔸 10:00 am: existing home sales (forecast 3.85m, previous 3.99m)

🔸 12:00 pm: 30-year mortgage rate (previous 7.18%) and government oil inventories

🔸 1:00 pm: 30-year Treasury bond auction

🔸 2:00 pm: monthly federal budget statement (previous: deficit of $27bn)

🔸 Fed speakers: Hammack, Barr, Daly and Williams

🔸 Any time: a decision from Nvidia's board

Coming up:

🔸 Fri 13 Nov, 8:30 am: producer prices, which measure inflation at the factory gate. 
Headline forecast: +0.4% for the month (previous +1.3%) and 6.6% for the year (previous 6.3%). 
Core forecast: +0.3% for the month (previous +0.7%) and 5% for the year.

💡 Even if monthly price rises cool, the annual rate is expected to climb to 6.6%. That is still a lot of cost pressure in the pipeline heading to shoppers.

🔸 30 Nov: Strategy leaves MSCI's indexes

🔸 8–9 Dec: Fed decision

🔸 17–18 Dec: Bank of Japan decision

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

🟢 WHAT IT MEANS

🔸 Nvidia's problem is about leadership and governance, not demand, at least so far. The rally in AMD and Broadcom shows money is moving within AI, not leaving it. But a low P/E only matters if earnings hold, and the board needs a credible succession plan quickly.

🔸 Interest rates are still the biggest driver of markets. The 10-year yield is near 5%, the 30-year is at 5.3%, and a December Fed rise is close to certain. Japan's 7.1% wholesale inflation shows the pressure is global, not only American.

🔸 Energy keeps inflation sticky into winter. Diesel is up 63% since February, heating-oil bills are up 70%, and the Russian diesel plan is stalling.

🔸 With both Hormuz and the Red Sea route under threat, oil has a floor even when peace headlines appear.

🔸 For crypto, Strategy's removal from MSCI's indexes was expected, but its 4.6% pre-market fall shows traders are already getting ahead of the forced selling. Expect more pressure between now and the 30 November close, when index funds must finish selling. After that, the pressure from forced sellers falls away.

Bull case: Nvidia quickly names a credible successor, producer prices cool, the Fed sticks to quarter-point steps, and Vance's diplomacy reopens oil flows through Hormuz.

Bear case: a messy leadership gap stalls Nvidia's deals, producer prices run hot, the Fed moves by half a point, a weak 30-year auction pushes yields higher, and talks collapse while Hormuz and Yanbu come under attack.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

💭 THOUGHT FOR THE DAY

"If I have seen further, it is by standing on the shoulders of giants."

— Isaac Newton

No great enterprise rests on one person alone. Thousands of engineers, ideas and years of work stand behind every breakthrough. The same is true of a portfolio: one setback rarely defines it. Keep building on solid foundations, and you'll see further too.

━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━

It will be the first full recovery of an orbital rocket in history. And if you want to watch it live, you'll need to know what time and where to tune in.

It is the 15th test flight of the giant stainless-steel reusable rocket, which SpaceX wants to use for everything from Starlink internet satellite launches to landing NASA Artemis astronauts on the moon in 2028, and even for a crewed flight to Mars. But first, SpaceX has to successfully recover and refly both stages, something it's never done before — and that's where Flight 15 comes in. It's the first time the company will try to land an entire Starship rocket. Here's when to tune in.
     What time is SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch (and landing)?
    The Starship Flight 15 test mission is currently scheduled to launch no earlier than Friday, Nov. 13, at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas. But there is a chance of a later liftoff time.
     SpaceX has said it has a 75-minute window in which to launch Starship Flight 15 to add some flexibility into its preflight countdown. That means the launch could take place anytime between 5:45 p.m. and 7 p.m. EST (2245-0000 Nov. 14). The local time for the launch window will be 4:45 p.m. to 6 p.m. CST.
     What time will SpaceX launch its 1st orbital Starship test on Flight 14 today? (Full mission timeline)
     SpaceX has not formally announced if it has backup days for the launch, but if the company does have those options, liftoff would likely occur at the same time, based on past Starship missions that saw delays.
     One thing that separates Starship Flight 15 from past Starship test flights is its length. The mission, if it runs its full duration, will last just over 22.5 hours until Ship lands back at Starbase. That landing would occur on Saturday, Nov. 14, at 4:17 p.m. EST (2117 GMT). If SpaceX launches at the end of its window on Friday, at 7 p.m. EST, the Ship landing would occur on Saturday at 5:32 p.m. EST (2232 GMT).
     Meanwhile, the Super Heavy, known as Booster 22, will land about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.
     Can I watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch?
Watch OnWatch live! SpaceX launches Starship Flight 15 with potential double catch attempts - YouTube.
     Yes, you'll be able to watch SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 launch online, and you have many ways to do so.
     https://t.co/iODbrq8Yli will host a livestream simulcast of Starship Flight 15 on this page, as well as on our homepage and our YouTube channel VideoFromSpace. That webcast will begin about 30 minutes before liftoff, at 5:15 p.m. EST (2215 GMT).
     SpaceX, of course, will offer its own Starship Flight 15 livestream on its Flight 15 mission page, as well as on its X account. That livestream will also begin 30 minutes before launch, at 5:15 p.m. EST (it's the same one as on https://t.co/iODbrq8Yli).
     A prelaunch show Watch OnWaiting for Flight 15 Full Stack | Countdown To Launch - YouTube.
     If you need your Starship launch preparations fix before the Nov. 13 launch, good news: You can see SpaceX's prep work live online.
     NASASpaceflight's YouTube channel offers live views of SpaceX's Starship pads at Starbase 24 hours a day, seven days a week.
     On Wednesday (Nov. 11), the channel will stream live views of the Starship Flight 15 rocket stacking, starting at 3 p.m. EDT (1900 GMT).
     The NASASpaceflight Flight 15 launch webcast will begin on Nov. 13 at 11:45 a.m. EDT (1645 GMT), about six hours before launch. NASASpaceflight typically offers live commentary and constantly changing views of the Starship launch pad via remote cameras positioned around Starbase.  Watch OnSPACEX LAUNCHES STARSHIP FLIGHT 15 - Launch & Booster Catch - YouTube.
     In-person launch options
     If there was ever a SpaceX Starship test flight to see in person, this just might be it.
     In addition to watching the world's largest rocket launch into space, Starship Flight 15 offers the chance to see both parts of that megarocket return to Earth and be caught in mid-air, 22 hours apart.
     If you've read our past Starship launch viewing guides, you'll know that SpaceX doesn't have an official viewing site for Starship launches. But you can see the spectacle from several public beaches (as well as private campgrounds).
     Cameron County Amphitheater at Isla Blanca Park on South Padre Island is always my first recommendation (I watched the first Starship launch from there in April 2023). The park offers a clear view of the Starship launch site across the bay and includes views of boats on the water. There are also bathrooms close by for your convenience. It's 5 miles (8 kilometers) from the launch site as the crow flies. But plan to head out early as traffic can be heavy, especially if you have to cross the bridge from Port Isabel.
     Speaking of Port Isabel, there are stretches along Highway 48 between Port Isabel and Brownsville, Texas where you can pull over to the shoulder to watch the launch from 6 to 8 miles (10 to 13 km) away. But it's just the side of a highway, so don't expect bathrooms there. 
     The website https://t.co/NPgvinQKQ3 does report that there are "open pull-offs" to park, from which you can get "wide wetland views." And, of course, it's free. 
     I've driven along Highway 48 during two Starbase visits but have not pulled over to the shoulder to test this site.
     If you're on the Mexico side of the border, you may be able to watch Starship Flight 15 from Playa Bagdad, a public beach with a "head-on view of the launch tower and a festive vibe," according to https://t.co/NPgvinQKQ3.
     Finally, there is the Rocket Ranch campground, where you can get a closer view of Starship launches — but you have to pay $200 a ticket (kids under age 17 are $40). The ranch is 3.8 miles (6.1 km) from the Starbase launch site, and your ticket allows you to camp there for one day and one night. Longer four-day stay packages are available.
     The Rocket Ranch has two primary viewing locations: The "Outpost" offers the closest view and "unmatched media service," so you can stay connected. The second location is a bit farther away on the campground itself. 
     Please note: Tickets include bus transportation from the ranch campground to a viewing site and back, but it is for one launch attempt only. Be sure to read the full Rocket Ranch FAQ for details on the site.
     How long is SpaceX's Starship Flight 15?
     If everything goes to plan, SpaceX's Starship Flight 15 orbital launch and landing test could last up to 22.5 hours and orbit the Earth 14 times.
     "If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in a mission overview.
     But the test flight could end early. That's what happened on SpaceX's first orbital Starship test mission, Flight 14 on Sept. 28, which was expected to last nearly 10 hours and orbit Earth six times. Instead, SpaceX ended the mission after three hours and two orbits of Earth as a safety precaution.
     "Starship’s initial return to launch site mission is expected to orbit the Earth at an altitude of ~275 km and complete approximately 14 orbits around the planet over the course of a more than 22-hour flight," SpaceX wrote in the mission description. "Similar to Starship’s first orbital mission, the flight profile has been designed with the opportunity to insert into a passively safe suborbital trajectory or safely deorbit at multiple pre-determined areas over the ocean after raising to an orbital altitude."
     SpaceX Starship Flight 15 Launch Timeline

     T+22:32:34 "An exciting landing!" SpaceX says.
     If SpaceX has to end the Starship Flight 15 test flight early, it has three primary splashdown zones to land the Ship upper stage in the ocean.
     The company could drop the Ship vehicle in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of Hawaii in early and late stages of the mission, according to a reentry overview. A mid-mission splashdown window off the coast of Chile is available if needed at that time. A late-mission splashdown zone in the Gulf of Mexico is also available.
     The Gulf is also a wave-off splashdown zone for SpaceX's Starship Super Heavy Booster 22 in case it is unable to land shortly after liftoff.
     As with Starship Flight 14, SpaceX is loading Flight 15 with 26 operational Starlink V3 internet satellites. They will be deployed in orbit within the first 90 minutes of the flight.
     "The Starship upper stage’s primary objectives include the deployment of 26 Starlink V3 satellites and the first return to launch site and catch at Starbase," SpaceX wrote in its overview. "Starship will only execute a return to launch site if the flight control team has ensured that the vehicle systems critical for reentry maneuvers and final landing burn and tower approach are healthy."
     What if Starship Flight 15 can't launch on Nov. 13?
     While SpaceX is hoping to launch Starship Flight 15 on time, there is a chance that a technical issue or bad weather could prevent liftoff on Nov. 13.
     SpaceX has not announced any official backup days for the Starship Flight 15 launch, but it is likely that the company has at least one if not two additional opportunities to try again, based on past Starship launches. Any backup launch attempts will depend greatly on the nature of a launch delay.
     A good website to watch is the official Starbase page for Boca Chica Beach and Highway 4 closure alerts here. Those beach closures can be a good indicator of SpaceX's available flight windows.

text:
I HAD AN AFFAIR WITH MY NEIGHBOR, AND HIS WIFE WAS THE BEST FRIEND I EVER HAD

My name is Colleen Frasier. I'm 37 and I live in Omaha, Nebraska. I've been trying to figure out how to tell this for a long time, and there's no version where I come out looking good, so I'll just say it plainly. I slept with my neighbor, Paul, for almost five months. His wife, Joanna, was my closest friend.

Joanna and I met the week I moved in, seven years ago. She showed up on my porch with a plate of lemon bars and a hand-drawn map of which local contractors to avoid. We were friends from that day on. Our kids grew up together, and our husbands tolerated each other. Joanna and I had a standing Thursday wine night for six years. She was at my bedside when I had my second baby. I was the first person she called when her father died.

My husband, Russell, and I were fine. Not great, not terrible. He'd taken a job that kept him on the road three weeks out of every month, and when he was home, he was tired. I'd stopped expecting anything else. I wasn't unhappy enough to leave, but I was lonely in a way I couldn't explain to anyone, least of all him.

Paul was easy to talk to. He worked from home, so he was around when nobody else was. He'd wave from his driveway, ask how Russell's trip was going, and offer to take my trash cans out. Small things. But after weeks of nobody asking how I was, even small things felt like warmth.

It started in February, during a snowstorm. Russell was in Denver, the power was out, and Paul came over to check on me and the kids. We ended up sitting in my kitchen by candlelight after the kids fell asleep, talking about nothing and everything. At some point I realized I didn't want him to leave. I knew exactly what that meant, and I let it happen anyway.
Afterward I sat on my kitchen floor and told myself it was a mistake that would never be repeated. I told myself that again the following week, and the week after that.

For the next five months, I became a person I didn't recognize. I'd wave to Joanna across the yard with Paul's scent still on my clothes. I'd sit across from her on Thursday nights and let her tell me about how distant Paul had been lately, and I'd nod and offer advice. Advice! I told my best friend to be patient with her husband, while I was the reason he was distant.
The guilt came in waves. Some days I'd decide to end it, and I'd tell Paul so, and he'd agree, and then within a week we'd be back. We weren't in love. I think that's the part that still haunts me. We were just two people who'd found a place to hide from our own lives, and we were willing to hurt the people closest to us to keep it.
It ended in July, at a barbecue in Joanna's backyard. Our families were all there. Russell had come home for the weekend. The kids were running through the sprinkler. I was holding a plate of potato salad when Joanna's seven-year-old daughter, Ellie, walked up to me and said, loud enough for half the yard to hear, "Colleen, why were you in our garage with my dad on Tuesday?"
The garage. I'd been in the garage with Paul on Tuesday. I hadn't known anyone was home.

Everything stopped. I watched Joanna's face move from confusion to understanding in about two seconds. She set down her drink very carefully and asked Ellie to go inside. Then she looked at Paul. Then she looked at me.
She didn't scream. She said, "Is it true?" and neither of us answered fast enough.
Russell was standing right there. He'd heard all of it. He looked at me for a long moment, put his plate down, and walked to the car. I followed him. He didn't say a word the whole drive home, and when we got there, he packed a bag and went to a hotel.
Joanna filed for divorce within the month. She told me once, through a closed door, that the affair was awful, but what she couldn't forgive was the Thursdays. "You sat there and listened to me cry about him," she said. "You held my hand."
I had.

text:
A Father in Gaza. A Genocide Inquiry. NVIDIA’s AI Chips. Who Answers?

A chief executive admits infidelity, and his private life becomes a public reckoning. His company’s processors appear in military systems, including a munition designed to kill, and the reckoning becomes harder to find. What an absurd moral arrangement: we can organize an inquiry into whom a man slept with while struggling to establish who profits from the machinery of mass killing. A UN commission has found genocide in Gaza. What did Jensen Huang know about the military uses of NVIDIA’s chips, what did his company earn, and what did he do when evidence of abuse became public? Those questions deserve an investigation at least as persistent as the scrutiny of his sex life.

By Alan Clements · November 12, 2026

Muhib was nineteen. His brother Elyas was seventeen. On February 12, 2024, in the Al-Shaboura refugee camp in Rafah, their father, Osama Abu Jama, heard gunfire outside the family tent. He stepped out to see what was happening. People were running. The sound woke his sons. Within a minute, he told the Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor, a quadcopter overhead opened fire on the tent. Osama was wounded. Both boys were killed. His testimony preserves a detail I have been unable to get past. Among the last things he could tell us about his sons was something a parent sees a thousand times and scarcely thinks to remember. They woke up.

Half a world away, five people who worked at NVIDIA helped The New York Times report on an alleged affair between Jensen Huang, the company’s chief executive, and an executive who reported to him. Five sources for one relationship. Think of the calls that went unanswered before someone agreed to speak. Think of the patience it takes to earn the confidence of a person whose livelihood may depend upon your discretion. That is a capacity I want the American press to keep—and bring, with equal appetite, to the business of killing. A newspaper can reconstruct the intimacies of a billionaire. What could that persistence discover about the machinery above a family’s tent?

I have no evidence that the aircraft over his tent contained an NVIDIA chip. An Israeli arms manufacturer does, however, identify an NVIDIA processor in a drone it designed to kill. The distance between those two sentences is where a reporter’s work begins. It is also where a great deal of public interest seems to end.

Huang acknowledged to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. He did not name his partner in that admission. The New York Times reported that American intelligence had identified a Chinese businesswoman with whom he had a close relationship as an intelligence asset. Beijing dismissed the allegation. NVIDIA’s board opened an investigation. In a separate story, the Times reported an affair with an NVIDIA executive who reported to him. Those are distinct accounts involving different women. The public knows less about the private circumstances of either relationship than a week of headlines might lead one to believe.

As for the bare fact that a married man had sex outside his marriage, my response as a citizen is simple. So, fucking what? His wife has standing to answer that question very differently. An employee whose career depends upon the judgment of the man she reports to has interests a board must take seriously. A foreign intelligence service obtaining privileged access to a chief executive would be a substantial public matter. Journalism earns its keep by making these distinctions. The sheer fact of intercourse, however, confers no public entitlement to the sheets.

Yet the sheets offer something the contracts do not: immediate moral fluency. Everybody knows how to have an opinion about adultery. Put a processor inside a weapon, move it through a reseller and a defense contractor, and suddenly the same public must acquire a graduate education in procurement before it is allowed to be appalled. Sex gives us a scandal we can understand over coffee. Mass killing comes with an explanation of why responsibility is complicated.

The absurdity lies in what happens next. A sexual relationship becomes a question of judgment, access, power and accountability. The sale of technology used by military institutions becomes a question of distribution channels. We recognize the obligations of a man who has power over someone across a desk. Put a purchasing ministry and six thousand miles between his company and a person exposed to its products, and we begin to lose our vocabulary. At what point along that route does the obligation expire? And who had the authority to decide?

The relationship disclosed in the accounts

In its fiscal year ending in January 2026, NVIDIA recorded $19.677 billion in sales to direct customers headquartered in China and Hong Kong. In the following six months it recorded another $12.430 billion. More than $32 billion across those eighteen months. You can find the numbers in the company’s financial filings. They tell you where the customer was headquartered. They do not tell you where every processor went, which government could ultimately draw upon its computing power, or what proportion served the People’s Liberation Army.

Here is the peculiarity of Washington’s alarm. A woman may have obtained access to a man whose company openly does tens of billions of dollars of business with customers headquartered in her country. Espionage is a serious allegation. Ordinary commerce offers no defense to it. Yet ordinary commerce presents questions of its own, and the Times turned up a remarkable one. Megaspeed, the Singapore-based company associated with the businesswoman, reportedly bought more than $4.8 billion in NVIDIA chips over two years. Who took delivery? Which customers bought access to the machines? One can ask both questions without learning another thing about anybody’s marriage.

On November 11, Reuters supplied an example of what that journalism looks like. A Chinese university with deep military ties bought two NVIDIA H200 chips for 874,700 yuan through a domestic supplier. The purchasing department was the management school. Its cybersecurity school rented computing capacity under separate agreements. Good reporting leaves the management school in the sentence. It resists promoting a university purchase to a missile program for the sake of a better headline. It also makes it considerably harder for the company to say the destination of its products is beyond the reach of human curiosity. Reporters found the paperwork.

Apply that curiosity at home. On May 1, the Pentagon publicly named NVIDIA among the companies with which it had reached agreements to deploy artificial intelligence on its classified networks. The public announcement gave no dollar figure for NVIDIA. At Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory, a single American supercomputer called Sierra contained more than 17,000 NVIDIA processors. Its work included assessing the nuclear weapons stockpile. Seventeen thousand in one machine. You need no speculative theory of Silicon Valley’s proximity to military power. You can count the processors.

Can I tell you the Pentagon puts billions of dollars a year into NVIDIA’s pocket? I cannot. Consider a modest purchase that illustrates why. The Air Force Research Laboratory bought two NVIDIA computing systems for $485,455. Look up the award by recipient and you will find Sterling Computers. A search for NVIDIA alone can miss it. Assign the entire sum to NVIDIA and you have made a different mistake. Multiply that problem across contractors, foreign resellers and computing time bought by the hour. A citizen can be taxed to pay for the machine and still be unable to discover how much the company whose name it bears earned from the sale.

Here, apparently, is where our appetite for disclosure becomes exhausted. We can pursue the identity of a sexual partner through frightened sources and private denials. Following public money into military computing is harder, so the unanswered questions remain unanswered. Difficulty is a reason to fund the reporting. It is a grotesque reason to accept the silence.

What a father can know

Elbit Systems, an Israeli arms manufacturer, identifies the onboard computer in its LANIUS loitering munition as the NVIDIA Jetson TX2. Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor reported the use of small drones in Gaza, including aircraft it classified as LANIUS, in the same investigation that recorded Osama Abu Jama’s testimony. His account identifies a quadcopter. There is no serial number in that testimony, no recovered processor identifying the aircraft that killed his sons. I return to that missing piece because it is precisely where an honest indictment of our priorities begins. Why should a wounded father carry the burden of tracing an international supply chain before anyone asks its beneficiaries to account for it?

In September 2025, the United Nations Independent International Commission of Inquiry concluded that Israel had committed genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. Israel rejects that finding. South Africa’s case against Israel remains before the International Court of Justice. I use the word genocide here deliberately, and I name the body that made the finding. The word war alone leaves too much unsaid about what that commission examined and concluded.

Read those matters beside each other. A chief executive has acknowledged infidelity. A UN commission has found genocide. An arms manufacturer names his company’s processor inside a killing machine. These facts do not establish his responsibility for that genocide. They establish the urgency of finding out what his company supplied, what it knew and what it could have done. The evidentiary gap calls for investigation. It does not make the bedroom the more consequential place to look.

But put the letters AI in front of genocide and something curious happens to the grammar. The machine seems to acquire a will. The human being who authorized its use can slip out of the sentence altogether. Investigators have documented Israel’s use of intelligence systems called Lavender and The Gospel. The Israeli military says analysts independently assess intelligence before designating a military objective. I have found no public record identifying the processors on which those systems ran. What I want to know is who decided their output was reliable enough to act on, who could call a halt, and what happened when a family said the machine, or the people relying on it, had got it wrong.

Journalism has already shown what such questions can accomplish. The Associated Press documented a three-year, $133 million Microsoft contract with Israel’s defense ministry. In September 2025, after reporting on the surveillance of Palestinians, Microsoft disabled specified cloud storage and AI services to one ministry unit. Its review found evidence supporting elements of the reporting. The company could examine its business records. It could identify subscriptions. It could withdraw a service. These are useful verbs for the next annual meeting of any technology company whose directors profess uncertainty about what, in practice, they can do.

A chip possesses no special faculty for concealing its use. People make choices about what to record, what to disclose, whom to supply and what to do when credible evidence of abuse arrives. Hardware sold years ago can change hands beyond the maker’s knowledge. A current contract with a named customer presents a different degree of visibility and a different opportunity to act. A company can reasonably be asked to account for the information it had at the moment it still had a choice.

That is a recognizable inquiry into human conduct. What did you know? Whom did you expose to harm? When could you have stopped? We ask versions of those questions about sexual betrayal without finding them impossibly abstract. A company’s commercial relationships deserve the same insistence, especially when the potential harm is measured in human lives.

The countries inside the question

Russia offers two pieces of evidence that belong beside each other. Bloomberg traced $300 million in Dell servers imported by two Russian trading companies in five months of 2024. Specifications identified NVIDIA H100 chips in 998 of the 1,111 servers. Separately, Ukrainian investigators identified NVIDIA hardware in a Russian Lancet loitering munition and reported finding it in an S-71 cruise missile. NVIDIA says it stopped direct sales to Russia in March 2022. Nothing in the server investigation establishes that those shipments supplied those weapons. Together the accounts establish an uncomfortable fact about the reach of an American commercial decision. Direct sales can end on a certain date. The life of the product continues on somebody else’s calendar.

Iran comes into view through an Iranian-manufactured Shahed recovered in Ukraine, in which Ukrainian investigators identified an NVIDIA module. In France, reporting describes a classified defense supercomputer with more than a thousand GPUs, most of them NVIDIA’s. In Spain, an €18 million initial drone tender selected Skydio aircraft that carry NVIDIA hardware. Different countries, different purposes, different degrees of responsibility. The question travels because the technology does. Its answer has to be earned in each place.

Burma is where that discipline costs me something personally. I have known people there for whom the sound of an aircraft overhead carries the whole history of what the state is capable of doing to a village. Mizzima reported a delivery of fifteen drones to Min Aung Hlaing’s military in April 2024. I have found no evidence identifying an NVIDIA processor in that delivery. I will leave the sentence there. After years of asking the world to believe Burmese witnesses, the last thing I would do is spend their credibility on a detail I cannot establish. What they deserve is somebody willing to go looking.

An inquiry into mass killing must be exact because the accusation is grave. It must distinguish a manufacturer from a reseller, knowledge from ignorance, a preventable sale from hardware already beyond a company’s control. Such distinctions make an investigation credible. They should never become the paperwork behind which everyone disappears.

I could call Huang the butcher of Silicon Valley. How convenient that would be for the official who authorized procurement, the minister who could release the records, the commander who selected the target, the director who approved the terms. All of them could read to the end of the piece secure in the knowledge that the butcher was somebody else. I would prefer to see Huang at a hearing with the contracts in front of him. Which military customers have you investigated? What did you learn? Has your company ever walked away from a sale it could legally have made because of what the evidence told you would happen to other human beings?

And I would like the people asking those questions to arrive as thoroughly prepared as the reporters investigating his affairs. Bring the correspondence. Establish the dates. Identify who knew. Examine the power relationship. Follow the money. The skills already exist. What remains in question is the scale of suffering required to command their sustained attention.

I have spent enough of my life in the company of Buddhist teachings to distrust the pleasure of catching another human being in disgrace. There is a small relief in discovering that a billionaire has made an ordinary mess of his life. For a moment we understand the whole story. We know whom to judge. We can even enjoy our own good judgment on the way to breakfast.

There is something almost unbearable about that breakfast. We sit with a device in our hands, reading about a man’s sexual conduct, while elsewhere a father is trying to explain how his children died. The affair supplies the recognizable drama: desire, secrecy, betrayal. The father supplies names, ages and a tent. Somehow, it is the father whose story requires the more elaborate justification for our attention.

Sex can wound. Coercion, exploitation and betrayal deserve serious scrutiny. But what a civilization reveals about itself when the possibility of mass murder has to compete with the revelation that a powerful man has been having sex. What an obscene disproportion between the intimacy we demand from his private life and the opacity we tolerate in the commercial arrangements that may expose strangers to death.

Osama Abu Jama offers us no such satisfaction. He could give investigators the place, the gunfire, the order in which things happened. He could give them his sons’ names. Imagine asking him for more. Imagine explaining that before a board of directors can reasonably be troubled, he must identify the aircraft, establish who supplied its electronics and produce a chain of invoices reaching back from Rafah to the country of manufacture. Then imagine turning to the people who keep those invoices and asking, with the same persistence we bring to the private life of one married man, to see them.

A married man’s admission of infidelity tells us nothing about his responsibility for a military supply chain. The records might. Open them. Establish what was sold, who received it, what warnings arrived and who decided to continue. If there is evidence of knowing assistance in unlawful killing, pursue it to the people responsible, however wealthy, celebrated or far from the bodies they may be.

Muhib was nineteen. Elyas was seventeen. They woke up. Their father has given his account. We have heard the admission about sex. Now let us hear from the people with the records about the business of death.

About the Author

Alan Clements is an American author, human rights journalist, spoken-word artist, and former Buddhist monk. Ordained in Rangoon in 1979, he studied with Mahāsi Sayadaw and Sayadaw U Pandita. He later returned to Burma as a writer. In 1995, soon after Aung San Suu Kyi’s release from house arrest, he began the conversations that became The Voice of Hope. His reporting on Burma and its borderlands has followed the lives of people who have risked imprisonment, exile and death to bear witness to military rule.

Clements founded World Dharma Publications and is the author of Politics of the Heart: Nonviolence in an Age of Atrocity — Psychedelic Activism to End War, a work of spoken-word theatre that brings his experience as a meditator and war correspondent onto the same stage. His forthcoming three-volume collection, Patriarchy, Authoritarianism and the Role of the Divine Feminine in Contemporary Society: Conversations with Visionary Women, grew out of three years of conversations with fifty-five women. Readers can find his books, essays, and performances at https://t.co/SE9uLs89dH.

text:
Good morning from Virginia. 🇺🇸

On November 12, 1775, Abigail Adams sat in the farmhouse at Braintree and wrote the words that marked the end of any remaining illusion about Britain. The Olive Branch Petition had gone out from Philadelphia that summer—Congress’s last formal plea for peace, drafted by men still hoping a loyal petition might reach the ear of King George III and restore the old relationship. The king never read it. He answered with a proclamation declaring the American colonies in open rebellion. When that news reached Massachusetts, Abigail refused to join the prayers for reconciliation that her minister still offered. She wrote John that she could no longer pray for what she now called a tyrant state.

Her letter was blunt. “Let us separate, they are unworthy to be our Brethren. Let us renounce them.” Instead of the old appeals for British prosperity, she called on Americans to ask Providence to frustrate their councils and bring their designs to nothing. This was no abstract theory. It came from a woman running a farm, raising children, and holding a household together while her husband sat in Congress. The regulars were still in Boston. Small skirmishes continued in the countryside. Winter was closing in. Yet she saw clearly what many still hesitated to say: the bond had already been broken by the other side. Continued loyalty would mean continued subjection.

That decision—to renounce rather than submit—was the core of the American founding. It was not a demand for better terms inside an empire. It was a refusal to remain subjects of a distant crown that had rejected every petition and answered with force. From the Virginia soil that produced Washington and the men who would later stand at Yorktown, the same spirit took root. Abigail’s private letter captured the public turning point: when a people decide that a foreign power is no longer worthy to rule them, separation becomes the only honorable course.

Two hundred and fifty years later the lesson remains. Nations that forget how they won their independence risk losing the will to keep it.

text:
SoftBank Group recorded a net loss of approximately $7 billion for the second quarter of its 2026 fiscal year (July to September), a sharp reversal from the profit of roughly $16 billion seen in the previous fiscal year. Of this loss, $3.7 billion stemmed from changes to a procurement plan for power generation equipment intended for AI data centers in the United States. SoftBank had made $9.5 billion in advance payments to secure this equipment, but subsequently abandoned $2.9 billion worth of it following a strategic adjustment—resulting in a non-refundable loss. The notion that "Big Tech" is shifting its focus toward Latin America—partly due to fatigue over the data center boom elsewhere—finds some support in SoftBank’s regional strategy; the company completed its acquisition of DigitalBridge in September 2026, which includes assets such as Scala Data Centers in Latin America. However, the CEO of SoftBank’s Latin American operations has publicly noted that the region faces structural hurdles, specifically a "lack of capital and energy capacity" for AI infrastructure.

SoftBank’s Quarterly Loss: Figures and Origins

Reports from CNBC and *Business Standard* confirm that SoftBank posted a net loss of 1.12 trillion yen (approximately $7 billion) for the second quarter of its 2026 fiscal year, falling well short of the 129 billion yen profit analysts had anticipated. This marks SoftBank’s first quarterly net loss in nearly two years. For the preceding fiscal year (FY2025), the company reported a full-year net profit of approximately 1.15 trillion yen (about $16 billion), consistent with the aforementioned $16 billion profit figure.

Within this loss, 597.2 billion yen (approximately $3.7 billion) is attributed to changes in the procurement plan for AI data center power equipment in the U.S. During the earnings call, SoftBank CFO Yoshimitsu Goto explained that the company had made advance payments—totaling $9.48 billion by the end of September—to secure equipment for projects such as "PORTS-Pike." Following a reassessment of its procurement strategy, SoftBank decided to cancel the purchase of $2.9 billion worth of this equipment. These advance payments were non-refundable, and the cancellation incurred additional costs related to contract modifications and settlement fees. A report by the Nikkei adds a crucial detail: on November 11, SoftBank revised its earnings presentation materials, explicitly stating that this loss is "unrelated to the Ports-Pike project in Ohio."

Drivers of the Loss: Beyond Equipment—A Shift in the AI ​​Narrative

Losses from equipment procurement represent only a portion of the quarterly deficit. According to a report by the *Business Standard*, SoftBank’s losses occurred against a backdrop of a "sharp downward revision in the global AI outlook," following the success of Democratic candidates in the U.S. midterm elections who campaigned against data center developments. Declines in the share prices of Arm, Intel, and Coupang—all held by SoftBank—further weighed on performance. Additionally, SoftBank’s financing costs more than doubled between July and September, and its credit default swap (CDS) spreads climbed to multi-year highs. Together, these factors point to a structural issue: SoftBank’s debt-fueled AI investment model faces a "double squeeze" during an AI valuation correction—shrinking asset values ​​coupled with rising liability costs.

Latin America: Opportunities and Structural Constraints

SoftBank’s interest in Latin America is genuine, though the narrative that "Big Tech is turning to Latin America due to a backlash in the U.S." requires nuance. On September 30, 2026, SoftBank completed its acquisition of DigitalBridge—a deal valued at approximately $3.1 billion—which includes assets in Latin America such as Scala (data centers), Highline do Brasil (wireless infrastructure), and Mundo (fiber optics). In Brazil, Scala is developing "Scala AI City" in Eldorado do Sul, with an initial investment of roughly $500 million and approval for up to 5GW of power access. The project’s positioning explicitly cites corporate reassessments of deployment strategies following "geopolitical tensions in the Middle East"—including drone attacks on data centers in Iran, the UAE, and Bahrain—with Brazil’s "relative distance from major conflict zones" serving as a key draw. However, in an April 2026 interview with CNN Brasil, Alex Szapiro, CEO of SoftBank Latin America, offered a more cautious assessment. He noted that Brazil and the broader Latin American region face a significant gap—requiring billions of dollars in investment and specialized human capital—when it comes to the "capital-intensive" aspects of AI, such as chip manufacturing and the development of foundational models. He argued that the region’s realistic opportunities lie at the "application layer," rather than in foundational models or supercomputing. Consequently, Latin America’s appeal as a destination for AI data centers hinges on factors like energy costs, geopolitical neutrality, and land availability, rather than the region’s own capacity to absorb the output of such AI infrastructure. Scala’s "AI City" project, for instance, requires "hyperscale tenants" to fill its capacity, as it is not driven by local demand.

Assessment

It is verifiable that SoftBank reported a quarterly loss of $7 billion—$3.7 billion of which stemmed from changes in the procurement of power-generation equipment for U.S. data centers—following a profit of approximately $16 billion in the previous fiscal year. SoftBank holds data center assets in Latin America through DigitalBridge, and the "AI City" project by Scala is currently underway. Yet, the narrative that "Big Tech companies are fleeing the U.S. for Latin America"—framing SoftBank’s regional strategy as a hedge against U.S. political risk—is contradicted by SoftBank’s own regional leadership. They position Latin America as an opportunity for the "application layer," not as an alternative hub for core AI infrastructure. Latin America offers land, energy, and a degree of geopolitical distance; it does not, however, provide the capital density, chip-manufacturing capabilities, or the R&D ecosystem required for foundational models. SoftBank’s bet on Latin America is less an escape from the U.S. and more a search for a physical location—within its global AI portfolio—that offers lower costs and fewer political hurdles. Ultimately, the success of this strategy depends on whether "hyperscale tenants" are willing to locate their computing operations thousands of kilometers away from their core markets and supply chains.

THE TORUS: THE POWER OF SACRED UNION 
AND THE CREATION OF NEW EARTH 

The torus, in its perfect balance of simplicity and complexity, remains one of the most compelling symbols in sacred geometry. 

From the human energy field to the cosmos, galaxies, and the Milky Way, it offers a model for understanding the interconnected nature of existence.

The toroid is a dynamic geometric figure that appears both in nature and in models of energy and consciousness. 

Your toroidal field is centered on your heart.
It produces your body’s strongest rhythmic magnetic field.

This continuous flow extends outward from the core,  loops above and below, and re-enters you at your base.

It represents a continuous flow that expands and contracts, symbolizing the balance between the internal and the external.

The outward, radiating expansion of the field reflects active, outward-moving masculine energy. 

The inward, drawing contraction back toward the center reflects receptive, inward-moving feminine energy. 

Together, they create a state of complete equilibrium.
Our own hearts operate like tiny toroidal fields. 

When we send out love, we don’t just give—it circles back through us. 
That’s the beauty of the torus: what you emit, you receive. 

This means love, healing, and even consciousness ripple outward and return, constantly shaping the world within and around us.

As humankind, we need our elimination system to purify our culture of all the toxic energy that builds up but which doesn’t belong here. 

We are responsible for repairing the flow of the human fountain in our own field, seeing where there is a resistance to unblock, a short circuit to fix, or a leak to patch.

It just needs to go so that the pure flow of the fountain can return, and we can know that together. 

Through the Spirit of Purification, we eliminate what does not belong so that we can enjoy the invigorating flow of our collective fountain.

We are the generating station for the flow of current through our human experience. 

We are the power source. 
But we are also the builders of the system. 

We grew our own human capacity, and together as humankind, we create the culture that holds the flow between us, for better or worse. 

An open heart reveals truth and allows true connection to the divine and the world.

It takes our conscious participation as human beings to allow that flow to move and let the circuitry between us be what it ought to be. 

So we become keepers of the fountain, spiritual pipefitters, plumbers, and electrical engineers.

Good to be fountaining together, allowing Creation to take its natural shape: the torus 💫

text: “Transparency” by Oliver R: an apparition at the threshold of the visibleWith Transparency, Oliver R extends and deepens one of his most fertile intuitions: the kaleidoscope as a mental space rather than a mere backdrop. After Doll K, in which a figure from the Dolls collection already conversed with a floral and chromatic explosion, the artist tightens the motif. The kaleidoscope is no longer a scattered field of colors; it contracts, deepens, and becomes a tunnel.The background is now bichrome: deep blue and burning orange. Perspective turns it into a hypnotic corridor, a succession of petals or scales receding toward a central point. We are no longer facing a decorative pattern, but inside an optical device. The gaze is drawn in. The kaleidoscope ceases to be an object one turns in one’s hands; it becomes a passage. At the center of this vortex appears a creature immediately recognizable as one of Oliver R’s Dolls — those hybrid beings, halfway between a luxury collectible doll, a Parisian department-store mannequin, and an animated character. Yet she is not sharp. She is an apparition. Her presence hovers at the edge of transparency, as if the tunnel both revealed and dissolved her. She does not fully occupy the space: she haunts it.Seated cross-legged, in a pose at once meditative and ceremonial, she wears a jumpsuit with dense blue and red patterns, almost like tapestry. On her head, a red headdress hesitates between turban and veil. Earrings, a necklace of red beads, red slippers: red returns as a connecting thread, both ornamental and ritual. On her right hand, a tattoo remains hard to decipher — a discreet, almost private sign that anchors the figure in a story the viewer will never be able to read completely.The eyes are closed. The nose and mouth are fine. The face does not express absence, but concentrated inwardness. Unlike many previous Dolls, often frozen in a wide, slightly uneasy gaze, this one has withdrawn. She does not look at us. She is elsewhere, or more deeply here.The title Transparency is not incidental. It resonates with the theme of a contemporary exhibition devoted to the interplay of light, layers, and perception. Oliver R does not treat transparency as a merely optical quality. He makes it an existential condition of his Dolls. These figures have always oscillated between object and living being, between artificial perfection and a nearly human emotion. Here, that oscillation becomes literal: the creature is both fully present and already fading into the pattern that surrounds her.The blue-and-orange kaleidoscope is no longer a background. It is the very medium in which the figure exists. Its repetitive, concentric forms evoke at once a mandala, an optical machine, and an organism. The tunnel-like perspective suggests an inner journey as much as a visual trap. One cannot tell whether the Doll appeared at the bottom of the kaleidoscope or whether the kaleidoscope was born from her. In Oliver R’s work, the Dolls are never mere mannequins. They carry a memory, a slight unease, an elegance a little too perfect to be reassuring. Transparency pushes this ambiguity further. By making the figure less sharp, more spectral, the artist does not weaken her presence: he makes it more insistent. What is not entirely visible demands more attention. Here one finds the artist’s signature: a cocktail of Pop Art, Surrealism, and digital Art Brut, obtained by assembling artificial intelligences and digital tools, then fixed in a unique work also intended for physical existence — fine-art paper, dibond, framing, anti-reflective plexiglass. But beyond technique, Transparency marks a shift. The kaleidoscope no longer illustrates a state of mind. It is the theater of that state.The creature with closed eyes, crowned in red, seated at the center of a tunnel of blue and orange, does not offer a single interpretation. She may be meditating, sleeping, absent, or simply dissolving into the pattern that brought her forth. Faithful to his method, Oliver R imposes nothing. He installs an atmosphere, a color, a tension between the sharp and the blurred, and leaves the gaze to do the rest.Transparency is not merely a new piece in the Dolls collection. It is the moment when the kaleidoscope stops surrounding the figure and begins to pass through her.

text:
Drive 100 kilometres in India and listen. The accent changes. The words change. You still manage to order lunch and argue about cricket.

So why does Modi want one of everything?

In Episode 555, I trace the RSS vision from Golwalkar’s call for a unitary India to today’s debates over Hindi, school funding, simultaneous elections and a common police uniform.

Tamil Nadu kept Tamil and English in its schools. The dispute over central funding shows how much leverage Delhi has even when a state can choose its own policy. Andhra Pradesh offers the reverse lesson. When the BJP fell short of a majority in 2024, the TDP’s 16 MPs gave a regional party real leverage in Delhi.

I ask the same question about each proposal. Once the slogan becomes policy, who gets to decide?

Which decision would you leave to your state, even if Delhi wanted a common rule?

text:
#Kyiv #Klitschko #MAFs #Kiosks #KyivKlitschko #MAFDismantling #Troieshchyna #SmallBusiness #Kyiv2026
Updated critical overview of the MAF/kiosk situation in Kyiv (November 2026), with the Troieshchyna example added.
The capital continues mass dismantling of small architectural forms (kiosks). Officially, only “illegal” ones that obstruct pedestrians or occupy green zones are removed. In practice, it often looks like the clearance of small businesses without a viable alternative — especially harsh during wartime.
Specific example from Troieshchyna (Desnianskyi district)
A shoemaker had worked in his kiosk for 25 years. The kiosk stood off to the side, bothered no one, and allowed him to earn a living. Municipal workers arrived and removed it. The man was left without work and without the spot that had been his livelihood.
Meanwhile, near the Silpo supermarket on Ronald Reagan Street 8, rental prices for spots have become astronomical. According to local accounts, the process is overseen by someone from the Desnianskyi district administration. The pattern is clear: an old small entrepreneur is removed “for beautification,” while prices at good nearby locations skyrocket and are controlled by “insiders.”
Overall picture
Similar stories are repeated across Kyiv (including other high-profile cases involving craftsmen and military personnel). People lose their only source of income while the city “cleans up” streets and sometimes transfers dismantled kiosks to the army. New locations are offered via auctions that are financially and connection-wise out of reach for many ordinary entrepreneurs.
Bottom line: beautification is happening at the expense of ordinary people. Instead of supporting small business during wartime, it is simply being destroyed, while control over land and trading spots tightens.
