text:
Nobody gave this sea creature a second look until someone decided to find out what it was hiding.

Studded with tiny dark-and-gold speckles, heavy as a stone, silent as one too. If you had seen it on a shoreline, you would have stepped over it. Most people would. That is exactly why this video exists.

Because the real question is not what it looks like on the outside. The real question is the one that has pulled humans toward closed shells, sealed boxes and locked doors for as long as we have been human: what is in there?

I am not going to tell you. I am going to tell you why you will not be able to look away once you start.

Here is a number that should bother you. By the estimates of ocean-mapping agencies, the majority of the seafloor has never been directly seen at high resolution by a human being. We have better maps of the surface of Mars than of the bottom of our own planet's oceans, and that sentence has been repeated so often that it stopped shocking people. It should still shock people.

Now zoom in from the whole ocean to a single animal. If we have not properly mapped the place, imagine how much we have not properly met the residents.

Marine biologists describe new species every single year. Not a handful. Thousands. The World Register of Marine Species, the database scientists use to keep the official count, adds roughly two thousand newly described marine species annually, and researchers who study the numbers generally agree that a large share of ocean life has never been formally named at all.

Read that again. Not a large share of the deep ocean is unexplored. A large share of the living things in it do not have a name yet.

Which means that when something spotted, round and strange shows up in a person's hands, the honest scientific answer to "what is it?" is sometimes a long, uncomfortable pause. And inside that pause is where the best stories live.

This is a story about that pause.

THE ANIMAL KINGDOM'S BEST DISGUISE

Evolution has a sense of humor, and it is mostly practical. For roughly half a billion years, soft-bodied sea animals have been solving one problem: how do you survive when you are slow, squishy and delicious?

Some answered with armor. Some answered with venom. Some answered by looking so boring, so plant-like, so rock-like, so completely uninteresting that predators lose interest before the thought of eating them forms.

The result is an ocean full of animals that fail the first test of being an animal. They do not run. They do not chase. They do not have a face you can read. A sponge, one of the oldest lineages of animal life on Earth, has no brain, no heart, no stomach and no muscles in the way we think of them, and yet it filters entire volumes of seawater and has been doing so since long before anything on land had a spine.

A sea squirt looks like a lumpy bag. A sea cucumber looks like something you might scrape off a boot. Some of them can expel parts of their own internal organs when threatened and then grow those organs back. That is not a myth and not an exaggeration. It is a documented defense, and biologists have studied it seriously, partly because of what it might teach us about regeneration.

So when we say an animal "looks like nothing," we should hear how that sentence sounds to biology. Looking like nothing is a strategy. Looking like nothing is often the whole point. And the animals that are best at it are frequently the ones with the strangest engineering tucked away out of sight.

The outside is a costume. The inside is the truth.

WHY A PATTERN MAKES YOU STOP

Look at how your own attention behaves around patterns. A smooth stone gets nothing. A stone covered in regular, tiny, glittering dots gets a second glance, then a third, then a quiet, involuntary thought: that is not random.

The human brain is a pattern engine. It treats regularity as a signal that someone or something made this on purpose, whether that someone is a god, an engineer or a few hundred million years of natural selection. Spots are not decoration in nature. Spots are information. They can be camouflage that breaks up an outline. They can be a warning that says do not eat me. They can be structures that sense light, release chemicals or house tiny symbiotic organisms that the animal depends on.

Every dot on a creature is a question the creature is asking you without a mouth.

And the more perfect the pattern, the louder the question. If the outside is this ordered, what kind of order is waiting on the other side of it? A body is not a rock. A body is an argument about survival, written in tissue, and the part you can see is only the first sentence.

THE OLDEST HABIT IN SCIENCE

There is a reason the most famous biology books in history are, at their core, books about opening things.

In 1543, a young anatomist named Andreas Vesalius published a massive work on the human body, built on the radical idea that you should look for yourself instead of repeating what ancient authorities said was inside. Doctors had trusted old texts for more than a thousand years. Vesalius said, in effect, let us check. The book changed medicine because it replaced assumption with observation.

Long before him, Aristotle spent time on the island of Lesbos studying the creatures of a coastal lagoon, and his notes on marine animals are still read today with a certain amazement at how much he got right using nothing but patience and his own eyes.

And then there is Charles Darwin, who, before he wrote the book that rearranged human thought, spent roughly eight years of his life on barnacles. Barnacles. Eight years. He dissected them, compared them, drew them, complained about them in letters and became one of the leading authorities on them. The man who eventually explained the diversity of life got his training by staring at some of the least glamorous animals in the sea and refusing to assume he already understood them.

That is the tradition this kind of curiosity belongs to. Not the loud kind. The quiet kind. The kind that says: I do not know what this is, and I am not comfortable leaving it that way.

Some of the biggest shifts in how people understand life started with a person, a strange specimen and a simple decision to look closer.

THE ITCH THAT HAS A NAME

Psychologists have a precise way of describing what happens in your head when you meet a mystery you cannot immediately solve. In the nineteen-nineties, the behavioral economist George Loewenstein proposed what became known as the information gap theory of curiosity. The idea is simple and slightly brutal: curiosity is not a love of knowledge. It is the discomfort of noticing a gap between what you know and what you want to know.

The gap hurts a little. That is why it works.

A child does not need to be taught to want to open a closed hand. An adult does not need a reason to pick up an unlabeled box. Put a covered object on a table and watch what happens to a room. Conversation slows. Eyes drift. Someone says, half joking, "what do you think is under there?" and every person nearby has already started guessing.

What matters here is how specific the pull is. Curiosity does not respond to vagueness. It responds to a shape. A closed door is a shape. A sealed shell is a shape. A strange, spotted sphere resting on rough stone, with no obvious head or limbs, is the most potent shape of all, because the mind keeps trying to assign it a category and keeps failing.

Is it plant, animal, mineral, egg, seed, shell, or something your brain has no folder for?

That failed categorization is the hook. And you are already inside it.

THE THING ABOUT "JUST A SEA ANIMAL"

We use that phrase as if it closes a case. Just a sea animal. Just an invertebrate. Just something from the shallows.

But consider what the word invertebrate actually covers. It covers every animal without a backbone, which is the overwhelming majority of animal species on the planet. The octopus is an invertebrate, and it has three hearts, blue copper-based blood and a nervous system so distributed that a large portion of its neurons sit in its arms rather than its head. The jellyfish is an invertebrate, and some species have been drifting through the oceans in essentially the same basic form for hundreds of millions of years. Corals are invertebrates, and together they build structures so large they can be seen from space.

The word "just" is doing a lot of lying in that sentence.

Every category we make for the sea is a convenience for us. The animals themselves have never heard of the categories. They have only ever had one job, which is to stay alive in water that is trying, constantly and without malice, to take them apart.

That is the context in which any single sea creature should be understood. Not as a curiosity. As a survivor. As a design that has passed a test lasting longer than mountains, whose full structure we only partly understand, and whose hidden architecture may be more sophisticated than anything we could draw on paper.

WHAT HIDDEN ARCHITECTURE LOOKS LIKE

Biologists who study soft-bodied marine animals often talk about a particular kind of astonishment. It is the moment when an animal that appears simple from the outside turns out to be intricately organized within.

A tunicate, for instance, can look like a shapeless lump on a dock piling, yet it carries a filtering basket, a heart that periodically reverses the direction in which it pumps blood, and a developmental history that places it, evolutionarily, surprisingly close to the lineage that eventually led to vertebrates. The lump is a cousin. A distant one, but a cousin.

Sea cucumbers move water through their bodies in ways that have attracted attention from researchers studying tissue that can shift between stiff and soft within moments. A starfish has no brain in the sense we mean it, yet coordinates the movement of hundreds of tiny tube feet with a precision that would be impressive in any machine.

None of this is visible from the outside. Every single one of these discoveries required someone to be curious enough to look past a boring surface.

Which brings us back to the strange, speckled, silent shape in this video, and the plainest of all questions.

What is the structure inside, and does it match what the outside promises?

THE PROMISE OF A SURFACE

Here is something almost nobody says out loud. We read surfaces like contracts.

A smooth surface says: nothing to see. A rough surface says: this has been through something. A glittering surface says: look closer. A hard surface says: protected. A pattern says: designed.

Then, occasionally, we are shown that the contract was a bluff, or that it understated what was inside, or that the exterior was a deliberate piece of misdirection from an organism that benefits from being underestimated.

This is why so many of the greatest moments in natural history are not about finding something new. They are about discovering that what we thought we understood was a mask.

A mimic octopus can imitate other animals so convincingly that predators misjudge it. Some deep-sea fish carry their own lanterns and use them as lures. Certain cephalopods change their skin texture and color in a fraction of a second, rewriting their surface faster than a person can blink. In the ocean, the outside of an animal is often the least reliable thing about it.

So the viewer who treats this creature's surface as the whole story is making the very error evolution has been betting on for hundreds of millions of years.

SOMEONE HAS TO BE THE FIRST TO LOOK

It is easy to imagine discovery as something grand. A research vessel, a submersible, a team in matching jackets, a press conference.

Much of it is not like that. Much of it is a single person on a shoreline or a boat deck or a reef flat, holding something unfamiliar and deciding whether to put it down or find out more.

The difference between those two decisions has shaped the history of human knowledge. People who put things down leave the world as they found it. People who look more closely, with respect and with attention, tend to leave the world slightly bigger.

There is a particular kind of person who does this. You have probably met one. They are the person who stops at a tide pool for twenty minutes while everyone else waits. They keep a small notebook. They know the names of animals nobody else around them has noticed. They are not performing curiosity. They simply cannot walk past an unanswered question.

This post is for them, and for everyone who secretly wishes they were one.

A QUESTION OF HOW WE LOOK

There is a second layer to all of this, and it is more uncomfortable.

When humans meet a living thing they do not understand, they choose, consciously or not, an attitude. Some choose awe. Some choose appetite. Some choose indifference. Some choose scientific hunger. Some choose all of these at once, in an order that depends on the day.

Different cultures along different coastlines have relationships with sea life that are generations deep. In many communities, knowing what is edible, what is useful, what is dangerous and what is simply not to be touched is a form of inherited intelligence, passed from parent to child along the waterline. That knowledge is not casual. It was earned over centuries of trial, observation and respect for the sea's moods.

At the same time, a viewer far away, sitting with a phone in a quiet room, meets the same creature with entirely different eyes and entirely different questions. Neither viewpoint is the whole truth. And the gap between them is part of what makes this kind of footage so compelling and so debated.

Who gets to be curious about a living thing? What does curiosity owe to the life it examines? Is there a line between studying and consuming, and if so, where is it, and who drew it?

Those questions do not have one neat answer, and anyone who offers you a neat answer is probably not looking at the full picture. But they are worth asking, and worth asking out loud, and the fact that a short video can raise them says something about how much weight can hide inside a small moment.

THE LONG MEMORY OF THE OCEAN

Consider the time scale involved.

The oceans have existed for billions of years. Complex animal life in them has existed for more than five hundred million years. Over that stretch, entire lineages have appeared, thrived, vanished and been replaced. Mass extinctions have erased the majority of marine species on several occasions, and each time life rebuilt itself from whatever was left.

Any creature you see today is the product of survivors descending from survivors descending from survivors. Every ancestor in an unbroken line made it long enough to reproduce. Not one failed. That is true of you as well, which is a strange thing to share with a spotted animal on a rock.

When you hold that thought, the spotted creature stops being an oddity and becomes a long answer to an ancient question. The answer is encoded in its shape, its texture, its internal organization, its chemistry. It is a living document, and the thing about living documents is that they can only be read by looking.

WHY THIS KIND OF CONTENT TRAVELS

You might wonder why a short clip about an unfamiliar sea animal travels the way it does.

Part of it is the information gap. Part of it is the pattern. Part of it is that it takes almost no explanation to feel the stakes. You do not need to speak a particular language. You do not need a biology degree. You do not need to know where it was filmed or what the animal is called. Anyone, anywhere, understands the shape of the question.

There is also something deeply calming about a single object and a single mystery. In a feed that usually throws fifty arguments at you per minute, a simple question that has nothing to do with politics, celebrities or outrage can feel like cold water on a hot day.

People send these clips to friends with captions like "what IS that" and "I have so many questions." That is the most honest form of sharing there is. Not "agree with me." Not "be angry with me." Just: be curious with me.

THE HUMILITY BUILT INTO GOOD SCIENCE

Ask a working marine biologist how much they are sure of, and the best ones will smile before answering.

The honest posture of serious science is not certainty. It is a disciplined willingness to say "I do not know yet." Entire careers are built on the edges of that sentence. A researcher who has spent thirty years on one group of animals will often tell you that the main thing those thirty years taught them is how much remains unanswered.

That humility is not weakness. It is the engine. The moment a person believes the book is finished, they stop reading the animal in front of them. The moment they admit the book is barely begun, every unfamiliar creature becomes a page.

There is an old and slightly funny truth in field biology: the specimen that does not fit the guidebook is usually the most interesting one in the bucket.

THREE QUESTIONS WORTH CARRYING INTO THE VIDEO

I will not describe what is in the clip. Describing it would spoil the only thing it has to offer, which is that you will see it for yourself without anyone narrating your reaction.

But I can give you three questions to hold while you watch. They are the same questions a naturalist would ask.

The first is about expectation. Before anything is revealed, what do you think is inside? Not what you hope. What you honestly predict. Be specific. Is it hollow or dense? Is it soft or structured? Is it one thing or many? Commit to your guess before you see anything. Predictions are the most underrated tool of curiosity, because they let you feel the exact moment reality corrects you.

The second is about proportion. Notice how your feelings change as the mystery shrinks. Most people expect the answer to feel like a relief. Often it feels more like a quiet second wave of wonder, because a good answer tends to raise more questions than it closes.

The third is about the animal itself. It is easy to treat a creature as an object in a story about us. Try the opposite for a moment. Ask what this body is for. What problem was it built to solve, and how well does the solution work?

If you carry those three questions, you will watch differently. You will not be a passive viewer. You will be doing what every naturalist in history has done: guessing, observing, adjusting.

THE GIFT OF NOT KNOWING

We live in a period of unusually fast answers. Almost any factual question can be settled in seconds. The side effect is that we have slowly lost practice at sitting with an open question.

A mystery used to last. A child who saw something strange on a beach might wonder about it for a week, a year, a lifetime, and the wondering itself became part of who they were. Many of the people who ended up studying the sea trace their entire path back to one unanswered moment like that, one animal they could not name, one afternoon of being genuinely stumped.

There is value in that state, and it is disappearing. Not knowing is not a defect to be eliminated as quickly as possible. It is a kind of attention. When you do not know what you are looking at, you look harder. You notice texture, spacing, symmetry, weight. You see more of the thing precisely because you cannot dismiss it with a label.

Experts sometimes envy beginners for exactly this reason. A beginner sees the animal. An expert, on a tired day, sees the category.

So consider this a small invitation to be a beginner for a few seconds. The category can wait.

WHAT THE SEA KEEPS

The ocean is generous with surprises and stingy with explanations.

It holds creatures that glow in total darkness. It holds animals that survive crushing pressure that would flatten a submarine built carelessly. It holds organisms that live off chemical energy near volcanic vents, a discovery that, when first made in the late nineteen-seventies, overturned a basic assumption in biology about what life needs in order to exist. Sunlight, it turned out, was not mandatory. Whole ecosystems were thriving in a place everyone had assumed was a desert.

That discovery came from people willing to look somewhere they had been told there was nothing to see.

It is a good reminder. Every time a field has declared a place or a kind of animal empty, boring or already solved, the ocean has eventually answered by producing something that made the textbook rewrite a chapter.

The sea keeps its secrets patiently. It does not hide them out of cruelty. It hides them because the cost of reaching them is high and the number of people willing to pay that cost has always been small.

Now and then, the secret ends up within arm's reach, on a quiet stretch of rock, in the hands of someone who decides to find out.

ON PAYING ATTENTION TO WHAT IS RIGHT THERE

There is a mistake we make when we think about wonder. We assume it lives far away. In deep trenches, distant planets, remote forests, places that require money, equipment and permission.

But the strangest thing about the living world is how often wonder sits at ordinary scale, in ordinary light, close enough to touch. A tide pool. A shoreline after a storm. A fishing boat deck at dawn. A piece of reef that looks like a stone until you give it a minute.

Every one of those places has a question hidden in it, waiting for anyone who slows down enough to ask.

What would change in your day if you assumed that the next unfamiliar thing you saw deserved a real look? Not a scroll-past. Not a verdict. A look. Thirty seconds of honest attention, with no goal except to see what is actually there.

Most of what we call boredom is just a habit of not looking.

WHY THE UNREMARKABLE ONES MATTER MOST

Natural history has a quiet bias. The animals that get attention are the ones with teeth, color, speed or size. Sharks, whales, big cats, eagles. They are easy to love because they behave in ways we recognize.

But the machinery of the living world is run largely by the animals nobody photographs. The filter feeders that clean the water. The grazers that keep reefs from being smothered. The burrowers that turn over sediment and move nutrients around the seafloor. The slow, round, unglamorous bodies that hold entire food webs together while the famous predators take the credit.

Remove the spectacular animals and an ecosystem is damaged. Remove the quiet ones and it can come apart in ways that take scientists years to understand.

There is a lesson in that about attention. We tend to assume importance announces itself. In nature, it often does the opposite. The most consequential creature in a patch of sea may be the one that looks least like a character in anyone's story.

So when a plain, speckled, unexplained animal appears on screen, it deserves the same seriousness we would give a whale. Perhaps more, because the whale already has a fan club.

A NOTE ON WHAT WE DO NOT CLAIM

Nothing here names the animal. That is deliberate. Putting a confident label on an unfamiliar creature is the easiest way to stop learning about it, and plenty of viral captions have been confidently wrong about what a sea animal is, where it lives or what it can do.

The honest position is simpler. Here is a living thing most viewers have never met, and here is a chance to meet it with open eyes. If you recognize it, say so, and say how you know. If you do not, enjoy the uncertainty. Both responses are a kind of respect.

One more thing worth keeping in mind: a short clip is a keyhole, not a window. It shows a moment, not a species, a habitat or a lifetime. Treat what you see as the start of a question rather than the end of one, and you will get far more out of it than a quick verdict ever gives.

WHO YOU SEND THIS TO

Think of the person in your life who always wants to know how things work. The one who took things apart as a kid. The one who reads the back of every label. The one who watches documentaries about animals nobody has heard of and then calls you at night to talk about them.

They are going to ask what it is the moment they see it. And you are going to have to say that you do not know, either, that the whole point is that nobody does until they look.

That is a good conversation to start. Better than most of what the internet offers on an average night.

THE LAST THING

Every living thing carries more inside it than its surface admits.

That is true of sea creatures. It is probably true of people. It is certainly true of the ocean, which has spent four billion years teaching one lesson over and over to anyone patient enough to listen: do not mistake what you can see for everything that is there.

Somewhere on a piece of coast, a closed, speckled, silent mystery is about to be answered.

You can read one more paragraph about it, or you can find out.

Press play, and decide for yourself what you think is inside. Then notice how close your guess landed.

text:
Rachel Reeves, "Andy Burnham deserves credit for facing reality head on"

"I firmly believe that Britain's future lies inside the European Union"

"Europe represents the single biggest opportunity to boost living standards and generate the revenue to invest in public service, while also deepening our security"

"The British government must prove to the public the benefits of a closer relationship"

"And it must prove to Europe that we are serious and open to compromise"

My view:

I agree with Rachel Reeves that Britain’s future belongs inside the European Union. Closer cooperation offers a route to greater prosperity, stronger public services and greater collective security. I welcome her support for making that argument.

But there is considerable irony in hearing her praise Andy Burnham for “facing reality head on” after spending six years helping Labour avoid that same reality. Her own record deserves a little attention:

• October 2020, at a LabourList event: “We won’t be back in the EU.” She also said: “I don’t think we have to rejoin the single market and customs union.”

• 12 October 2021, writing in the Guardian: “You need a plan to make Brexit work.”

• 11 January 2022, in the Commons: “We want to make Brexit work.”

• 20 January 2022, in her Bury economic speech: “The first step is to make Brexit work for the British people.”

• 20 January 2022, reporting her Financial Times interview: “I don’t want to go back to a system of free movement.”

• 18 May 2022, in the Commons: “We will make Brexit work.”

• 26 September 2022, at Labour conference: “If you are remotely serious about growth, then you have got to make Brexit work.”

• 24 May 2023, in her Washington speech: “While there’s no going back into the single market or the customs union”, Labour would improve trade with Europe.

• 22 September 2023, on Radio 4’s Today programme: “We don’t want to rejoin the EU in name or any other way; we accept the result of the referendum.”

• 9 December 2024, after meeting EU finance ministers, she reiterated Labour’s commitment to “not rejoining the European Union, the single market or the customs union”.

• 16 May 2025, in a Guardian interview, she again defended excluding single market membership, a customs union and free movement.

• 23 June 2026, in the Commons, she acknowledged that Britain was poorer outside the EU, yet reaffirmed the restrictions on rejoining: “Those red lines stand.”

That last example is particularly revealing. She recognised the economic damage while defending political commitments that limited how far Britain could go to repair it.

The economic warning signs were already there in 2022. The OBR was forecasting that Brexit would leave long-term productivity 4% below what it would otherwise have been. This was evidence available while Reeves was insisting that anyone serious about growth had to make Brexit work.

I’m glad she has changed her position. But welcoming that change does not mean overlooking her responsibility. Reeves and Starmer helped entrench a policy that accepted avoidable economic damage, spending years promising to make Brexit work while ruling out the relationships that could help repair it.

If we already knew in 2022 that Brexit was making us poorer, and global insecurity was already plain to see, why did she and Starmer waste years trying to make it work?

LVMH Moet Hennessy Louis Vuitton (LVMUY) at $89.40, -$0.92 / -1.02% on Wednesday.

LVMH is still on none of the Momentum, Quality-Value, Deep-Value and Special-Situations, Hypergrowth or Income Len5es. We said its November rally had no new figures from LVMH behind it, and its US shares have since given back about three-fifths of it while France's larger companies held their ground. Oil rose as LVMH took most of that loss, then fell back without lifting it. Morgan Stanley trimmed its price target on Monday over weaker demand. We also left out a buyer, money leaving AI stocks, and it looked to be back in Paris on Thursday morning.

Quality-Value is still the near miss. It wants a durable profit at a discount, and the drop has taken LVMH back to about 18 times the past year's profit, from about 19 in our post. The durable half is still missing, because Fashion and Leather Goods, the division that sells Louis Vuitton bags, shrank 5% in the September quarter. What would put LVMH on the Quality-Value Len5: that division growing again in the December quarter, reported in late January, with the shares near this multiple. LVMH still passes the Quality Len5, which wants profit with debt under the owners' stake: it earned 5.7B euros in the first half of 2026, and its net debt, borrowings minus cash, was about an eighth of its equity. A losing half-year would knock it off the Quality Len5.

Hermes International (HESAY) at $150.65, -$0.64 / -0.42% on Wednesday, sells to the richest luxury buyers, and LVMH lost more than it did. iShares MSCI France ETF (EWQ) at $43.94, -$0.19 / -0.43% on Wednesday, tracks France's larger companies. From the November 4 closes, in US trading:
- LVMH: -$4.90 / -5.2%.
- Hermes: -$4.71 / -3.0%.
- The France fund: +$0.08 / +0.2%.
LVMH's Wednesday close sat under its $89.64 close of November 3, the last before the midterm results. More than half of the drop came on Friday, November 6, when the shares fell 2.8%. Hermes is on none of the five Len5es LVMH misses; at about 30 times profit it offers no discount.

Oil first moved against LVMH, then stopped mattering to it.
- US crude, November 6 settlement: $90.83 a barrel, +$2.71 / +3.1% from November 4.
- US crude at about 6:15am ET Thursday: $85.86, -$2.26 / -2.6% from November 4.
Crude fell back on hopes for more talks between Washington and Tehran, the force behind LVMH's Monday gain in our post, and LVMH kept slipping.

Morgan Stanley weighed in on Monday, November 9, and its note pointed to weaker demand. The bank cut its price target, its estimate of what a share will be worth in about a year, to 415 euros from 420, and kept its equal-weight rating, a neutral call, MarketScreener reported. It cited weak demand in China and worsening business in France and South Korea, and trimmed its Hermes target too. LVMH's shares in Paris, where they trade in euros, fell 1.5% that day.

We left out a third buyer. Kevin Smith of MarketScreener wrote on November 5 that money leaving AI stocks had finally spread to luxury companies, with the US election result reinforcing the bet. Our read: that money was back Thursday morning, when technology stocks fell overnight and LVMH's Paris shares rose.
- LVMH in Paris: 411.50 euros at about 6:10am ET, +8.40 / +2.1% from Wednesday's close.
That is still under its November 4 close in Paris.

LVMH's price has moved for a week on forces from outside the company, and the one fresh look at the business found weaker demand. China's National Bureau of Statistics is due to publish October retail sales at 9pm ET Sunday, the first count of China's shoppers since Morgan Stanley's cut.

text:
In the quiet elegance of Paris’s 16th arrondissement, just before an ordinary morning appointment, a bronze figure interrupts the rhythm of the street. On Place Rochambeau, amid autumn leaves, plane trees, and the pale stone of Haussmann buildings, Jean Baptiste Donatien de Vimeur, Count of Rochambeau, stands with one arm extended in command. The statue, sculpted by Fernand Hamar and inaugurated in 1933, captures the marshal in full eighteenth century military dress, tricorne hat on his head, a map in his other hand, a cannon at his feet. Pigeons settle casually on the outstretched arm, as if the city itself has claimed the gesture.

Born in 1725 and later named Marshal of France, Rochambeau commanded the French expeditionary force that crossed the Atlantic in 1780 to support the American colonies. At the siege of Yorktown on 19 October 1781, his strategic leadership alongside George Washington and the Marquis de Lafayette proved decisive. The British surrender under Lord Cornwallis that day effectively secured American independence after more than seven years of conflict. Washington’s own words, inscribed on the pedestal, acknowledge the shared struggle and the independence obtained. The monument itself was raised through Franco American subscription under the auspices of the Friendly Society of Loir et Cher in Paris, a lasting tribute to that alliance. The triangular square, created in 1934 at the meeting of Avenue Pierre Ier de Serbie, Rue Freycinet, and Rue de Chaillot, faces the Palais Galliera and offers a small green pause in the elegant quarter.

A contemporary plaque nearby asks visitors to look further. It recalls the complex legacy attached to the family name, specifically that of Donatien Marie Joseph de Vimeur, Count of Rochambeau (1755 to 1813), the son who served under his father in America yet later, as governor of Saint Domingue (today’s Haiti) in 1802, directed an exceptionally brutal campaign to suppress the Haitian Revolution and reinstate slavery. Under his command thousands were executed, often in horrific conditions that included the use of trained dogs and mass reprisals. These actions, now recognized as stark examples of colonial violence, form a dark chapter in French and global history. The plaque invites reflection on collective memory: honoring military contributions must not overshadow the violence and injustices committed under his authority. This space, like the statue, serves as a reminder of the importance of understanding history in all its complexity and of giving voice to the victims of these events.

The bronze marshal continues to point forward. In a city layered with memory, the pause before an appointment becomes something more. It is a moment that holds both the triumph of an alliance that helped birth a nation and the necessity of facing the full weight of the past. Statues do not freeze history; they ask us to keep reading it.

text:
At Six Years Old, She Left Japan. Decades Later, She Changed Education for Japanese Women. 🇯🇵

In 1871, a six-year-old Japanese girl boarded a ship bound for the United States.

Her name was Umeko Tsuda.

Japan had only recently emerged from centuries of rule under the Tokugawa shogunate.

The new Meiji government was determined to learn from the outside world.

It sent the Iwakura Mission abroad to study Western institutions, industry, and society.

Among those traveling were five young Japanese girls selected to study in America.

Umeko was the youngest.

Imagine leaving your family and homeland at six years old, knowing almost nothing about the country where you would spend the next decade.

She lived with an American family near Washington, D.C., learned English, and received an American education.

When she finally returned to Japan in 1882, she was seventeen.

But the country she came home to was very different from the one she had learned to navigate abroad.

Opportunities for women to pursue advanced education remained severely limited.

For Umeko, this was not simply an abstract social problem.

She had experienced what education could offer women, and she wanted Japanese women to have similar opportunities.

She worked as a teacher, then returned to the United States in 1889 to study biology at Bryn Mawr College.

There, she deepened her academic training and developed connections that would help support educational opportunities for Japanese women.

In 1900, she took a decisive step.

She founded Joshi Eigaku Juku, the Women’s English School, in Tokyo.

It opened with just ten students.

From that small beginning grew the institution that would eventually become Tsuda University.

Umeko believed that women deserved serious education, intellectual independence, and opportunities to develop their abilities.

Her work challenged the narrow expectations placed on women in Meiji-era society.

She did not live to see all the changes that would come in later generations.

But her influence continued through the women who studied at her school and pursued careers in education, public service, and other fields.

In 2024, Japan placed her portrait on its new 5,000-yen banknote.

text:
THE COLD FRONT HAS CLEARED, AND NOW THE REAL COOLDOWN BEGINS! 🥶❄️ We're now in somewhat of a weird "transition zone" across Southern Middle Tennessee as cooler air slowly begins filtering into the region. We've still got a few minor weather changes to get through over the next 24–36 hours before our coldest temperatures of the fall season arrive this weekend!

Today will feature a mix of sun and clouds, with afternoon highs approaching the upper 50s. After lunchtime, we could see a few scattered light showers and areas of drizzle develop as the upper-level trough associated with our departing cold front swings through the region. However, widespread rainfall is NOT anticipated, and many communities may not see much of anything. A few light showers or patches of drizzle could linger into Thursday evening before coming to an end around midnight. By Friday morning, temperatures will have fallen into the upper 20s and lower 30s across Southern Middle Tennessee, making for a rather chilly start to the day!

We'll see another mix of sun and clouds throughout much of Friday, although there's one little wrinkle in the forecast that I'm keeping an eye on. The latest HRRR short-range forecast model is trying to bring an additional piece of weak atmospheric energy across our region Friday evening. If this materializes, we could see a few scattered light showers develop across our eastern communities, with some of that precipitation potentially falling as LIGHT SNOW across the higher elevations of the Cumberland Plateau, generally above 1,500 feet. The best chance for a few flakes would be in Grundy County and around Sewanee in Franklin County. Now, before anyone gets too excited, we're NOT expecting any snow accumulations or travel impacts, and there's still some uncertainty as to whether we'll see any precipitation at all. Believe it or not, around this same time last year, we were dealing with our first light snow event along the Cumberland Plateau! So, while it may seem a little early to be talking about snowflakes, it's really not all that unusual for the higher elevations to see a few flakes flying this time of year.

Once we get past that small chance for precipitation Friday evening, skies will begin clearing out, setting the stage for our coldest temperatures so far this fall. Overnight lows are expected to drop into the MID TO UPPER 20s Friday night, Saturday night, and potentially Sunday night as well! We're talking about our first widespread HARD FREEZE of the season, accompanied by a heavy, killing frost that will likely put an end to the growing season across much of Southern Middle Tennessee. If you've got outdoor plans after sunset or around sunrise Saturday and Sunday, you'll definitely want to break out the winter coat!

Tension prevailed in Madikeri after a family that had visited a temple to offer prayers during a festival was allegedly assaulted by a group of men over previous enmity.

Three members of the family sustained injuries and were admitted to a hospital for treatment.

The incident took place on Sunday evening at Sri Kanchi Kamakshiyamma Temple on Gauli Street in Madikeri town.

According to reports, G.R. Satish, a resident of Hosa Badavane, had visited the temple along with his wife and children, Sampreeth and Abhisheeth, to offer prayers. At the time, Sharat, Suraj and Umesh Subramani, along with a group of local residents, were allegedly gathered outside the temple.

The group reportedly attacked Satish and his sons Sampreeth and Abhisheeth over previous enmity.

The incident is said to have been captured on CCTV cameras installed in the area.

A complaint has been registered at the Madikeri Town Police Station in connection with the incident.

The family has alleged that the accused had previously issued death threats against them and that a complaint regarding the threats had also been submitted to the police.

Satish and his sons, who are undergoing treatment at a hospital, told the media that the attack was allegedly carried out with the intention of killing them. They also expressed concern over the alleged lack of action despite their earlier complaints.

The injured family members have urged the police department to take strict action against the accused, investigate the alleged death threats and ensure adequate protection for their family.

Further investigation into the incident is awaited.

text:
Aleksandr Shevchenko vs Thiago Agustin Tirante — the qualifier who beat the second seed against the higher-ranked Argentine

Preview · ATP 250 Stockholm · Quarter-final · Thursday 12 November 2026

Aleksandr Shevchenko came through qualifying in Stockholm and has now won four matches here, the last of them against the second seed, Casper Ruud. Thiago Agustin Tirante is ranked 56 places higher, but has completed only one match this week after a walkover in the last 16. The ranking points one way and the results here point the other, which keeps this a cautious call.

THE MATCHUP

Tirante is ranked No.51 and Shevchenko No.107. Both are 25 and right-handed; Tirante, from Argentina, stands 1.85m, and Shevchenko, from Kazakhstan, 1.88m.

They have never met in a tour-level match. Their one meeting came in qualifying at the ATP Masters 1000 event in Miami in 2025, on an outdoor hard court, where Tirante won 6-3 6-3 in the second qualifying round. That result counts for something, but it is a single qualifying match, played outdoors rather than indoors, and it does not appear in their tour-level record.

FORM & CONTEXT

Shevchenko, the seventh seed in qualifying, has played four matches in Stockholm. He beat Viktor Durasovic 6-1 6-1 in 57 minutes on Saturday and the fourth qualifying seed, Jacob Fearnley, 6-2 6-4 in 1h15 on Sunday. In the main draw he beat the lucky loser Adrian Mannarino 6-1 6-3 in 1h09 on Tuesday, and yesterday he beat Ruud 6-7(5) 6-4 6-3 in 2h17. He has lost one set in four matches.

Tirante beat Jaume Munar 7-6(3) 6-3 in 1h44 on Sunday. His last-16 match against the fifth seed, Tomas Martin Etcheverry, was a walkover on Tuesday, so he has completed one match here.

Away from Stockholm, neither arrives with much. Tirante lost the final qualifying round in Paris to Mattia Bellucci 4-6 4-6, then lost to Jan-Lennard Struff 7-6(5) 3-6 6-7(3) in the round of 32 of the main draw. Before that he lost in the first qualifying round in Vienna to Mannarino and in his first match in Almaty to Facundo Diaz Acosta. Shevchenko lost to Luka Pavlovic 3-6 6-4 4-6 at an event in Bratislava on 2 November, and lost the final qualifying round in Almaty to Stefanos Sakellaridis 6-7(4) 4-6. In mid-October, at an event in Jinan, he beat Miomir Kecmanovic 6-3 6-4 and Jay Friend before losing to Bellucci 4-6 4-6 in the quarter-finals.

THE DECIDING FACTOR

The deciding factor is what each has shown in Stockholm. Shevchenko has won four matches in five days, including a win over the second seed. Tirante has one completed win here. Their results elsewhere offer little to separate them, so the week in Sweden carries most of the weight.

THE CALL

The 56-place ranking gap and the 2025 qualifying win both favour Tirante, and neither should be dismissed. Shevchenko's results this week are the stronger evidence on court, but against a higher-ranked opponent that is enough only for a low-confidence call.

Aleksandr Shevchenko to win, low confidence.

Have you heard of the Isreali Dahiya doctrine that says, “If rockets are fired from an Arab or Palestinian village, destroy the village. Not just the launcher. The whole area”. He brought the doctrine as a military commander. He is ruthless. 

Today, Arab parties reportedly walked out of a meeting with him, apparently unwilling to describe Hamas as a terrorist organisation. Meanwhile, I have read reports suggesting that Israeli fighter jets are being prepared for possible military strikes against Iran.

The question, therefore, is worth asking: if Benjamin Netanyahu were to leave office, would his departure necessarily bring the Palestinians and the wider Arab world the relief they might be expected to celebrate? Or is it from frying pan to volcanic magma!!??
~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~~
WHO IS GADI EISENKOT?
When President Herzog gave Gadi Eisenkot 28 days to form a government, the world expected celebration in Gaza, Ramallah, Beirut, and across the Arab world.

It didn't come.

Because for Palestinians and Arabs, this is not the end of an era. It is the beginning of a more dangerous one.

Netanyahu is a politician. Eisenkot is a soldier.

They feel Eisenkot will be more lethal than Netanyahu. 

Netanyahu talked about total victory. Eisenkot wrote the doctrine for how to achieve it.

THE DAHIYA DOCTRINE

In 2006, as Commander of the Northern Command, Eisenkot created what became known as the Dahiya Doctrine: If rockets are fired from a village, destroy the village. Disproportionate force. Not just the launcher. The whole area.

That is not a slogan. That is a military plan. And it was used in Lebanon. And its logic was used in Gaza.

Palestinians know that name. Lebanese know that name. They know what it means on the ground.

Eisenkot IS NOT COMING TO MAKE PEACE,

Eisenkot does not support a Palestinian state.
He does not support ending the occupation.
He does not support a full withdrawal.

His promise is clear: Hamas must be destroyed or dismantled. Within 18 months, Hamas rule in Gaza must be replaced — by deal, or by force.

His criticism of Netanyahu is not that Netanyahu went too far. His criticism is that Netanyahu promised victory in one year, and after three years, he failed.

In other words: Netanyahu was too slow. Eisenkot says he will finish it.

Eisenkot is GENERAL WHO HAS PAID IN BLOOD

Eisenkot lost his son in Gaza. He lost two nephews in Gaza.

To Israelis, that makes him credible. To Palestinians, that makes him terrifying. A leader who has buried his own child in this war will not be the one to stop it halfway. He will be the one to see it through to the end.

THE CONSENSUS HAS NOT CHANGED

Look at the election. No major Jewish party campaigned on Palestinian rights. No major party campaigned on ending settlements. No major party campaigned on a sovereign Palestine.

The debate was about who is more competent to run the war, not whether the war should end.

That is why many Arabs say: Changing Netanyahu for Eisenkot is like changing the driver, but keeping the same destination.

AND THE COALITION WILL KEEP HIM HARD

Eisenkot has only 48 seats. He needs 61. To get there, he needs the ultra-Orthodox, or Likud, or outside support.

None of them want concessions. None of them want a Palestinian state.

And he has already said he will NOT form a government with the Arab parties, even though they gave him the 67 recommendations to get the mandate. He used their votes to block Netanyahu, but he will not share power with them.

SO WHY NO CELEBRATION?

$SPB Q4 2026 earnings: Spectrum Brands lifts profit, but sales fall across all units

Spectrum Brands, the maker of Spectracide bug spray and Remington shavers, expanded its profit margins even as fourth-quarter sales slipped in all three divisions. Underlying sales excluding currency fell 3% because bad weather and full store warehouses hurt lawn and garden restocking, while North American appliance sales dropped. However, higher prices and factory savings lifted gross margin by 2.6 percentage points, pushing operating cash profit excluding tariff refund costs up 15%, well above what the company's own full-year plan pointed to. Chief executive David Maura set a fiscal 2027 plan for flat to low-single-digit sales and underlying profit growth.

• Sales from businesses owned a year ago, ex-currency: -𝟑.𝟏% (reported net sales $713.2M (-2.8%))
• Q4 Adjusted EBITDA, excluding tariff refund costs: $𝟕𝟑.𝟏𝐌 (+15.3% from a year ago)
• Net debt to Adjusted EBITDA: 𝟎.𝟕𝟕𝐱 (1.58x a year ago)
• Fiscal 2027 sales and Adjusted EBITDA outlook: 𝟎–𝟑% 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 (flat to low single digits, ex-refunds)

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪ Neutral

The story is unchanged because wider profit margins and tariff refund cash balanced out weaker store restocking and a stalled appliance deal. Beating the fourth-quarter profit implied by the prior plan shows management set a cautious bar, and collecting tariff refunds cut net debt below one times cash profit. The bad news: Home and Garden sales fell 9% on leftover retailer stock, and rival Helen of Troy rejected a takeover bid from the company's Oaktree-backed appliance unit.

The question now is whether pet and garden sales can grow without favorable currency while the appliance unit pursues a contested takeover. Either new products drive real volume gains and a disciplined deal, or store overstock and appliance shelf losses keep total underlying sales flat for another year. Retailer spring restocking orders and Helen of Troy's response to the public bid will tell.

[Model: Gemini 4 Argon. Full article with charts - link in bio]

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🟢🟢 𝐋𝐨𝐰𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐝𝐮𝐜𝐭 𝐂𝐨𝐬𝐭𝐬 𝐋𝐢𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐌𝐚𝐫𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐬
Spectrum Brands makes pet supplies, bug sprays, and small kitchen appliances. Chief executive David Maura said that in Home and Personal Care (HPC), the appliance and grooming unit, "while top-line pressures persisted as expected, the team delivered strong margin expansion, a direct reflection of disciplined execution and a clear focus on profitability." Across the group, gross margin rose 2.6 percentage points to 37.6% because the cost of making products fell 2.7 points of sales.

• Cost of goods sold: 62.4% of sales, down from 65.0% a year ago
• Selling and administrative overhead: 34.2% of sales, up from 30.9% a year ago
• HPC Adjusted EBITDA margin excluding tariff refunds: 8.8%, up 3.5 percentage points

Higher prices, lower retail promotional spending, reduced tariff rates, and factory cost savings drove the gross margin gain. That improvement easily covered a 3.4-point rise in selling and administrative overhead, lifting company Adjusted EBITDA (operating cash profit before interest, taxes, and one-off items) by 15.3% excluding tariff refund costs.

What to watch: first-quarter gross margin and appliance profit margins. Holding gross margin above 37% without the help of early retailer orders ahead of the software rollout would show the cost savings are permanent.

🟢 𝐅𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐐𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐭 𝐚 𝐂𝐚𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐥𝐚𝐧
Three months ago, management raised its full-year target for Adjusted EBITDA excluding tariff refunds to mid-single-digit growth. By our math, that full-year outlook pointed to $56.4–62.1 million of fourth-quarter Adjusted EBITDA, which would have meant a decline of 2% to 11% from a year ago.

Instead, the consumer products maker delivered $73.1 million excluding $3.2 million of tariff refund expenses, up 15.3% from a year ago. Full-year Adjusted EBITDA excluding refunds grew 9.8% to $317.4 million. Beating the implied fourth-quarter target proves the prior outlook was cautious, though it does not erase the fourth-quarter sales drop.

What to watch: whether management raises its fiscal 2027 outlook after the first half. Starting the new year with a plan for flat to low-single-digit profit growth after nearly 10% growth this year tests if leadership is setting another low bar.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞

🔴🔴 𝐀𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐁𝐢𝐝 𝐑𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐍𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐡 𝐀𝐦𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐚 𝐒𝐥𝐮𝐦𝐩𝐬
Spectrum Brands wants to separate its Home and Personal Care (HPC) unit, which sells Remington shavers and George Foreman grills, and use its clean balance sheet for deals. In May, it partnered with investment firm Oaktree Capital Management to form Empower Brands. Last week, Empower Brands "announced its interest to acquire Helen of Troy", a rival consumer goods company, but Maura said leadership was "disappointed by their rejection of our offer".

While the company pursues a public takeover fight to build scale, the appliance unit's own sales are still shrinking. Underlying sales in HPC fell 2.3% in the fourth quarter and 6.1% for the full year. Worse, fourth-quarter sales "benefited from retailer orders in advance of the S4/Hana ERP go-live", meaning customers stocked up early before the company switched software systems.

Even with those early orders, North American appliance and personal care sales dropped in the low double digits because of "distribution losses in Home Appliances and increased competitive pressure in Personal Care". That makes an acquisition more urgent to fix the division's scale, but a public pursuit after a rejected bid raises the risk of overpaying.

What to watch: any revised offer terms for Helen of Troy and first-quarter HPC sales in North America. When the early software-related orders reverse next quarter, the underlying sales drop in North America will look steeper.

🔴 𝐆𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐒𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐎𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐞𝐝 𝐚𝐬 𝐏𝐞𝐭 𝐆𝐚𝐢𝐧𝐬 𝐒𝐥𝐨𝐰
"The underlying performance across all three segments demonstrates the strength of our business fundamentals," chief executive David Maura said. Supporters point to full-year sales growth of 5.1% in Global Pet Care (GPC), which makes dog chews and aquarium supplies, and 3.9% in Home and Garden (H&G), which makes Spectracide and Cutter bug sprays. In the fourth quarter, however, sales excluding currency fell in all three divisions.

• Home and Garden underlying sales: down 9.3% in Q4, after rising 19.1% in Q3
• Global Pet Care underlying sales: down 1.1% in Q4, with Aquatics down low double digits
• Total company underlying sales: down 3.1% in Q4 and down 0.3% for the full year

In Home and Garden, "unfavorable weather conditions and elevated retailer inventory levels adversely impacted replenishment orders", flipping the division from an expected fourth-quarter gain to a 9.3% drop. In Pet Care, North American dog and cat treat sales grew, but European sales fell and aquarium demand stayed weak. Full-year reported sales only grew 1.5% because a weaker dollar added $51.6 million.

What to watch: retailer restocking orders for Home and Garden in the second quarter ahead of spring. If stores are still working through leftover bug spray inventory from this summer, full-year sales will struggle to grow.

🔴 𝐑𝐢𝐬𝐤𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐬 𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐝𝐢𝐝𝐧'𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐰𝐞𝐫
The fourth-quarter earnings release left three standing operational and financial questions without updated numbers ahead of the annual report.

• Price versus volume in Pet Care: the release credits pricing for margin gains and blames lower volume for profit dips, but the exact full-year volume growth table awaits the annual 10-K filing.
• New product sales share: management credits new products for market share gains in pet treats and bug sprays, yet still does not disclose what percentage of sales comes from recent launches.
• Retailer concentration: two large retail customers account for roughly a third of company sales, and the release does not detail whether the North American appliance shelf losses occurred at those top accounts.

👓 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

𝐆𝐥𝐨𝐛𝐚𝐥 𝐒𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐑𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐨𝐮𝐭 𝐅𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐒𝐜𝐡𝐞𝐝𝐮𝐥𝐞
Maura said "the completion of our S/4 HANA ERP deployment across the entire organization marks a pivotal milestone in our multi-year transformation". The company now runs all divisions on one software system for tracking orders and inventory. Spectrum Brands excluded $3.8 million of software project costs from Adjusted EBITDA in the fourth quarter and $12.1 million for the full year, up from $9.2 million last year, with final deployment costs wrapping up in calendar 2026.

𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐑𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬 𝐓𝐮𝐫𝐧 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐨 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐚𝐬 𝐁𝐮𝐲𝐛𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐏𝐚𝐮𝐬𝐞
Following a court ruling on International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) duties, Spectrum Brands booked $57.4 million of net tariff refunds in fiscal 2026, including $3.2 million of related costs in the fourth quarter. Other receivables on the balance sheet dropped by $46.7 million from last quarter to $74.0 million as the government paid out most of the cash. Meanwhile, the company bought back no shares in the fourth quarter, keeping full-year repurchases at $58.2 million versus $326.4 million last year.

— • — • —

💲 𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 (𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔): $𝟐𝟒𝟕.𝟑 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧  ⇗ accelerating
Rose 44.9% from $170.7 million last year. By our math, the company generated $111.2 million of that cash in the fourth quarter alone as seasonal working capital wound down and tariff refund checks arrived. Capital spending on property and equipment rose to $47.8 million from $38.3 million a year ago, finishing slightly below the $50–60 million plan.

𝐍𝐞𝐭 𝐝𝐞𝐛𝐭 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐥𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐠𝐞 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟐𝟖𝟗.𝟗 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 (𝟎.𝟕𝟕𝐱)  ⇘ decelerating
Net debt — total debt of $629.8 million minus $339.9 million of cash — fell by $84.2 million during the fourth quarter. That brought net debt down to 0.77 times full-year Adjusted EBITDA, down from 1.58 times a year ago and well below management's long-term target of 2.0 to 2.5 times.

𝐈𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐫𝐞𝐜𝐞𝐢𝐯𝐚𝐛𝐥𝐞𝐬 (𝟐𝟔𝐐𝟒): $𝟒𝟔𝟔.𝟎 𝐦𝐢𝐥𝐥𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲  ⇒ stable
Inventory on the company's balance sheet rose 4.5% from a year ago to $466.0 million even though fourth-quarter sales fell 2.8%, though inventory came down from $499.6 million at the end of the third quarter. Trade receivables — money owed by retail customers — fell 6.3% from a year ago to $488.8 million alongside the lower fourth-quarter shipments.

— • — • —

🔮 𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐑𝐞𝐩𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐧𝐞𝐭 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡: 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟎–𝟑%)  ⇗ accelerating
New. The plan calls for reported sales to be flat to up a few percent in fiscal 2027, matching the 1.5% reported growth delivered in fiscal 2026 and improving from the 2.8% drop in the fourth quarter. Management expects growth in Global Pet Care and Home and Garden to carry the year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐠𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 (𝐞𝐱𝐜𝐥𝐮𝐝𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐫𝐞𝐟𝐮𝐧𝐝𝐬): 𝐅𝐥𝐚𝐭 𝐭𝐨 𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐬𝐢𝐧𝐠𝐥𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐬 (𝟎–𝟑%)  ⇘ decelerating
New. Starting from the $317.4 million fiscal 2026 base that strips out $57.4 million of one-off tariff refunds, management plans for operating cash profit to be flat to up a few percent. That is a slowdown from the 9.8% underlying growth achieved in fiscal 2026, though last year also started with a low-single-digit plan before two upward revisions.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟕 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐟𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐟𝐥𝐨𝐰 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧: ~𝟓𝟎% 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀  ⇘ decelerating
New. Spectrum Brands targets turning about half of its Adjusted EBITDA into adjusted free cash flow, excluding tariff refund impacts. By our math, 50% of the guided EBITDA base equals roughly $161 million of cash flow, down from $247.3 million in fiscal 2026 when tariff refunds boosted collections.

— • — • —

❓ 𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐖𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐧𝐞𝐱𝐭 𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐩𝐬 𝐚𝐟𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐇𝐞𝐥𝐞𝐧 𝐨𝐟 𝐓𝐫𝐨𝐲'𝐬 𝐫𝐞𝐣𝐞𝐜𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧?
Empower Brands made its acquisition offer public after Helen of Troy's board rejected it. Investors need to know how high Spectrum Brands and Oaktree are willing to bid, and how much debt the appliance unit would take on to fund a deal.

𝐇𝐨𝐰 𝐦𝐮𝐜𝐡 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐲 𝐬𝐨𝐟𝐭𝐰𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐨𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐫𝐬 𝐛𝐨𝐨𝐬𝐭 𝐟𝐨𝐮𝐫𝐭𝐡-𝐪𝐮𝐚𝐫𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐚𝐩𝐩𝐥𝐢𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐬𝐚𝐥𝐞𝐬?
Retailers ordered appliances and personal care items early ahead of the SAP software launch, helping the division's European sales grow. Because North American sales still fell low double digits, sizing that pull-forward is needed to judge the first-quarter drop-off.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐧 𝐰𝐢𝐥𝐥 𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐞𝐬 𝐟𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐡 𝐜𝐥𝐞𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐥𝐞𝐟𝐭𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐥𝐚𝐰𝐧 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐠𝐚𝐫𝐝𝐞𝐧 𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐨𝐫𝐲?
Home and Garden sales dropped 9.3% in the fourth quarter because bad weather left retailers with full warehouses. Management did not say whether store inventories are now back to normal or if excess stock will weigh on winter and spring orders.

𝐖𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐝 𝐟𝐮𝐥𝐥-𝐲𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐜𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐭𝐚𝐱𝐞𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐫𝐮𝐜𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐩𝐚𝐲𝐦𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐬 𝐥𝐚𝐧𝐝?
Management previously planned for $40–50 million of cash taxes and $25–35 million of cash restructuring and deal payments in fiscal 2026. The condensed earnings release does not break out those two cash lines, leaving their final totals for the annual filing.

Dwight begins exploring the city, trying to understand how things work in his unfamiliar surroundings.

text:
A technique known as “machine unlearning” could teach AI models to forget specific voices—an important step in stopping the rise of audio deepfakes, where someone’s voice is copied to carry out fraud or scams.

Recent advances in artificial intelligence have revolutionized the quality of text-to-speech technology so that people can convincingly re-create a piece of text in any voice, complete with natural speaking patterns and intonations, instead of having to settle for a robotic voice reading it out word by word. “Anyone’s voice can be reproduced or copied with just a few seconds of their voice,” says Jong Hwan Ko, a professor at Sungkyunkwan University in Korea and the coauthor of a new paper that demonstrates one of the first applications of machine unlearning to speech generation.

Copied voices have been used in scams, disinformation, and harassment. Ko, who researches audio processing, and his collaborators wanted to prevent this kind of identity fraud. “People are starting to demand ways to opt out of the unknown generation of their voices without consent,” he says. 

AI companies generally keep a tight grip on their models to discourage misuse. For example, if you ask ChatGPT to give you someone’s phone number or instructions for doing something illegal, it will likely just tell you it cannot help. However, as many examples over time have shown, clever prompt engineering or model fine-tuning can sometimes get these models to say things they otherwise wouldn’t. The unwanted information may still be hiding somewhere inside the model so that it can be accessed with the right techniques. 

At present, companies tend to deal with this issue by applying guardrails; the idea is to check whether the prompts or the AI’s responses contain disallowed material. Machine unlearning instead asks whether an AI can be made to forget a piece of information that the company doesn’t want it to know. The technique takes a leaky model and the specific training data to be redacted and uses them to create a new model—essentially, a version of the original that never learned that piece of data. While machine unlearning has ties to older techniques in AI research, it’s only in the past couple of years that it’s been applied to large language models.

Jinju Kim, a master’s student at Sungkyunkwan University who worked on the paper with Ko and others, sees guardrails as fences around the bad data put in place to keep people away from it. “You can’t get through the fence, but some people will still try to go under the fence or over the fence,” says Kim. But unlearning, she says, attempts to remove the bad data altogether, so there is nothing behind the fence at all. 

The way current text-to-speech systems are designed complicates this a little more, though. These so-called “zero-shot” models use examples of people’s speech to learn to re-create any voice, including those not in the training set—with enough data, it can be a good mimic when supplied with even a small sample of someone’s voice. So “unlearning” means a model not only needs to “forget” voices it was trained on but also has to learn not to mimic specific voices it wasn’t trained on. All the while, it still needs to perform well for other voices. 

To demonstrate how to get those results, Kim taught a recreation of VoiceBox, a speech generation model from Meta, that when it was prompted to produce a text sample in one of the voices to be redacted, it should instead respond with a random voice. To make these voices realistic, the model “teaches” itself using random voices of its own creation. 

According to the team’s results, which are to be presented this week at the International Conference on Machine Learning, prompting the model to imitate a voice it has “unlearned” gives back a result that—according to state-of-the-art tools that measure voice similarity—mimics the forgotten voice more than 75% less effectively than the model did before. In practice, this makes the new voice unmistakably different. But the forgetfulness comes at a cost: The model is about 2.8% worse at mimicking permitted voices. While these percentages are a bit hard to interpret, the demo the researchers released online offers very convincing results, both for how well redacted speakers are forgotten and how well the rest are remembered. A sample from the demo is given below. 

Ko says the unlearning process can take “several days,” depending on how many speakers the researchers want the model to forget. Their method also requires an audio clip about five minutes long for each speaker whose voice is to be forgotten.

In machine unlearning, pieces of data are often replaced with randomness so that they can’t be reverse-engineered back to the original. In this paper, the randomness for the forgotten speakers is very high—a sign, the authors claim, that they are truly forgotten by the model. 

 “I have seen people optimizing for randomness in other contexts,” says Vaidehi Patil, a PhD student at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill who researches machine unlearning. “This is one of the first works I’ve seen for speech.” Patil is organizing a machine unlearning workshop affiliated with the conference, and the voice unlearning research will also be presented there. 

She points out that unlearning itself involves inherent trade-offs between efficiency and forgetfulness because the process can take time, and can degrade the usability of the final model. “There’s no free lunch. You have to compromise something,” she says.

Machine unlearning may still be at too early a stage for, say, Meta to introduce Ko and Kim’s methods into VoiceBox. But there is likely to be industry interest. Patil is researching unlearning for Google DeepMind this summer, and while Meta did not respond with a comment, it has hesitated for a long time to release VoiceBox to the wider public because it is so vulnerable to misuse. 

The voice unlearning team seems optimistic that its work could someday get good enough for real-life deployment. “In real applications, we would need faster and more scalable solutions,” says Ko. “We are trying to find those.”

text:
134 years ago today, a Yale football star was secretly handed $500 to play one game, and football was never the same.

William "Pudge" Heffelfinger was a three-time All-American guard at Yale, widely considered the best player of his day. Football was officially an amateur sport. Players could be paid expenses, but not salaries.

In 1892, two Pittsburgh teams, the Allegheny Athletic Association and the Pittsburgh Athletic Club, were bitter rivals who both wanted an edge. The Pittsburgh club offered Heffelfinger $250 to play. He felt that wasn't enough to risk his amateur standing. The Allegheny club doubled it to $500.

On November 12, 1892, he played for Allegheny. He recovered a fumble and scored the game's only touchdown, which was worth four points at the time. Allegheny won, 4 to 0.

The payment was never published or admitted. It stayed secret.

Then, in the 1960s, a man known only as "Nelson Ross" walked into the office of Steelers president Art Rooney with a typed 49-page manuscript on the early history of pro football. His research pointed to Heffelfinger as the first. The Pro Football Hall of Fame soon found a page torn from Allegheny's 1892 ledger, with the line item showing a $500 game performance bonus to Heffelfinger.

Heffelfinger kept playing. He joined the Hennepin County Board in Minnesota, serving 24 years, and he played his last game at age 65.

He is in the College Football Hall of Fame. He has still not been inducted into the Pro Football Hall of Fame.

Football's first paid pro got paid in cash, in secret, and the receipt waited seventy years to be found.

Disclaimer: Based on the Pro Football Hall of Fame, College Football Hall of Fame, and Allegheny Athletic Association records. Details of the ledger discovery vary slightly by account.

text:
OpenAI has finally released its first open-weight large language models since 2019’s GPT-2. These new “gpt-oss” models are available in two different sizes and score similarly to the company’s o3-mini and o4-mini models on several benchmarks. Unlike the models available through OpenAI’s web interface, these new open models can be freely downloaded, run, and even modified on laptops and other local devices.

In the company’s many years without an open LLM release, some users have taken to referring to it with the pejorative “ClosedAI.” That sense of frustration had escalated in the past few months as these long-awaited models were delayed twice—first in June and then in July. With their release, however, OpenAI is reestablishing itself as a presence for users of open models.

That’s particularly notable at a time when Meta, which had previously dominated the American open-model landscape with its Llama models, may be reorienting toward closed releases—and when Chinese open models, such as DeepSeek’s offerings, Kimi K2, and Alibaba’s Qwen series, are becoming more popular than their American competitors.

“The vast majority of our [enterprise and startup] customers are already using a lot of open models,” said Casey Dvorak, a research program manager at OpenAI, in a media briefing about the model release. “Because there is no [competitive] open model from OpenAI, we wanted to plug that gap and actually allow them to use our technology across the board.”

The new models come in two different sizes, the smaller of which can theoretically run on 16 GB of RAM—the minimum amount that Apple currently offers on its computers. The larger model requires a high-end laptop or specialized hardware.

Open models have a few key use cases. Some organizations may want to customize models for their own purposes or save money by running models on their own equipment, though that equipment comes at a substantial upfront cost. Others—such hospitals, law firms, and governments—might need models that they can run locally for data security reasons. 

OpenAI has facilitated such activity by releasing its open models under a permissive Apache 2.0 license, which allows the models to be used for commercial purposes. Nathan Lambert, post-training lead at the Allen Institute for AI, says that this choice is commendable: Such licenses are typical for Chinese open-model releases, but Meta released its Llama models under a bespoke, more restrictive license. “It’s a very good thing for the open community,” he says.

Researchers who study how LLMs work also need open models, so that they can examine and manipulate those models in detail. “In part, this is about reasserting OpenAI’s dominance in the research ecosystem,” says Peter Henderson, an assistant professor at Princeton University who has worked extensively with open models. If researchers do adopt gpt-oss as new workhorses, OpenAI could see some concrete benefits, Henderson says—it might adopt innovations discovered by other researchers into its own model ecosystem.

More broadly, Lambert says, releasing an open model now could help OpenAI reestablish its status in an increasingly crowded AI environment. “It kind of goes back to years ago, where they were seen as the AI company,” he says. Users who want to use open models will now have the option to meet all their needs with OpenAI products, rather than turning to Meta’s Llama or Alibaba’s Qwen when they need to run something locally.

The rise of Chinese open models like Qwen over the past year may have been a particularly salient factor in OpenAI’s calculus. An employee from OpenAI emphasized at the media briefing that the company doesn’t see these open models as a response to actions taken by any other AI company, but OpenAI is clearly attuned to the geopolitical implications of China’s open-model dominance. “Broad access to these capable open-weights models created in the US helps expand democratic AI rails,” the company wrote in a blog post announcing the models’ release. 

Since DeepSeek exploded onto the AI scene at the start of 2025, observers have noted that Chinese models often refuse to speak about topics that the Chinese Communist Party has deemed verboten, such as Tiananmen Square. Such observations—as well as longer-term risks, like the possibility that agentic models could purposefully write vulnerable code—have made some AI experts concerned about the growing adoption of Chinese models. “Open models are a form of soft power,” Henderson says.

Lambert released a report on Monday documenting how Chinese models are overtaking American offerings like Llama and advocating for a renewed commitment to domestic open models. Several prominent AI researchers and entrepreneurs, such as HuggingFace CEO Clement Delangue, Stanford’s Percy Liang, and former OpenAI researcher Miles Brundage, have signed on.

The Trump administration, too, has emphasized development of open models in its AI Action Plan. With both this model release and previous statements, OpenAI is aligning itself with that stance. “In their filings about the action plan, [OpenAI] pretty clearly indicated that they see US–China as a key issue and want to position themselves as very important to the US system,” says Rishi Bommasani, a senior research scholar at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence. 

And OpenAI may see concrete political advantages from aligning with the administration’s AI priorities, Lambert says. As the company continues to build out its extensive computational infrastructure, it will need political support and approvals, and sympathetic leadership could go a long way.

text:
The Department of the Interior has formally adopted a policy goal of reducing federal land ownership, reopening one of the most contentious debates in Western land management.

In its strategic plan released November 10, the department says it intends to offer federal lands for purchase by states, local governments and Tribes.

The stated objective is to reduce federal management costs while concentrating resources on lands the department considers nationally significant.

Interior also proposes using conservation funding to expand recreational access through easements on private land rather than increasing federal land ownership.

The announcement is consequential for the American West, where federal lands support hunting, fishing, livestock grazing, energy production, mining and recreation.

But the plan leaves several important questions unanswered.

It identifies no specific parcels, acreage targets, prices or schedule for proposed sales.

It also does not explain how the department would determine which lands qualify as nationally significant.

Supporters of greater state and local control argue that transferring selected federal parcels could improve land management, accommodate growing communities and reduce administrative costs.

Opponents warn that transferring public land could eventually threaten recreational access, wildlife habitat and the long-term protection of landscapes currently managed for multiple uses.

The legal obstacles are substantial.

Federal agencies cannot simply sell every parcel they manage. Existing statutes establish restrictions, procedures and public-interest requirements, and some transfers would require congressional authorization.

Previous proposals to sell substantial acreage in Utah and Nevada encountered opposition from both political parties.

The new document is a strategic plan, not a completed land sale or a blanket authorization to dispose of protected public lands.

For Western hunters, ranchers, counties and outdoor businesses, the next important development will be whether Interior identifies actual parcels and explains the legal process for transferring them.

Until that happens, the administration has announced a direction, but not a specific land-sale program.
