text:
$AG First Majestic Silver has developed in recent years into one of the most prominent pure silver producers and has meaningfully expanded its production base. With the acquisition of Gatos Silver in January 2025, the company secured a 70 percent interest in the high-grade, cost-attractive underground mine Cerro Los Gatos in Mexico. This integration proceeded according to plan and contributed significantly to First Majestic setting a new annual record in 2025 with 15.4 million ounces of silver - an increase of 84 percent compared with the previous year. Overall, silver-equivalent production reached 31.1 million ounces, exceeding both the original and the upwardly revised guidance issued during the year. Revenues rose by 124 percent over the same period to around US$1.26 billion, while the balance sheet was strengthened by a liquidity position of nearly one billion US dollars.

In addition to organic growth through higher throughput and improved mining rates at the existing operations of Santa Elena, San Dimas and La Encantada, the company benefits from targeted exploration. New high-grade veins such as Santo Niño and Navidad in the vicinity of Santa Elena expand the resource potential and offer additional production leverage in the medium term. At the same time, First Majestic operates First Mint, the only publicly listed silver mine that mints and markets its own silver - a vertically integrated element that enables premium prices relative to the spot market and reduces dependence on pure concentrate sales. The dividend policy raised in light of strong earnings, which will in future distribute two percent of net quarterly revenues, underscores the focus on shareholder returns while retaining sufficient flexibility for investments in throughput increases and the potential restart of the Jerritt Canyon project in Nevada.

This operational setup underpins the pronounced share-price elasticity with respect to the silver price. As a producer with a silver share of roughly 55 to 58 percent of revenue and a notable proportion of fixed costs, First Majestic possesses high operating leverage. Rising silver quotations increase revenues almost linearly, while production costs - apart from price-linked components such as certain bonus payments - rise far less than proportionally. The difference flows largely into the margin, so that EBITDA and free cash flow grow disproportionately. The market anticipates this development and values the stock with a high beta to the silver price: historically, the share has exhibited price movements in phases of clearly rising quotations that significantly outpace the increase in the metal. This mechanism intensifies once the silver price remains sustainably above all-in sustaining costs and management simultaneously focuses on margin-rich tonnages and capacity expansion. The downside lies in the same sensitivity when prices fall; in an environment of rising silver prices, however, the combination of production growth, cost control and operating leverage translates into above-average stock performance.

First Majestic prints with 9-bagger potential at $7,000 gold and $200 silver and is the must-own silver stock.

text:
The U.S. dollar has lost 51% of its value over the past seven years against a basket of crude oil, corn, copper, natural gas, sugar, and soybeans.

That is the backdrop for Royal Gold $RGLD and Franco-Nevada $FNV, both closing in on new all-time highs.

Gold has spent more than two decades revaluing to keep up with the flood of new currency units. Governments keep spending and borrowing well beyond tax revenue.

Neither party wins elections by promising cuts. That makes hard assets a long-term defense, not a short-term trade.

Royalty companies offer a cleaner way to own that theme than miners.

They do not develop or operate mines. They provide upfront capital to mine projects in exchange for a share of future production.

The result is high margins, steady cash flow, and leverage to the gold price, without the cost overruns and operating headaches that come with running a mine.

$RGLD and $FNV are the largest and most diversified of the six royalty names we highlighted this summer.

$RGLD had a big run through 2025 and early 2026, then corrected and moved sideways. It has rallied again and is now a chip shot from a record. $FNV is following the same script.

A breakout from a long consolidation is often where the next leg starts.

Would you rather own the royalty or the miner here?

Coverage begins at 10:30 this morning on WNBS AM and FM and the Varsity App. 

WBB OFFERS COURTSIDE SEATING
Thanks to CFSB, admission to all women's basketball games is FREE for all fans, and new for this season, Murray State Athletics is offering a premium experience for fans who want to be closer to the action. Courtside seating will be reserved and available for purchase at $250 for the season for those who want to catch the game up close. The CFSB Courtside Club will be open for select women's basketball home games. For more information, call the Murray State Ticket Office at 270-809-3000.

WBB SIGNS GORDON
Murray State women's basketball has announced the signing of 5-foot-9 guard Ryenn Gordon of Centralia High School in Missouri for the 2028 recruiting class. Gordon is a three-time All-State, All-Region and All-District selection and a two-time district and conference player of the year. Ranked among the nation's top 100 recruits by Prep Girls Hoops, she helped lead Centralia to a Class 3 Final Four appearance. 

WEDNESDAY WBB ROUNDUP
Kentucky women's basketball took down Evansville 98-30 last night at home.  UK freshman guard Emily McDonald set a new single-game school record by racking up nine three-pointers.  The 12th-ranked Wildcats are back in action this Sunday hosting Eastern Michigan. 

In other MVC games, Illinois State rallied from a halftime deficit to remain unbeaten with a 75-66 win over Green Bay. Danyella Mporokoso led ISU with 20 points. 

UIC rolled to an 87-50 victory over Chicago State, extending its winning streak to three games. The Flames jumped out to a 19-0 lead and never looked back. Nevaeh Foster led UIC with 18 points.

WEDNESDAY'S MBB ROUNDUP
In MVC games, Milwaukee used a strong offensive performance to pick up an 82-73 road victory over Indiana State. Milwaukee shot 52% from the field and built a 14-point second-half advantage before holding off the Sycamores. Maguire Mitchell led Indiana State with 19 points. 

South Dakota State remained unbeaten with an 81-69 victory over Valparaiso. The Beacons made a second-half push but could not overcome the deficit. Carter Hopoi paced the Valpo with 16 points and nine rebounds. 

In other action WKU improved to 3-1 with a convincing 78-51 win over Campbellsville at Diddle Arena. Emondrek Erkins-Ford led the Hilltoppers with a season-high 14 points.

PROS

AREA NBA ROUNDUP
The Grizzlies fell to the Nuggets 123-118 last night at FedEx Forum.  Ty Jerome and Jaylen Wells each led Memphis with 22 points apiece in the setback.  The Grizzlies are now 7-4 and will visit the Pelicans Friday night in NBA Cup Group Play. 

The Indiana Pacers have won their first home game of the season, defeating the Washington Wizards 114-101.  Pascal Siakam led Indiana with 28 points, while Ivica Zubac added 20 points and grabbed 12 rebounds.  The Pacers host the New York Knicks tomorrow night. 

The Spurs extended their winning streak to double-digits after taking down the Bulls 124-119 in Chicago.  Victor Wembanyama led all scorers with 32 points.  San Antonio has won 10 straight.  Jalen Smith sunk 23 points for Chicago which has lost 8 straight games. 

AREA NHL ROUNDUP
The Predators extended their winning streak after taking down the Ducks 4-2 in Anaheim.  Jayden Struble and Nils Hoglander netted goals for an early 2-1 lead.  Shane Wright and Steven Stamkos put the game on ice with third-period goals as Nashville has won six in-a-row.  Cutter Gauthier and Mikael Granlund lit the lamp for Anaheim, which had a five-game winning streak snapped.

MLB CY YOUNG WINNERS
Major League Baseball revealed which pitchers were at the top of their game in 2026.  Milwaukee Brewers ace Jacob Misiorowski and New York Yankees starter Cam Schlittler were named unanimous Cy Young Award winners.  

Misiorowski finished first in the National League ahead of Cristopher Sanchez of the Philadelphia Phillies and Chris Sale of the Atlanta Braves.  

Schlittler won the American League award after Dylan Cease of the Toronto Blue Jays finished second and Parker Messick of the Cleveland Guardians was third. 

TNF PREVIEW
Week 10 of the regular season kicks off with a divisional matchup when the Giants host the Commanders on Thursday Night Football from MetLife Stadium.  JJ McCarthy will be making his first start at home for the G-Men since being traded from Minnesota.  New York leads the NFC East at 5-2-1.  The Commanders will be looking to overcome a disappointing finish to their first battle.  Washington, which is third in the division at 2-5-1, failed to get off a final snap in overtime resulting in a tie.  

AREA NFL ROUNDUP
The Tennessee Titans are preparing to debut a special new look when they host the Jacksonville Jaguars Sunday.  The team will wear its "Music City" Rivalries uniforms, featuring navy blue jerseys and pants, a light blue helmet and neon-inspired numbers celebrating Nashville's musical heritage.  The design also includes a six-string stripe and a "Music City" logo across the chest.  The uniforms are part of an NFL and Nike program highlighting divisional rivalries, and Tennessee plans to wear them just once this season.  Sunday's game kicks off at noon at Nissan Stadium.

Kansas City Chiefs kicker Harrison Butker will keep his job despite ongoing struggles.  Head coach Andy Reid said today that he's not making a change for Sunday's game versus the Atlanta Falcons.  Butker has missed field goal tries in each of the last three games and is just 12-of-19 for the season, prompting the Chiefs to sign veteran Justin Tucker to the practice squad.

WAKE UP, WORLD! THE RAPTURE WILL CHANGE EVERYTHING — ARE YOU READY FOR WHAT COMES NEXT?
🌍 The world continues with its ordinary routines. People are making plans, pursuing their ambitions, building their futures, and living as though everything will continue just as it is today. But there is a prophetic event approaching that this world cannot afford to ignore: THE RAPTURE OF THE CHURCH.
The Bible does not teach that the present world system will continue indefinitely. Jesus Christ is coming for His Church, and the moment will come when believers are caught up to meet the Lord in the air.
📖 1 Thessalonians 4:16–17 (KJV)
"For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God: and the dead in Christ shall rise first:
Then we which are alive and remain shall be caught up together with them in the clouds, to meet the Lord in the air: and so shall we ever be with the Lord."
WHAT HAPPENS AFTER THE RAPTURE?
According to the dispensational understanding of Bible prophecy, the catching away of the Church marks the close of the Church Age. The prophetic seventieth week of Daniel, commonly understood as the seven-year Tribulation, follows. This is not a period the Church is appointed to endure as God's object of wrath.
📖 1 Thessalonians 5:9 (KJV)
"For God hath not appointed us to wrath, but to obtain salvation by our Lord Jesus Christ."
The Tribulation will bring a time of unprecedented trouble, divine judgments, and events foretold in the Book of Revelation. The world should not mistake God's present patience for an absence of coming judgment.
⏳ THIS IS WHY THE WARNING MATTERS NOW!
Do not assume you have unlimited time. Do not postpone the most important decision of your life. The Gospel of God's grace is being preached today. The invitation to be saved is not something to treat lightly.
✝️ THE GOSPEL OF YOUR SALVATION
But understand this: salvation is not earned through religious activities, good deeds, church attendance, or personal righteousness. Jesus Christ has already accomplished the work necessary for your salvation.
📖 1 Corinthians 15:1–4 (KJV) gives us the Gospel:
• Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures.
• He was buried.
• He rose again the third day according to the scriptures.
Jesus Christ paid the price for sin through His death, burial, and resurrection. He offers eternal life as a free gift to everyone who believes.
📖 Ephesians 2:8–9 (KJV)
"For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast."
❤️ WAKE UP, WORLD!
The question is not whether you are religious, whether you consider yourself a good person, or whether you have plans for tomorrow.
The question is: HAVE YOU BELIEVED THE GOSPEL AND TRUSTED JESUS CHRIST AS YOUR SAVIOUR?
Do not wait for the Rapture to discover the seriousness of Bible prophecy. Believe the Gospel NOW, while it is being preached in this present Church Age.
JESUS CHRIST DIED FOR YOUR SINS, WAS BURIED, AND ROSE AGAIN. BELIEVE ON HIM AND RECEIVE THE GIFT OF ETERNAL LIFE.

text:
THESE ARE SEVEN TRUTHS YOU CANNOT AFFORD TO IGNORE!
📷 The world is consumed with making money, pursuing success, acquiring possessions, and enjoying the pleasures of this life. People spend years planning their future, yet many give little thought to what lies beyond the grave.
But there are eternal realities that no amount of wealth, success, or worldly achievement can change.
📷 1. YOUR SOUL HAS AN ETERNAL DESTINY.
Your earthly life will not last forever, but the question of eternity is far more important than anything you can gain in this world.
Matthew 16:26 KJV
“For what is a man profited, if he shall gain the whole world, and lose his own soul? or what shall a man give in exchange for his soul?”
You could possess everything this world has to offer and still lose what matters most. Nothing you acquire on earth can compensate for the loss of your soul.
📷 2. YOUR DAYS ON EARTH ARE LIMITED.
Nobody knows how much time they have left. Tomorrow is not guaranteed, and life can pass far more quickly than we realize.
James 4:14 KJV
“Whereas ye know not what shall be on the morrow. For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away.”
Do not keep putting off the things that matter eternally. Life is short, and the time to consider your relationship with God is now.
📷 3. EVERY PERSON NEEDS FORGIVENESS FOR SIN.
No one is righteous in God's sight through personal goodness or religious achievements. Every human being has sinned and needs a Saviour.
Romans 3:23 KJV
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God;”
Sin is humanity's greatest problem, and no amount of good deeds can remove its penalty. We all need the forgiveness that God offers through Jesus Christ.
📷 4. GOOD WORKS CANNOT EARN YOUR SALVATION.
Being religious, attending church, helping others, giving to charity, or trying to live a good life cannot purchase eternal life. Salvation is not something we earn through our efforts.
Ephesians 2:8–9 KJV
“For by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God:
Not of works, lest any man should boast.”
Good works have their proper place in the Christian life, but they are not the means of salvation. We are saved by God's grace through faith, not by our own accomplishments.
📷 5. JESUS CHRIST DIED FOR YOUR SINS.
God did not leave humanity without hope. Jesus Christ willingly went to the cross and gave His life to pay for our sins.
1 Corinthians 15:3 KJV
“For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;”
The cross reveals the seriousness of sin and the greatness of God's love. Jesus paid the price that we could never pay ourselves.
📷 6. JESUS CHRIST ROSE AGAIN FROM THE DEAD.
The Gospel does not end with His death and burial. Jesus Christ rose again on the third day, just as the Scriptures declared.
1 Corinthians 15:4 KJV
“And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:”
The resurrection is central to our faith. Jesus Christ is alive, and His victory over death is the foundation of our hope.
📷 7. SALVATION IS GOD'S FREE GIFT.
Eternal life is not something you can buy, earn, or deserve. It is a gift of God's grace, made available through Jesus Christ.
**Romans 6:23 KJV**
“For the wages of sin is death; but the gift of God is eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.”
Sin brings death, but God offers eternal life through His Son. Salvation is not a reward for being good enough; it is a gift received through faith in Jesus Christ.
📷 NOW, THE MOST IMPORTANT QUESTION: HAVE YOU BELIEVED THE GOSPEL?
Do not mistake religious activity for salvation. Do not place your confidence in your good deeds, church attendance, or personal righteousness. None of these can save you.
📷 THE GOSPEL OF YOUR SALVATION
The Apostle Paul clearly declares the Gospel in 1 Corinthians 15:1–4 KJV.
1 Corinthians 15:1 KJV
“Moreover, brethren, I declare unto you the gospel which I preached unto you, which also ye have received, and wherein ye stand;”
1 Corinthians 15:2 KJV
“By which also ye are saved, if ye keep in memory what I preached unto you, unless ye have believed in vain.”
1 Corinthians 15:3 KJV
“For I delivered unto you first of all that which I also received, how that Christ died for our sins according to the scriptures;”
1 Corinthians 15:4 KJV
“And that he was buried, and that he rose again the third day according to the scriptures:”
This is the Gospel of Grace: JESUS CHRIST DIED FOR OUR SINS, WAS BURIED, AND ROSE AGAIN THE THIRD DAY!
He accomplished what we could never accomplish through our own efforts. Salvation is received by grace through faith in His finished work, not by trying to earn God's favour.
📷 A FINAL WAKE-UP CALL TO THE LOST
You may have plans for tomorrow, dreams for the future, and ambitions you hope to accomplish. But have you considered where you will spend eternity?
The things of this world are temporary. Your achievements will not save you, your possessions cannot redeem you, and your good works cannot take away your sins.
Do not allow the distractions of this world to keep you from the truth that matters most.
The invitation of the Gospel is still being proclaimed. Jesus Christ has paid for your sins. Believe the Gospel and put your trust in Him.
YOUR LIFE ON EARTH IS TEMPORARY. ETERNITY IS FOREVER. YOUR SOUL MATTERS!

text:
The Pasta That Held a Town Together

A story about creamy shrimp pasta with cheeses and herbs

The Night the Lights Went Out
At 3:12 a.m., in the middle of the worst storm the town had seen in forty years, a stranger kicked open the door of a tiny kitchen and shouted: “Whatever you’re cooking, I will pay anything for it.”
Marta did not look up. She was standing over a wide skillet, wooden spoon in hand, a headlamp strapped to her forehead because the power had been dead for six hours. The only reason her stove worked at all was the old gas line her late husband had refused to remove during the renovation. “It’s only pasta,” she said.
“Lady,” the stranger said, water pouring off his yellow jacket, “I have not smelled anything that good since I was a kid.”
She finally turned. He was a lineman for the electric company, one of the crews that had been out in the wind since midnight, trying to climb poles that were swaying like reeds. His lips were blue. His hands shook. Behind him, in the dark street, other figures were moving toward the warm yellow square of her doorway, drawn the way moths are drawn to a lamp.
Marta looked at the skillet. Then she looked at the door. Then she did what she had done her whole life when too many people showed up hungry: she reached for more cream.
By sunrise, she would feed four hundred people from a kitchen built for twelve. By the end of that week, two brothers who had not spoken in nine years would share a table. A widower who had stopped eating would ask for a second plate. A girl who had lost everything would find a reason to stay in town. And the whole thing would start with a dish so simple that Marta herself could not explain why it worked.
Creamy pasta. Shrimp. Cheese. Herbs.
That was all.
But that night, in the dark, with the wind screaming against the shutters, that was everything.
The Recipe Nobody Wrote Down
Marta had learned the dish from her grandmother, though not in the way people learn recipes today. There was no paper, no measuring spoons, no photograph. There was a hand on her shoulder in a warm kitchen, and a voice that said: “Don’t rush the garlic. Garlic is shy. If you scare it, it turns bitter and never forgives you.”
Her grandmother had come from a fishing village where shrimp were pulled from the water in the morning and eaten by noon. She believed that good food was a conversation between three things: something from the sea, something from the field, and something from the cow. Shrimp, herbs, and cream. Everything else was decoration.
So Marta made it the way she was taught.
First, the shrimp. About four hundred and fifty grams, peeled, patted dry. “Wet shrimp steam,” her grandmother used to say. “Dry shrimp sing.” She seasoned them with salt, black pepper, and a generous pinch of smoked paprika, the kind that smelled like a campfire in the mountains. Then she seared them in a hot pan, just until they curled and turned pink at the edges, and set them aside. Not cooked through. Never cooked through. They would finish later, in the sauce, soaking up everything.
Then, in the same pan, in the glossy leftovers of the shrimp, she melted sixty grams of unsalted butter. Half a stalk of leek, sliced thin, went in first. Leeks are gentle. They do not bite back the way onions do. They melt, they sweeten, they perfume the butter until the whole kitchen smells like a Sunday. Two cloves of garlic followed, only for a moment, only until the scent bloomed. Half a teaspoon of thyme. Half a teaspoon of red pepper flakes, just enough to leave a small, warm glow at the back of the throat.
Then the cream. Three hundred and fifty milliliters, poured in slowly, whisked as it bubbled. A tablespoon of cream cheese went in next and dissolved into the sauce like snow into warm water, making it thick and velvet-smooth. Three tablespoons of grated parmesan followed, salty and sharp, tying everything together.
The pasta, precooked, three hundred grams of penne, went into the sauce to drink it in. The shrimp came back. A handful of halved cherry tomatoes tumbled in, bright and sweet, cutting through the richness. And last, a spoonful of chopped parsley, scattered like confetti.
That was it. Ten minutes of work and a lifetime of habit.
Marta never thought it was special. For thirty years she served it at her little restaurant, a place with eight tables and a hand-painted sign that said Cozinha da Marta because her family had come from Portugal and she refused to translate her own name. The tourists liked it. The locals liked it. But nobody wrote songs about it.
That changed on the night of the storm.

The First Hundred
The lineman’s name was Dariusz, and he sat at the corner table with a plate in front of him, staring at it as if it might disappear.
“Eat,” Marta said.
“I’m afraid to,” he admitted. “I’ve been awake for twenty hours. If this is a dream, I don’t want it to end.”
He took one bite. Marta watched his face. It was the face of a man being quietly, unexpectedly forgiven by the universe. The cream was warm. The shrimp were juicy, still carrying that faint smoky edge of paprika. The parmesan lingered. The thyme whispered. His shoulders, which had been up near his ears for hours, slowly dropped.
“Okay,” he said, in a small voice. “Okay. I can go back out there now.”
He ate the whole plate in under three minutes. Then he went to the door and shouted into the storm, to the crews working in the dark: “There is food! Real food! Come in! Ten minutes!”
They came in waves. Linemen first, then two paramedics who had been running from call to call without stopping. A couple of truck drivers stranded on the highway. A young family carrying a sleeping baby wrapped in three jackets, the mother’s eyes red from worry. An old woman with a flashlight in her teeth. A teenage boy who had walked two miles in the rain because his phone said there was a shelter nearby, and nobody had the heart to tell him it was closed.
Marta’s kitchen had a single skillet big enough for the sauce. She worked it like a conductor. Shrimp in, shrimp out. Butter, leek, garlic, thyme, chili. Cream, cheese, pasta. Again. Again. Again. Her hands knew the rhythm so well that she stopped thinking, and when she stopped thinking, she started noticing.
She noticed that nobody spoke while they were eating. The restaurant, usually loud, was silent except for forks on plates and the howl of the wind outside. It was the silence of people who had been holding their breath for a very long time and were finally, finally exhaling.
She noticed that the baby woke up and the mother, without thinking, offered the child a tiny taste of cream sauce on her fingertip. The baby smiled. The mother burst into tears, and the paramedic sitting next to her, a woman twice her age, simply put an arm around her and said nothing.
She noticed that strangers began passing plates to one another. A trucker handed his second helping to the teenage boy without a word. The old woman divided her portion into three and shared it with people who had not yet been served.
Around 4 a.m., Dariusz came back in, soaked again, and set a car battery on the counter. “For your fridge,” he said. “So the shrimp don’t spoil.”
“You don’t have to do that.”
“Lady,” he said, “you just told a hundred people that the night is survivable. I’d say I owe you a battery.”
Marta laughed, and then, to her own surprise, she cried a little, right there over the skillet, and the tears went into the cream and no one ever knew.
4. The Brothers at Table Nine
By morning the storm had softened into a grey, dripping drizzle. The power was still out across half the town, and the restaurant was still full. Word travels quickly when there is hot food in a cold place, and people kept arriving from farther and farther away.
Around seven, two men came in separately, a minute apart, each carrying a bag of groceries from his own half-empty kitchen. One was big and silver-haired, with the careful posture of a man who sat behind a desk. The other was thinner, weathered, with sawdust still clinging to his sleeves. They were Henryk and Tomasz Vilar, owners of the two competing hardware stores on opposite sides of the main square.
Everyone in town knew the story, or thought they did. Nine years earlier their father had died and left one store to be shared between them. Within a year, they had split it in two. Within two years, they had stopped speaking. The reasons had grown so tangled that neither brother could have explained them anymore. A loan. A comment at a funeral. A missed phone call. A lawsuit that went nowhere. Pride, mostly, which is a heavy thing to carry for nine years.
They saw each other at the door. Both froze.
“I brought candles,” said Henryk, holding up his bag stiffly.
“I brought flour,” said Tomasz. “And eggs.”
There was a long, awful silence. The room watched.
Marta, sensing a disaster, did the only thing she could think of. She pointed at Table Nine, the one by the window, the only table with two empty chairs left, and said: “Sit. Both of you. It’s the last seat in the house.”
They sat. Not because they wanted to. Because it is very hard to refuse a seventy-year-old woman holding a wooden spoon.
She brought them two plates of the pasta, steam rising in curls, a few cherry tomatoes glowing red against the creamy white sauce, parsley bright as new grass. Neither brother touched it.
“Our mother used to make something like this,” Tomasz said finally, quietly, to nobody in particular.
Henryk looked up. “She did,” he said. “With the little shrimp. On Sundays.”
“You used to steal the parmesan from the grater.”
“You used to steal the parmesan. I took the blame.”
Tomasz’s mouth twitched. “That’s a lie.”
“It’s not a lie. I was nine. I got grounded for a week.”
Something in the room shifted. Marta, pretending to wipe the next table, held perfectly still.
They both picked up their forks at the same moment, as if by agreement. They ate slowly. Between bites, they spoke in short, awkward sentences about nothing: the roof of the hardware store that had probably leaked, the dog that had died last spring, the way their mother used to hum while she cooked. There was no apology. Not yet. Apologies are for another day, for days when the lights are on and the hands do not shake.
But when they stood up to leave, Henryk laid his hand, only for a second, on his brother’s shoulder. Tomasz did not pull away.
“Tell your wife,” Henryk said, voice rough, “that I have a generator. If your freezer needs it.”
“Tell yours,” said Tomasz, “that I have a truck, if she needs the roof fixed.”
It was not a reconciliation. Not yet. But it was a door, opened a crack, after nine years of slammed ones. And it had been opened by cream, shrimp, and a little bit of thyme.
5. The Girl Who Was Going to Leave
On the second day, a girl named Lucia came to the back door asking if the restaurant needed dishwashers.
She was nineteen, thin, with a backpack that looked far too heavy for her shoulders. She had arrived in town three weeks earlier, on a bus, with a plan that had since fallen apart: a job at a factory that had closed before she even started, a room she could no longer afford, a phone with a cracked screen and a battery that wouldn’t hold a charge. She had been sleeping in the bus station and eating crackers from a vending machine.
Marta looked at her for exactly four seconds.
“Have you eaten?”
“I’m fine.”
“That was not the question.”
Lucia hesitated. “Not since yesterday.”
Marta did not say anything. She simply pulled out a chair, pushed a plate of the creamy shrimp pasta in front of the girl, and went back to the stove. When she glanced over a minute later, Lucia was crying silently while she ate, wiping her face with the back of her sleeve, shoveling pasta into her mouth like it was the first warm thing she had ever been given.
“It’s only food,” Lucia whispered, apologizing.
“No,” said Marta. “It’s never only food.”
She put Lucia to work that afternoon. Not because she needed help, though she did, but because she understood something about hunger that went beyond the stomach. There is a hunger for warmth, and a hunger for usefulness, and a hunger for someone to look at you and say: you belong here, at least until the dishes are done.
Lucia learned fast. She learned to dry the shrimp before searing, how to slice a leek so it melted instead of burning, why you must never let garlic brown. She learned that the cream cheese goes in after the cream, never before, and that one spoonful is enough to turn a good sauce into a magical one. She learned to taste constantly. She learned to love the sound of the pan.
By the end of the week, the power was back on, but the line outside the restaurant had not shrunk. If anything, it had grown. People who had eaten the pasta that night had told others, and those others had told others, and soon Cozinha da Marta was the only place in three counties where you could get a plate of something that tasted, as one customer put it, “like being hugged by a very good-looking cow.”
Marta was seventy-one. Her knees hurt. Her husband had been gone for six years, and the kitchen had been quiet for most of them. She had been thinking, quietly, about closing.
One evening, as they scrubbed the last pan together, she said to Lucia: “I’m too old to run this place alone.”
“I know,” said Lucia.
“I’m not asking you to stay.”
“I know.”
“But if you wanted to, there’s a room upstairs. It’s small. It has a window that sticks.”
Lucia did not answer for a long time. When she did, her voice was very small. “Nobody’s ever offered me a room before. Not one that was warm.”
“Then it’s about time,” said Marta, and handed her the dish towel.
6. The Old Man Who Stopped Eating
In the third week, a woman named Ilse came into the restaurant and sat at the counter with her hands folded. She did not order. She just sat and stared, and after a long while, she said: “It’s my father.”
Her father was Anselm, eighty-three years old, a retired ship’s engineer who had lost his wife in the spring. Since the funeral, he had been fading. Not sick, exactly. Not in any way a doctor could name. He simply wasn’t hungry, anymore. He would push food around his plate. He would say he’d already eaten. He drank tea, sometimes, and that was all. Ilse had cooked for him every night for months: soups, stews, his favorite roasted chicken. Nothing worked. He grew thinner. His clothes began to hang on him like borrowed coats.
“I heard,” she said, awkwardly, “that people have been … that your pasta …” She trailed off, embarrassed. “It sounds ridiculous.”
“It sounds like a woman who loves her father,” said Marta. “Sit. Wait.”
She cooked it carefully, the way her grandmother had taught her. She seasoned the shrimp, seared them just until pink, and set them aside. She melted the butter, sweated the leek, bloomed the garlic, added the thyme and the pepper flakes. She poured the cream, whisked in the cream cheese, stirred in the parmesan, folded in the pasta, and returned the shrimp. She tossed in the tomatoes. She finished it with parsley. Then she packed it in a container, still warm, and handed it to Ilse.
“Don’t reheat it in the microwave,” she said. “Use a pan, a little splash of milk. And sit with him while he eats. Don’t watch. Just sit.”
Ilse did as instructed. That evening, in her father’s quiet kitchen, she warmed the pasta in a pan and set it down in front of him, then sat across the table and pretended to read a magazine.
Anselm looked at the plate for a long moment.
“What is this?” he asked.
“Pasta. With shrimp.”
“Hm.” He picked up the fork. He took a small bite, almost out of politeness. And then he stopped, fork frozen in the air.
Ilse held her breath.
“Your mother,” he said slowly, “used to make something like this. For our anniversary. In the little apartment, in Gdynia. We didn’t have any money, and she bought four shrimp and made them stretch for two people. She said it was a feast.”
“Dad …”
“It was a feast,” he said, his voice cracking. “I never told her that. I never told her it was the best meal of my life.”
He ate the entire plate, slowly, tears running down his weathered cheeks, and Ilse sat across from him and did not say a word, just as she’d been told. When he finished, he leaned back, and for the first time in months, there was something alive behind his eyes.
“Is there more?” he asked.
There was. There was a second plate, and a third the next day, and a fourth the day after that. Not every meal after that was easy. Grief does not disappear because of cream and parmesan. But Anselm began to eat. Then he began to talk. Then, one rainy Thursday, he put on his old captain’s cap and walked all the way to Cozinha da Marta by himself.
He stood in the doorway, a little unsteady, and said to the woman at the stove: “I would like to meet the person who cooked for my wife.”
“I never cooked for your wife,” said Marta gently.
“You did,” said Anselm. “You just didn’t know it.”
And that was how Marta gained a new regular, who ate at the counter every Thursday for six years and always, always ordered the same thing.
7. What Spread Through the Town
It is difficult to explain what happened next, because it was not a miracle, and nobody would have called it one. Nothing dramatic occurred. No headlines were written. The pasta did not cure anything or fix anyone.
It simply began to appear in places where kindness had gone missing.
The volunteer firefighters began cooking it on Friday nights, in a huge pot at the station, for anyone who wanted to drop in. It started as a joke, and ended as a tradition. The paramedics took a batch to the night-shift nurses at the hospital. A schoolteacher made it for her class on the last day before winter break and told the children, “This is what it means to feed someone you care about.” The two Vilar brothers, who had finally, awkwardly, begun to talk again, started a monthly dinner at which each of them had to bring one ingredient and neither was allowed to bring a grudge.
The local newspaper wrote a small article, buried on page eleven, about a restaurant that had stayed open through the storm. Someone clipped it and pinned it to a corkboard at the library. Someone else posted a photo of the dish online, a plain shot of a steaming plate under a kitchen light, and wrote underneath: This saved my week. Recipe in the comments.
Marta, who did not own a smartphone, would never see it. But Lucia did, and she read the comments aloud to Marta in the kitchen one evening, scrolling slowly.
Made this for my mom after her surgery. She cried.
I cooked this for my husband on our tenth anniversary. We were fighting. We’re not anymore.
First meal I ever cooked on my own after leaving home. I ate it on the floor of my empty apartment and felt like an adult.
Made this for my neighbor who just lost her dog. Didn’t know what else to do.
My son won’t eat anything except chicken nuggets. He asked for seconds of this. Seconds!
Cooked it for the first time after my divorce. It was the first thing I made that I wasn’t ashamed to eat.
Marta listened without speaking. When Lucia finished, the kitchen was quiet for a while, except for the soft tick of the cooling stove.
“I didn’t invent anything,” Marta said at last. “It’s my grandmother’s dish. And hers before her. It’s just shrimp and cream.”
“Maybe that’s the point,” said Lucia.
“What do you mean?”
“Maybe people don’t need something fancy. Maybe they just need something warm, made on purpose, by someone who’s paying attention.” She shrugged, a little shyly. “That’s all you ever did. You paid attention.”
Marta looked at the girl who had come to her back door with a heavy backpack and an empty stomach, who now ran the line like a veteran, who sang under her breath while she seared the shrimp, who had once said she was going to leave and never had.
“When did you get so wise?” Marta asked.
“I had a good teacher,” said Lucia. “She said garlic is shy.”
Marta laughed, loudly, the way she had not laughed in years.
8. Why It Works
People have asked Marta, over the years, what the secret is. Journalists, curious cooks, a television producer who once offered her a lot of money to “bottle the magic.” They wanted the trick. They wanted the thing she did differently.
She always gave them the same answer, and they never believed her.
“Dry your shrimp,” she would say. “Season them with salt, pepper, and smoked paprika, and do not overcook them. Sear them quickly and let them finish in the sauce. Use real butter. Cook the leek until it’s soft, not brown. Add the garlic last, and only for a moment. A little thyme. A little chili, just to wake things up. Pour in the cream, stir in a spoonful of cream cheese, and let the parmesan melt slowly. Toss in the pasta, whatever kind you have. Add tomatoes for brightness. Finish with parsley. Taste. Adjust. Serve it hot.”
“But what’s the secret?” they would ask.
And she would look at them with eyes that had seen a storm, a feud, a lost girl, and a grieving man, and say: “Make it for someone.”
That was the secret. Not the paprika, not the thyme, not the cheese, though all of them mattered. The secret was the person on the other side of the plate. The recipe worked because it was never really about the recipe. It was about the moment when somebody, tired, cold, afraid, or lonely, put down their bag and picked up a fork, and for ten minutes, the world stopped being so hard.
A plate of pasta cannot fix a broken heart. It cannot mend a family or end a war. But it can say: You are not alone https://t.co/C6ulPIfdov can say: Someone thought of you. It can say: Sit. Eat. It will be okay.
And sometimes, on the longest nights, that is exactly enough.
9. Epilogue: The Yellow Jacket
The following winter, a storm came through again. Smaller, this time, but with enough wind to knock out the lights on the north side of town.
At 2 a.m., Marta, now seventy-two, was asleep upstairs when she heard a sound from below: the clink of a pan, the hiss of butter, the unmistakable smell of leeks softening in the dark. She put on her robe and crept down the stairs.
The kitchen was lit by a single headlamp. At the stove stood Lucia, wooden spoon in hand, shrimp already seasoned and waiting in a bowl. Beside her stood Dariusz the lineman, in his yellow jacket, slicing cherry tomatoes with surprising delicacy. At a small table sat Henryk and Tomasz Vilar, arguing amiably about whose turn it was to bring the candles. Anselm, in his captain’s cap, was folding napkins and humming an old sailor’s song.
None of them had been asked. None of them had been told. They had simply seen the dark windows, felt the wind, and thought: Marta’s kitchen.
Lucia looked up and saw her standing there.
“Go back to bed,” she said, grinning. “We’ve got this.”
Marta did not go back to bed. She sat down at Table Nine, by the window, and watched. She watched her recipe, the one nobody ever wrote down, move through six pairs of hands. She watched the cream bubble. She watched the parmesan melt. She watched the shrimp curl pink in the pan, and the first cold, tired figures appear at the door, shaking the rain from their coats, their faces already lifting at the smell.
“Welcome,” Lucia called to them. “Sit anywhere. There’s plenty.”
And there was. There always was.
Because the best recipes are not the ones you keep. They are the ones that keep on feeding people long after you’ve stopped cooking.
Now go cook it for someone. Season the shrimp with salt, pepper and smoked paprika. Melt the butter, soften the leek, bloom the garlic. Add thyme, chili flakes, cream, a spoon of cream cheese, parmesan. Fold in the pasta and the shrimp, scatter tomatoes and parsley. And remember: it was never only food. #Cooking #pastacooking

text:
#PoeVive 

This morning, I woke up smiling. Perhaps you'd been there in that little space between sleep and waking, where I can still turn towards you without remembering the distance.

I wish you could have seen yourself, half asleep, trying to pull me closer while I told you something terribly important.

Listen to me, I'd whisper.

I'm listening, love, you'd mumble, eyes still closed.

And I'd laugh, knowing you'd ask me to repeat every word.

By morning, I've told you three things, argued with you twice, and forgiven you for something you haven't even done. Our conversation is already well underway.

Later, something happens, and you're the first person I want to tell. I've forgotten what it was, but I remember smiling. You know what?— the words almost reach my lips before the silence catches them.

Funny how I still turn to you, even for the smallest things.

You're doing it again, you'd say if you were here.

Doing what?

Thinking about me.

I'd pretend to consider it.

Well, whose fault is that?

I can almost hear you laugh.

By afternoon, the light has shifted. My hand reaches across the little space beside me, meeting only the rumpled sheet. For a moment, I imagine your fingers finding mine, your head tilting as you catch the words I'm keeping to myself.

Oh, to look up mid-sentence and find your eyes waiting for mine. To tell you something utterly ordinary and watch you make a moment of it.

The afternoon slips away. I keep saving little things for you.

By evening, I'm telling you about my day. You offer some infuriating opinion; I disagree, naturally. Somewhere between my argument and your imaginary reply, I find myself smiling at the empty room.

Tell me, love, when did you become so familiar to my solitude?

When did my thoughts begin to sound like you? I can't remember. Only that even my silences seem to know what to say to you.

Night comes softly. I draw the covers around me and leave a little space for the impossible.

What are you thinking? you'd ask.

You.

Again?

Always finding new reasons.

I'd smile into the darkness and let the rest remain unsaid.

That's how I miss you...

In the little things I turn to tell you,
in the smile that comes before I know why.

The quiet beneath my days,
the second skin I only notice
when the world grows still.

Tomorrow, I'll wake and turn towards that familiar space beside me. Perhaps I'll have something to tell you. Perhaps I'll simply smile.

And somewhere, a conversation will begin again.

Goodnight, my love.

There's something I forgot to tell you today.

I'll tell you tomorrow.

      ♡♡

A Day with You

text:
I Write the Letters That Tell Congress Its Job Is a Crime.

I'm an associate counsel in the White House Counsel's Office. Most lawyers respond to subpoenas. I respond to subpoenas that don't exist yet. The new Congress isn't sworn in until January. We have already objected.

On Monday our office sent a letter to Robert Garcia, the top Democrat on the House Oversight Committee and its likely next chairman. Garcia had spent election week telling administration officials to "lawyer up." He seemed to think that was a threat. We are the lawyers. We were already up.

The letter's best sentence took me 3 drafts: "threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality."

Look at the word "may." "May" is the most useful word in American law. It lets you call someone a criminal without becoming a defendant. Notice also "blatant." If it were blatant, we wouldn't have needed "may." The 2 words cancel each other out, and what's left is the feeling. The feeling is what we send.

There's a second sentence I'm proud of: "issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation." We are investigating the investigation before it starts. In my field this is called getting ahead of the story. In physics it's called time travel. Both are easier with letterhead.

Then the closing: "The administration will not be extorted and will not be cowed by unlawful process motivated by animus, pettiness, hatred, or any other unlawful motive." I fought for "pettiness." My colleagues said it isn't a crime. I said that's what makes it beautiful. Once you've listed pettiness as an unlawful motive, every subpoena that arrives in January is evidence of a crime, and every follow-up question is a second count.

Garcia replied that "it appears Donald Trump has something to hide" and that Congress doesn't need the "permission of the White House." He's right about the permission. We never offered it. You can't revoke what you never granted. That's the elegance of the format.

Mark DeSaulnier, likely the next Ethics chairman, said: "I don't work for a mafia, a mob organization." Neither do I. The mob never put a threat on letterhead. We have a seal. That's the whole difference between organized crime and organized government, and it's embossed.

Now the awkward part. Article I, Section 6 of the Constitution says that for "any Speech or Debate in either House," members of Congress "shall not be questioned in any other Place." Courts have read that to cover hearings and investigations. So our letter questions Congress, from another place, about its speech and debate. I've read the clause many times. It doesn't say anything about letters. It also doesn't need to. The letter was never meant to win in court. A court is where you go when you want a ruling. We wanted a headline.

The same section protects members from arrest "in going to and returning from" the Capitol. The founders thought of everything. They didn't think of a bus. On Tuesday several Democrats missed the Hegseth vote when a police escort for the incoming class's buses blocked their way. No one was arrested. No one had to be. That's the most efficient enforcement of executive privilege I've ever seen, and I'd like it in my file.

The same day, a colleague of ours, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, sent a letter to Senator Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, who has been asking corporate donors about the White House ballroom. The letter told the senator to preserve his documents. A federal prosecutor in Houston has written to a senator from Connecticut about a ballroom in Washington. Jurisdiction is a state of mind.

I want you to appreciate the irony that everyone else has missed. The Interior Department recently called reports of missing construction records "100% false." The executive branch keeps its own paperwork on a retention schedule. We asked the Senate to keep everything.

Blumenthal answered that night. He said we were "weaponizing the Department of Justice to baselessly target Congress in direct violation of the Constitution." Then he did something I didn't expect. He sent a preservation demand back: "I accordingly direct you to preserve all records and correspondence, including all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter."

So 2 branches of the United States government are now ordering each other to save paper. The National Archives has never been so popular. It's a preservation standoff. Whoever deletes first loses.

The Pentagon, for its part, told reporters before the Secretary's briefing on Tuesday that they'd be "physically removed" if they "get out of line." Different agency, same sentence. They say it in the Defense dialect. We say it in Counsel's. It translates beautifully: you may ask your question, and we may decide your question was a crime.

People ask whether this is the plan for the next 2 years. There is no plan. There is a sequence. First you call the oversight a crime. Then the oversight arrives, which proves you were right to be afraid of it. Every subpoena becomes a sequel. Every hearing becomes the persecution we predicted. We're writing the investigation's reviews before it opens.

Blumenthal wants every record related to "the decision to draft and post" our letters. I've searched. There's nothing to preserve. The decision wasn't made in writing. It was made in a mood. Moods have no retention schedule.

I have, however, placed the letter itself under a litigation hold. It's the only document in this building we're certain we'll want later. It's dated November 9. The new Congress arrives January 3.

In Washington, the first man to file the grievance gets to be the victim. We filed 55 days early.

text:
THEY STOOD ON GUARD

NOVEMBER 12, 1944

John Brine Johnson: A Young Airman Who Never Came Home

He was just 21 years old, a young Canadian airman who had left behind his family, his hometown and the promise of an ordinary life to serve his country during the Second World War.

Flying Officer John Brine Johnson was born on April 21, 1923, in Sarnia, Ontario, the son of John Francis Johnson and Blanche Brine Johnson.

Growing up in Ontario, he attended Kimberley Public School and Malvern Collegiate. His family had connections to Milliken and Agincourt, communities that were then far removed from the sprawling Toronto suburbs of today.

Before joining the military, Johnson worked as a clerk with General Motors Acceptance Corporation. His employment records described his duties as payment bookkeeping.

He enjoyed swimming, boxing, badminton and skating. His military application also listed carpentry among his interests.

These small details, preserved in his own handwriting, offer a glimpse of the young man behind the uniform.

On November 8, 1942, Johnson enlisted in the Royal Canadian Air Force.

After completing his training, he graduated from Hagersville in May 1943 and proceeded overseas.

He eventually served with No. 159 Squadron of the Royal Air Force, a bomber unit operating Consolidated B-24 Liberators in the Far East.

From bases in India, the squadron carried out dangerous long-range operations against Japanese-held territory, including bombing, reconnaissance and aerial mine-laying missions.

On November 12, 1944, Flying Officer John Brine Johnson was lost during overseas operations.

He was 21 years old.

A newspaper back home reported that the young airman from Agincourt had been declared missing. His parents, John and Blanche Johnson, had received the news every wartime family dreaded.

For Johnson, there would be no homecoming.

His remains were never recovered or identified, and today his name is commemorated on Column 442 of the Singapore Memorial, among thousands of Commonwealth servicemen who have no known grave.

His name also appears on Page 346 of Canada’s Second World War Book of Remembrance.

Eighty-two years later, the surviving photographs, handwritten service papers and newspaper clippings remind us that behind every name on a war memorial was a person with a family, a home and a future.

Flying Officer John Brine Johnson gave his life at 21.

He deserves to be remembered.

Source: Veterans Affairs Canada, Canadian Virtual War Memorial; RCAF service records and contemporary newspaper clippings.

The Dragon Challenge was hosted by the 18th Air Support Operations Group with the support of the 818th Operations Support Squadron at Pope. The competition began in 1999 as a means to push the best Airmen from each squadron to compete, improve and bring new skills back to their units.

text:
Chizarira National Park, Zimbabwe🇿🇼

Located in northwestern Zimbabwe, Chizarira National Park is one of Africa’s most beautiful and remote wilderness destinations. Overlooking the spectacular Zambezi Valley, the park is known for its dramatic escarpments, deep gorges, rugged mountains and breathtaking natural scenery.

The park is home to diverse wildlife, including elephants, lions, leopards, buffalo, sable antelope and roan antelope. Its rich birdlife also makes it an excellent destination for birdwatching, with hundreds of recorded species.

For travellers seeking adventure, nature and an escape from crowded tourist destinations, Chizarira National Park offers an unforgettable opportunity to experience the wild beauty of Zimbabwe.

text:
Ramesses III Cartouche Discovered in Jordan

In 2025, a remarkable discovery that bridged the ancient lands of the Nile and the Levant was revealed, archaeologists in southern Jordan uncovered a hieroglyphic inscription bearing the royal cartouche of Pharaoh Ramesses III, who reigned from 1186-1155 B.C.

This is the first known instance of Ramesses III’s cartouche being found within the borders of modern Jordan, and it offers striking new insights into Egypt’s far-reaching influence during the twilight of the New Kingdom.

The inscription, carved into a rock face in the dramatic red sandstone landscapes of Wadi Rum, an area renowned for its ancient petroglyphs and prehistoric settlements, contains the throne and birth names of Ramesses III: “Usermaatre-Meryamun”.

These cartouches, emblematic of Pharaonic authority, suggest a royal presence or expedition, possibly military or diplomatic in nature, extending deep into the Arabian Peninsula’s northwestern corridor.

During the Late Bronze Age and into the Early Iron Age, the region now known as Jordan was home to a number of emerging cultural and tribal groups, including the Edomites, Moabites, and Ammonites. Prior to their ascendancy, this area was part of the broader sphere of Canaanite civilisation. Though politically fragmented, it was strategically positioned along key trade and migration routes linking Egypt to Mesopotamia and Arabia.

Ancient Egypt, particularly in the New Kingdom period, maintained intermittent contact with this region through military campaigns, tribute relations, and trade. Wadi Rum, near the modern border with Saudi Arabia, lies along one such historic corridor. It is entirely plausible that Egyptian expeditions, whether for conquest, resource extraction, or control of trade, reached into these territories, especially during the reigns of powerful warrior-pharaohs like Ramesses III.

text:
I texted the wrong number that I'd be eating a frozen pizza alone on Thanksgiving. By Thursday afternoon, 31 strangers had cooked me dinner, and my mom was walking through their front door.

The text was: "Sorry Mom, I can't make it home for Thanksgiving. I'll just eat a frozen pizza by myself this year."

I was 26, three months into a new job in Columbus, and too broke to fly home to Oregon. I'd stared at my phone for an hour trying to word that message without crying. When I finally sent it, I'd typed one digit of Mom's number wrong.

A reply came in under a minute. "I think you've got the wrong number, sweetheart. But I'm Frank, I'm 72, and my turkey has won awards at our church. Nobody eats frozen pizza on Thanksgiving. Come over."

I laughed, felt stupid, and told him no thanks. I wasn't going to a stranger's house.

He wrote back, "Fair enough. The offer stands. You can decide Thursday."

text:
Scientists discover that necks didn't evolve for the reason we thought | Penn State, ScienceDaily

The first animals to make the transition from water to land nearly 380 million years ago may have had a surprising limitation: they could barely turn their heads. Although scientists have long believed that the evolution of necks gave these pioneering creatures greater freedom to look around, new research suggests their necks were actually remarkably stiff.

The discovery challenges a decades-old explanation for why animals developed distinct necks in the first place. Rather than evolving to improve head movement, necks may have emerged as part of broader changes to the skeleton that allowed animals to use their front limbs for movement.

To investigate this possibility, an international team of researchers combined new fossil evidence with experiments on living fish and computer models of ancient anatomy. Their findings, published October 14 in the journal Nature, offer a new perspective on one of the most important evolutionary transitions in Earth's history.

"This is a really interesting time in Earth's history where some of the first forests are forming, and there's a really radical reorganization of the Earth," said Tom Stewart, an assistant professor of biology at Penn State and a member of the research team. "So, understanding exactly when our lineage made that transition from water to land, how it was achieved, and which anatomical systems were changing is an important part of that story. What's cool is that many of the changes that were occurring in the skeleton at this time, about 380 million years ago, are still reflected in our own bodies today."

Why Scientists Thought Animals Evolved Necks

For decades, the prevailing explanation was that necks evolved to give early tetrapods, the ancestors of four-limbed vertebrates, greater control over their heads as they adapted to life outside the water.

The reasoning seemed straightforward. An animal living in shallow water or moving onto land would benefit from looking downward or turning its head from side to side to locate prey, recognize threats, and explore its surroundings. A flexible neck would allow it to do this without repositioning its entire body.

Modern fish generally lack a distinct neck because their shoulder structures connect directly to their skulls. To look in another direction, they typically have to turn their bodies instead. Separating the head from the shoulders therefore appeared to be an important step toward greater mobility.

However, determining how these ancient animals actually moved has been difficult. Much of their backbone consisted of soft tissue that rarely survives long enough to become fossilized, leaving scientists with an incomplete picture of how their necks functioned.

"The fish that were undergoing these changes had a vertebral column that was largely made up of soft tissue, which, unlike bone, is rarely preserved in the fossil record," Stewart said. "In these cases, we can look to modern animals to serve as analogues for the past, like how living birds can teach us about now extinct dinosaurs."

Ancient Fish Fossils Reveal a Turning Point in Evolution

Some of the best evidence for the transition from water to land comes from fish that lived during the Devonian Period, approximately 420 to 360 million years ago.

These ancient animals possessed an unusual combination of features. While they retained many characteristics of aquatic fish, some had stronger, more substantial fins that may have helped support their weight. Such adaptations could have allowed them to lift themselves off the bottom or push through shallow water.

At the same time, certain species began showing a clear separation between the skull and shoulders, creating the first distinct necks.

One especially important example is Tiktaalik, a fossil fish first described in 2006. Its remains were discovered on Ellesmere Island in Nunavut, Canada, in the northern Arctic. Because Tiktaalik is closely related to the earliest vertebrates with limbs, its anatomy provides valuable clues about the evolutionary changes that eventually made life on land possible.

"Tiktaalik is one of these fossil fish, and it was first described in 2006," Stewart said. "It has been reasonably assumed for decades that this separation of head and shoulders must have allowed the head to move more freely, so the hypothesis that neck mobility was an evolutionary driver for this change in the tetrapod body plan has prevailed, at least until now."

Tiktaalik also helps researchers understand other major changes that occurred during this evolutionary transition, including the shift from drawing food into the mouth through suction underwater to biting on land, as well as the gradual transformation of swimming structures into limbs used for walking.

"The materials have been really important because Tiktaalik is one of the closest relatives to limbed vertebrates," Stewart said. "It helps us to reconstruct a lot of intermediary steps in the transition to life on land, such as the move from suction feeding in water to biting on land or from swimming to walking."

How Modern Sturgeon Helped Solve an Ancient Mystery

The key to testing the traditional explanation for neck evolution came from an unexpected

Early tetrapods had backbones that were very different from those of most vertebrates living today. Instead of relying primarily on a series of large vertebrae connected by joints, their spinal columns contained a prominent structure called the notochord.

The notochord is a long, flexible rod of tissue that runs through the vertebral column and helps support the body. In these ancient animals, the individual vertebrae were relatively small and arranged around a much larger tube of soft tissue.

Because this arrangement responds to forces differently from a modern backbone, researchers had struggled to determine how much flexibility it would have allowed. That uncertainty prevented them from directly testing the idea that necks initially evolved to improve head movement.

Sturgeon provided an opportunity to overcome that problem. Although they are only distantly related to the ancient animals being studied, their backbones have a similar notochord structure.

The research team measured the stiffness and mechanical properties of the notochord in modern sturgeon. They then incorporated those measurements into models of fossil animals, including early tetrapods such as Tiktaalik, to estimate how far their necks could actually move.

The results were striking. Even when the head and shoulders were anatomically separated, the structure of the backbone would have severely restricted movement. The earliest necks appear to have been much less flexible than researchers had assumed.

"We know that tetrapods did eventually gain higher neck mobility," said Dana Korneisel, a postdoctoral researcher at Uppsala University in Sweden and first author of the paper. "Clearly it was advantageous eventually, but it was not an advantage available to these early tetrapods yet because of the limitations of their anatomy."

The First Necks Were Surprisingly Stiff

The researchers had expected the new models to clarify how much additional movement early necks provided. Instead, they found that most of the animals they examined would have gained little ability to reposition their heads.

"I undertook this study to find out how big of a difference this change in anatomy made for these animals," Korneisel said. "The vertebral columns of sturgeon are built a lot like those of early tetrapods, but they didn't seem terribly stiff. So, after doing the modeling, the lack of significant head mobility for almost all of these animals was a huge surprise."

The findings suggest that the first animals with distinct necks could not simply turn their heads to survey their surroundings the way many modern land animals can.

Their ability to lift their heads was also extremely limited, sometimes falling below what would be expected in fish.

"Head elevation in these animals was no more than what you would expect in fish and, sometimes, even less," Korneisel said. "We found that the kind of head twisting that we can do when we shake our heads was not feasible in any of these animals."

The researchers also cautioned that their estimates may actually overstate how much movement was possible.

Their models considered the mechanical properties of the backbone itself, but other structures would have added further restrictions. Muscles, skin, and even bones embedded within the skin of some early tetrapods may have made their necks still more rigid.

Necks May Have Evolved for Walking Before Looking

Together, the findings point to a different explanation for the origin of the neck.

Instead of first appearing because animals needed to turn their heads, the separation of the skull and shoulders may have developed alongside anatomical changes that allowed the front limbs to support and move the body.

In other words, the earliest necks may have been a consequence of adaptations for locomotion rather than an adaptation for improved vision or head movement.

Greater neck flexibility eventually evolved and became an important advantage for land vertebrates. But the new evidence suggests that this benefit came later, after the basic structure of the neck was already established.

The discovery also highlights the importance of the notochord in understanding animal evolution. Backbones dominated by this structure are uncommon among living vertebrates, but they were widespread during much of Earth's history. Studying modern animals that retain similar anatomy can therefore help scientists reconstruct how extinct creatures moved and behaved.

"We want to understand how these early tetrapods were living and how that is reflected in changes to their bodies," Stewart said. "Trying to reconstruct where an animal lived, how it moved, what its behavior was, is a really difficult thing. The cool part of this story is that it combines data from fossils and studies of living animals in a mechanical, functional perspective to reconstruct what the changes we see in the animal's anatomy mean for their behavior."

By bringing together fossil discoveries, experiments on living fish, and biomechanical modeling, the researchers have challenged a familiar explanation for an anatomical feature that remains central to the bodies of humans and many other vertebrates today.

text:
FLORIDA STATE’S NEXT HEAD COACH: FIVE CANDIDATES WHO COULD RESTORE THE SEMINOLES 🏈

With Mike Norvell’s firing, Florida State faces a defining moment. The Seminoles need a program builder who can restore accountability, rebuild the roster, recruit elite talent, and return FSU to national championship contention.

Five candidates offer distinctly different approaches:

1. Manny Diaz (Duke)

Proven Credentials: Diaz is 25–11 at Duke and led the Blue Devils to the 2025 ACC Championship. A 1995 FSU graduate, he began his coaching career as a Seminoles graduate assistant under Bobby Bowden and Mickey Andrews.

Projected Fit: Diaz offers the strongest combination of FSU roots, Florida recruiting connections, defensive expertise, and proven ACC success. He’s demonstrated he can win without elite recruiting resources.

2. Jake Dickert (Wake Forest)

Proven Credentials: Dickert went 9–4 in his first season at Wake Forest in 2025 and has followed it with an 8–1 start in 2026. Previously, he built a competitive Washington State program despite resource limitations.

Projected Fit: Dickert emphasizes defensive toughness, discipline, player development, and maximizing talent. He offers a potentially high-floor option for restoring accountability and stability.

3. Kenny Dillingham (Arizona State)

Proven Credentials: Dillingham served as FSU’s offensive coordinator from 2020–21 before taking over at Arizona State. He engineered an 11–3 turnaround in 2024, winning the Big 12 Championship and reaching the College Football Playoff.

Projected Fit: His offensive innovation, quarterback development, and firsthand knowledge of Florida State make him intriguing. He understands Tallahassee, the recruiting landscape, and the expectations surrounding the program.

4. Rhett Lashlee (SMU)

Proven Credentials: Lashlee guided SMU to an 11–3 record, an ACC Championship Game appearance, and a College Football Playoff berth in 2024. The Mustangs followed with another winning season in 2025.

Projected Fit: Lashlee brings offensive creativity, quarterback development, and ACC experience. His ability to build explosive offenses could help Florida State rediscover its offensive identity.

5. Jason Eck (New Mexico)

Proven Credentials: Eck built Idaho into an FCS contender, improving its record in each of his three seasons and reaching the playoffs every year. He then led New Mexico to a 9–4 record in 2025.

Projected Fit: Eck represents the unconventional program-builder option. His emphasis on physicality, discipline, and player development could provide the cultural overhaul Florida State needs. His lack of Power Four head coaching experience remains a consideration.

THE BOTTOM LINE

Florida State doesn’t need a celebrity hire or another expensive gamble based on reputation. It needs a leader with a clear vision, an outstanding staff, recruiting ability, player-development expertise, and the discipline to build a sustainable winner.

Diaz offers institutional familiarity. Dickert brings defensive toughness. Dillingham provides offensive innovation. Lashlee brings proven offensive production. Eck offers a culture-first rebuilding approach.

There is no risk-free candidate. The right hire must restore the standard, rebuild the culture, and make the Seminoles a legitimate national championship contender again.

text:
Fictional Obituary: Jonathan Kent (Absolute Superman comic spoilers)

Jonathan Kent, the Smallville farmer who shared his home with his wife, Martha, and briefly gave refuge to Kal-El, is remembered for the welcome he offered a young stranger far from home.

Kal arrived at the Kent farm as a teenager. Jonathan and Martha met him after he had already known his own family and suffered the loss of his world. They offered him a place in theirs. The time they shared was short, but it was long enough for the possibility of becoming a family to matter to all of them.

Their home became dangerous when the Peacemakers came looking for Kal. Jonathan and Martha understood the threat and urged him to escape. Letting him go meant losing the future they had begun to imagine together, but his safety came first.

Jonathan died before Kal could return openly to that life. Martha outlived him, carrying her own memories of the young man they had welcomed and continuing to think of him as their son.

His place in Kal’s life rests on ordinary acts of care performed under extraordinary circumstances: making room for someone, offering safety, and protecting him when that welcome brought danger to the door. The life they might have shared was interrupted. The kindness Jonathan had already shown remained.

Most companies hire salespeople the way they hire everyone else. Here is the seven-step process built for sales.

I've spent 33 years working with sales teams. Here's the innovative hiring model built exclusively for hiring superior sales talent.

1. Establish the standards for an A-Player. List the must-avoid weaknesses and the must-have strengths.

2. Search: describe the person, not the position.

3. Assess every candidate before reviewing a single resume. Every applicant's hidden weaknesses and strengths surface. Resumes never reveal them.

4. Conduct a 20-minute screen with only A players.

5. Conduct structured audition interviews, applying questions built from the assessment.

6. Get a decision for a decision. Before the final interview, ask candidates if they are in a position to accept an offer, if made. It surfaces other obstacles, so you can adapt accordingly.

7. Close the deal and onboard using a structure specifically for sales.

Rules for the HR team:

1. Do not recruit salespeople with the same process as other candidates. Test first for courage, resilience, rejection tolerance and the other distress factors.

2. Past sales success does not predict future success. Learn how a candidate accomplished success, and critically assess that.

3. Make a list of must-avoid weaknesses. Set the floor.

4. Make the search a competition. Give candidates obstacles to defeat. The best will relish the contest.

Great salespeople are not hard to find. They are findable applying the right method.

text:
Mike Macdonald was making $450 a month in college football when KPMG offered him $60,000 a year. He said yes. He never started, and in February he won the Super Bowl as head coach of the Seahawks.

At Georgia they told him he could volunteer on staff if he got into grad school. Admissions had already closed, so he went down to the graduate office: "I have to get in." He was ready to take out a $20,000 loan for it. If it didn't work out, he says, he'd just go get a job.

Four years later his old boss, now at Louisville, offered him another GA job. He'd had a couple of beers that night and his answer was "no, screw you." He admits now it was probably a pretty good offer.

So he took KPMG and figured "it's time to get out of football." Then John Harbaugh called from the Ravens.

What stands out to me is the KPMG offer. He wasn't stuck at $450, he had a real job waiting, and I think that's why he could say no.
