text:
AUDI'S $7 BILLION AMERICAN BET: Trump's tariffs are bringing German luxury cars to Georgia | Lauren Fix, Blaze Media

German luxury automaker Audi is preparing to build cars in America for the first time, and its investment could reach $7 billion.

Last month, Audi announced plans for a $4 billion manufacturing plant in Georgia that would employ approximately 4,500 workers and produce up to 200,000 vehicles annually. Now, documents obtained by the Atlanta Journal-Constitution reveal that the company is considering a second phase worth another $3 billion, potentially adding 3,000 jobs.

If Audi can sell a luxury SUV for $90,000, moving production to Georgia doesn't mean it will suddenly offer that vehicle for $80,000.

That would bring Audi's total investment to $7 billion and its workforce to 7,500, although the expansion remains a possibility, not a commitment. Even the original plant still awaits final corporate approval.

For an automaker that has spent decades selling German luxury cars to Americans without building a single one here, it's a major change. And President Donald Trump's tariffs are helping drive it.

The cost of importing cars

Until now, every Audi sold in the United States has been imported from factories in Europe or Mexico. But that business model has become considerably more expensive. According to Reuters, Trump's tariffs on vehicles, steel, aluminum, and parts cost Audi approximately $1.4 billion in 2025.

That's a substantial expense for a company competing against BMW and Mercedes-Benz, both of which already manufacture vehicles in the United States.

Building cars domestically would allow Audi to avoid tariffs on imported finished vehicles produced at its new factory. It would also give the company greater control over production costs and reduce its exposure to future trade disputes.

Audi isn't simply accepting the current tariffs while it builds a factory, however. The company is also negotiating with Washington for relief. Reuters reported October 29 that Audi wants the Trump administration to reduce the 15% tariff on European Union vehicle imports to 7.5%. Administration officials were reportedly considering a reduction to approximately 10% for automakers making substantial investments in American manufacturing.

In other words, Audi wants to make cars here while also paying less to import the ones it will continue building overseas.

The negotiations illustrate how tariffs are reshaping manufacturers' decisions. Imported cars have become more expensive, while companies willing to invest in American factories may qualify for favorable treatment.

Audi's investment is a particularly striking example.

Why Georgia?

The new factory will occupy the Middle Georgia Mega Site in Peach County, near Macon. Audi plans to begin site work in 2027, with full production projected for 2031.

The plant is expected to manufacture premium SUVs designed for the American market. Audi has not announced specific models, but the emphasis on SUVs makes sense. American buyers continue to favor larger vehicles, particularly in the luxury market, and Audi has been looking to strengthen its position against BMW and Mercedes-Benz.

Georgia also has something Audi needs: an established automotive manufacturing industry.

BMW builds SUVs in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes-Benz has manufactured vehicles in Alabama for decades. Closer to Audi's proposed factory, Kia operates a plant in West Point, Georgia, while Hyundai has invested billions in its own Georgia manufacturing operations.

Those companies have helped create a network of suppliers, skilled workers, and transportation infrastructure that Audi can now draw upon.

Georgia is also offering substantial financial incentives.

According to the Atlanta Journal-Constitution, state and local officials proposed at least $958 million in tax breaks, grants, and other support for the first phase. That includes approximately $459 million in property tax savings over 20 years, along with investments in roads, utilities, site preparation, and workforce training.

Those incentives are a significant public expense. Georgia is betting that thousands of jobs, new suppliers, and decades of economic activity will justify the investment.

Will American buyers pay less?

For consumers, the most immediate question is whether building Audis in America will make them more affordable.

The answer depends on what Audi does with the savings.

When an automaker imports a vehicle, tariffs increase the cost of bringing it into the country. The manufacturer can absorb that expense, raise the sticker price, reduce discounts and incentives, or combine those approaches. The customer can end up paying more even when the manufacturer's suggested retail price doesn't change.

Building vehicles in the United States removes the tariff on the imported finished car. That gives Audi more room to compete on price, but it doesn't require the company to pass those savings along to buyers.

And even an American-built Audi won't necessarily be free of tariff-related costs. Imported engines, electronics, transmissions, and other components may still be subject to duties.

There's another consideration. Automakers don't necessarily price vehicles according to what they cost to manufacture. They price them according to what customers are willing to pay and what competing brands charge. If Audi can sell a luxury SUV for $90,000, moving production to Georgia doesn't mean it will suddenly offer that vehicle for $80,000.

What domestic production could do is help Audi hold prices steady, offer more competitive financing or incentives, and protect its margins without making customers absorb every increase in import costs. The company would also have more flexibility to build vehicles specifically for American buyers.

For someone shopping for a new Audi today, however, none of this will change the price at the dealership tomorrow. The first American-built vehicles are still years away.

A long-term American commitment

Audi's announcement came during an October 24 campaign rally in Perry, Georgia, where Trump appeared alongside company CEO Gernot Döllner.

Trump celebrated the project as evidence that his trade policies were bringing manufacturing investment to the United States.

Audi has been more cautious about the politics. In an October 26 statement, the company acknowledged concerns about its appearance with Trump but emphasized the economic reasons for building in America.

Audi also made an important admission: Its U.S. business is currently unprofitable. That puts the Georgia investment in perspective. Tariffs are an important factor, but Audi also needs to improve its American operations. Building vehicles closer to customers could help accomplish both goals.

text:
Suggestions on the Sustainable Development of the MSN Project— Focusing on Community Interaction and Player Base Expansion
Dear MSU Team Members and Fellow Long-term Players：

 Whether in Web2 or Web3, whether a game project can truly endure in the long run ultimately depends on whether it can form a stable small-scale society built on interpersonal interaction and mutual support. Technical architecture, economic models, and gameplay design are certainly important,but they can only generate continuous value and vitality when supported by a sufficient scale of real user participation. 

Without the flow and recognition of people, even the most refined product is prone to gradually falling into a state of “desertification.”

Let us use a simple analogy：

A well-crafted game that long lacks effective user growth and external communication is like a fine bottle of wine hidden deep in a cellar—only the owner and a few close friends know its taste. They may sincerely praise its quality and value, yet it remains difficult for a broader group to resonate with it. 

The outside world has neither experience nor awareness of it, so the so-called “preciousness” stays at the level of self-evaluation and struggles to transform into a consensus that can be jointly verified by a larger gaming community. This is one of the core contradictions currently facing MSN.

As players who have been deeply involved for more than two years, we clearly understand the project’s strengths and limitations. There is no overly burdensome daily task pressure, monetization is relatively restrained, the trading system is highly free, overall progression is newer compared with most similar servers, and the content has undergone targeted specialization. 

More importantly, measured by current token prices and entry costs, MSN indeed offers relatively high cost-effectiveness for those whose primary goal is pure entertainment—the same investment that can often only support a mid-to-upper-tier experience on other servers has the opportunity here to reach higher-level content.

These characteristics objectively exist and form the project’s differentiated foundation. However, if advantages cannot be seen and experienced by enough people, they are difficult to convert into a positive ecological cycle.

1、Clear supply-demand imbalance has already appeared within the server: players who want to buy equipment and items struggle to find suitable sellers, while those who want to sell assets lack sufficient buyers.
2、Insufficient liquidity directly constrains players’ long-term retention and willingness to reinvest. The root of this problem is not the design of any single economic model, but the fact that the overall user base has long failed to expand effectively.

I once had an experience with the MapleStory TMS mobile game:

At the time, I purchased an account for approximately RMB 10,000 and spent another RMB 10,000 on equipment. When adjusting the account or gear, I was often able to complete matching between buyers and sellers in a relatively short time. 

The logic behind this is not complicated: a sufficiently large player base makes value anchoring more transparent and price fluctuations relatively controllable; 

there are ample participants on both the supply and demand sides, so “where there is demand, there is production, and where there is production, more people can obtain what they need at a reasonable cost.” 

When I eventually left, the account as a whole still achieved a certain profit.

I am not citing this case primarily to emphasize the profit. What I want to say remains the same point: without people, nothing else matters. It must be people mutually recognizing and identifying with something. But when the population base is too small, recognition cannot take hold. 

Everyone understands the difference between riding a roller coaster alone and riding it with another person, right?
This case illustrates that the key variables determining asset liquidity and value stability have never been the labels of “Web2” or “Web3” themselves, but the number and activity level of real participants. 

People have always been the starting point of everything.
Therefore, if the project truly wishes to go further, progress must be advanced simultaneously on two levels:

First, strengthen in-depth communication with existing players. In addition to routine replies on social media, it is recommended to establish more systematic and direct communication mechanisms so that players can genuinely feel the team’s continuous investment and sincerity toward the project. Transparent information synchronization and responses to issues are themselves important supports for community confidence.

Second, substantive expansion of the user base must be treated as a priority. Relying solely on natural spread within the existing circle makes it difficult to break the current closed state.

Consideration can be given to targeted content placement and advertising on platforms such as YouTube, collaborations with creators or public figures who possess real influence, or in-depth linkages with Web3 communities that have a good atmosphere and higher user quality. 

The key is to choose channels that truly possess communication power and user foundations, rather than partnerships that appear lively on the surface but lack substantive effect.

Only when external users continue to enter can internal supply-demand relations possibly return to health, allowing trading, social interaction, and content experience to form a positive feedback loop. 

Ultimately, Web2 and Web3 are not a matter of superiority or inferiority, but choices under different stages and entry points.

What remains truly constant is human participation and recognition. Only when enough people are willing to enter, experience, interact, and stay will the project’s value move from the self-evaluation of a minority to a consensus that can be verified by a broader group.

 This is also the direction we, as long-term players, sincerely hope to see.

The above suggestions are proposed based on actual gameplay experience and are offered for the team’s reference. We look forward to more substantive communication and progress in the future.

text:
Paul Atreides didn’t simply forget that the Emperor had secretly helped destroy House Atreides. In fact, one of his earliest plans was to use that betrayal to bring Shaddam before the Landsraad and turn the Great Houses against him.

But there’s a fascinating detail in Frank Herbert’s original novel that changes how you understand Paul’s decision.

Before the fall of House Atreides, Paul actually asks Duke Leto why they can’t expose the Emperor to the Landsraad.

Leto explains the problem.

Shaddam would simply deny everything. The Sardaukar had been disguised in Harkonnen uniforms, making it difficult to prove that the Emperor had personally authorised the attack.

Exposing their suspicions without solid evidence would only warn Shaddam that the Atreides knew the truth. It could also create political chaos while giving their enemies time to prepare another attack.

But Paul doesn’t abandon the idea.

After escaping into the desert and joining the Fremen, he develops a plan that could finally give him the evidence he needs.

He tells Kynes that the Fremen might be able to provide proof that Sardaukar soldiers were operating in Harkonnen uniforms.

His intention is to let the Emperor become further entangled in the destruction of House Atreides, then present a formal case against him before the Landsraad.

And Paul’s reasoning is incredibly important.

The Great Houses are already terrified of the Emperor using his Sardaukar to eliminate powerful rivals one by one.

Paul understands that every House would see his father’s fate as a warning of what could happen to them.

As he explains, Arrakis could become a rallying cry. Every Great House would see itself in Duke Leto, a powerful ruler singled out and destroyed by the Emperor.

In other words, Paul wants to turn the destruction of House Atreides into a political crisis that threatens the entire Imperial system.

But there’s a problem.

Kynes warns him that even if the Landsraad accepts the case, the likely result would be general warfare between the Imperium and the Great Houses.

Paul knows this is a dangerous gamble, but he believes he can offer the Emperor another option: surrender political power and avoid the destruction of the Imperium.

And then the situation changes.

Paul gains control of the Fremen, becomes the leader of an army capable of defeating the Sardaukar, and discovers the ultimate leverage over the entire civilisation: spice.

The Spacing Guild cannot risk losing its supply. Without spice, its Navigators cannot safely guide interstellar travel.

So instead of depending entirely on the Landsraad to remove Shaddam, Paul threatens the one thing the Emperor and every Great House cannot afford to lose.

He forces the Guild to support his demands, makes Shaddam surrender the throne and marries Princess Irulan to secure his political claim.

But here’s the part people often overlook.

Taking the throne doesn’t mean the Great Houses accept him.

In the novel, they refuse to recognise his ascendancy, and Paul knows the Fremen Jihad is becoming impossible to stop. His victory over Shaddam has not united the Imperium behind him. It has created an even greater conflict.

The film makes this confrontation more direct, with Paul ordering the Fremen to attack the Great Houses after they reject him.

So Paul didn’t ignore the possibility of exposing Shaddam. He considered it, developed a plan around it and eventually found a more immediate weapon than political accusations.

He could expose the Emperor’s betrayal and hope the Great Houses united against Shaddam. Or he could control the spice and make the entire Imperium answer to him. He chose the weapon nobody could afford to challenge.

text:
Coromandel International Ltd Concall Summary (Q2 FY27, 12 November 2026) #COROMANDEL

🟡 Management Guidance: 
Management expects H2 FY27 to be significantly better than H1, supported by revised Rabi NBS subsidy rates, moderation in raw material prices, improved farm economics and a recovery in fertilizer consumption. The company expects fertilizer production, sales and consumption to improve during Rabi. Management indicated that NPK prices could see a 10% to 15% moderation in certain grades such as 20:20, depending on the final subsidy notification and the scope for MRP correction. The newly commissioned phosphoric acid and sulfuric acid plant at Kakinada is back to full-capacity operations, with backward integration spreads expected to improve in H2. Management considers a $300 to $350 spread a reasonable assumption. The new granulation facility is expected to be commissioned by February, with the target of operating close to full capacity next year. The retail network is targeted to increase from 1,300 stores to 2,000 over the next two years. Management expects the retail white-label brand to cross ₹100 crore in annual sales this year. One key crop protection molecule's expanded capacity is expected to come on stream by the end of November. The fluorination launch plant will be used to qualify products with customers before committing ₹200 crore to ₹300 crore towards a commercial facility, potentially 1 to 2 years later. Management expects to provide a further update on the Daksha defence order next quarter.

🟢 Green Alert: Consolidated Q2 revenue increased 6% YoY to ₹10,348 crore, while EBITDA declined 18% to ₹944 crore and PAT fell to ₹523 crore from ₹793 crore. H1 revenue grew 10% to ₹18,563 crore, but EBITDA declined 12% to ₹1,705 crore and PAT fell to ₹905 crore from ₹1,295 crore. The Kakinada phosphoric acid and sulfuric acid plant has resumed full-capacity operations following the sulfur subsidy announcement, improving the company's backward integration economics. Management expects the value gap from backward integration to benefit H2 performance. Crop protection revenue grew 22% in Q2, supported by exports, while Coromandel's standalone crop protection export revenue grew 44% and exports contributed more than 40% of segment revenue. New products contributed 36% of crop protection business during the year. Retail added 80 stores during Q2, taking the network to 1,300, with several recently opened stores reaching breakeven faster than expected. Specialty nutrients, organic fertilizers and biological products performed well, supported by increased farmer adoption and demand for differentiated products. The company launched 10 new products across nutrients and crop protection. The revised Rabi NBS rates and special sulfur subsidy have received cabinet approval. Subsidy collections were ₹4,478 crore during H1, and the company received another approximately ₹1,200 crore in October. Management also indicated that channel inventory is not significantly elevated, with industry inventory estimated at only 5% to 7% above last year's level.

🔴 Red Alert: Q2 was severely affected by deficient rainfall of around 20% to 30% across key markets, rupee depreciation, elevated raw material prices, weak agricultural consumption and unfavorable subsidy rates. Industry NPK production and consumption declined approximately 40% during the quarter. Coromandel's fertilizer primary sales declined 30% to 10 lakh tonnes, while production fell 15% to 7.7 lakh tonnes as management deliberately moderated supplies to protect working capital. H1 industry NPK sales declined to 60 lakh tonnes from 77 lakh tonnes, while DAP remained flat at 44 lakh tonnes. The widening price gap between DAP and NPK fertilizers caused farmers to shift towards DAP, hurting domestic complex fertilizer manufacturers. Consolidated EBITDA and PAT declined despite revenue growth, highlighting the impact of margin compression. NACL reported Q2 revenue of ₹374 crore, down 18%, and EBITDA of just ₹12 crore, due to high-cost inventory that could not be passed on to customers amid falling market prices. Management expects a recovery but acknowledged that crop protection portfolio improvements and new product registrations will take time, potentially 2 to 3 years. Restrictions on the sale of non-subsidy fertilizers in Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and Maharashtra have also affected business. The government's pilot fertilizer sales framework applies to all fertilizers and could restrict farmers' ability to purchase the required NPK quantities if implementation issues are not resolved. Battery-grade phosphoric acid development has been delayed for 2 to 3 quarters because management is prioritising the core fertilizer business. The proposed fluorination commercial plant requires customer validation and signed commitments before investment. The Daksha defence drone business is still awaiting progress on its earlier defence order, and no confirmed order timeline was provided.

🔵 Blue Alert: Coromandel is gradually diversifying beyond conventional subsidized fertilizers into crop protection, specialty nutrients, biologicals, retail, nano fertilizers, specialty chemicals and drones. Its retail network is becoming an important distribution advantage, allowing the company to sell organic fertilizers, water-soluble nutrients, biologicals and proprietary products directly to farmers. Management believes biologicals can deliver sustainable growth through neem-based biopesticides, microbials, plant extracts and organic fertilizers. These products have relatively strong entry barriers due to proprietary research, product registrations, branding and farmer engagement, although scaling volumes requires time. Specialty nutrients have historically delivered 20% to 25% volume growth, according to management, and the company is working to reduce dependence on imported Chinese raw materials through captive sourcing. In crop protection, Coromandel is leveraging NACL's spare manufacturing capacity, R&D capabilities and product portfolio to develop new-age chemistries and pursue CDMO opportunities. The proposed fluorination business could use hydrofluoroacetic acid generated from its phosphoric acid operations, providing a potential raw material advantage over competitors using the phosphor route. Management wants customer commitments before investing in this business. The company is also expanding its presence in nano DAP, with exports beginning and registrations being pursued in Latin America, the Middle East and Southeast Asia. Daksha is developing agricultural and defence drones, with two new agricultural drone variants introduced and demonstrations conducted for the Army in the Kargil region. The company has a 1,30,000 sq. ft. drone facility and is developing an indigenous vendor ecosystem.

🧠 Deep Insight: Coromandel's Q2 performance reflects a combination of industry-wide demand weakness and unfavorable fertilizer economics rather than simply a company-specific operational problem. The most important near-term variable is whether the revised NBS subsidy rates translate into lower NPK prices, improved farmer affordability and a recovery in consumption during Rabi. The company's deliberate reduction in production and primary sales has helped contain inventory and working capital risk, while the Kakinada backward integration facility provides an opportunity to improve margins as production scales up. However, the recovery should not be judged only by improved subsidy economics. Actual fertilizer volumes, NPK market share and the company's ability to maintain profitability after MRP corrections will be critical. Beyond fertilizers, retail, biologicals, specialty nutrients and crop protection exports are developing into meaningful diversification opportunities. NACL remains a weak point in the near term, although its manufacturing capacity and R&D capabilities could create longer-term synergies. The fluorination project is promising but remains at the customer-validation stage, while defence drones are still awaiting order conversion. The central investment thesis is that Coromandel is combining its established fertilizer and backward integration business with a growing retail-led specialty agriculture and crop protection platform. A recovery in fertilizer consumption could improve near-term earnings, while biologicals, specialty nutrients, exports and new chemistries offer longer-term growth opportunities. Key monitorables are Rabi fertilizer volumes, NPK market share, EBITDA per tonne, backward integration spreads, Kakinada utilisation, granulation plant commissioning, NACL margin recovery, retail store profitability, crop protection exports and customer commitments for the fluorination project.

One funny story:

I was the Maintenance Officer in the VF-154 Black Knights in Atsugi, Japan (1998-2000).  At one point we desperately needed a Tomcat nose strut and the part wouldn't arrive in time for the next at sea period.

One of my Chiefs offered: "Why don't we inspect the nose strut on the static Tomcat at the main gate and if it's in good shape we can use that one."

That bird had been sitting there for years, but the Tomcat is notoriously tough, thanks to Grumman Ironworks.

My response: "OK, let's do it.  And Chief?  I didn't hear that."

(I would, of course, have backed them up if it went sideways.)

God Bless the Goat Locker.

text:
Deal Attorneys: The Purchase Agreement Is Signed. The Client's 2026 Tax Question Is Still Open.

To the business-transaction, M&A, and corporate attorneys working Texas: this one is for you.

You see a sale long before the tax return does. You know the closing date, the price allocation, and the payment terms. Often you are also the first person the seller asks, "What does this do to my taxes this year?"

Here is a scenario. A business owner (and accredited investor) signs a purchase agreement in October and expects to close before year end. The attorney's work is done well. Then the owner asks what can be done about the 2026 tax bill.

Three things are worth noticing early:

1. Allocation can change the character of the income.

How the price is allocated among the assets can change how much of the gain is taxed as ordinary income and how much as capital gain. That is a CPA question, and it is easiest to raise before the allocation is final.

2. Payment terms can change the year the income lands.

An installment structure, an earnout, or a holdback can move income into a later year. A closing in 2026 with a full cash payment puts all of it in 2026.

3. A high-income year starts a planning conversation.

When income is concentrated in one year, owners often ask about categories such as intangible drilling cost programs, Opportunity Zone funds, and Delaware Statutory Trusts. Each comes with real limits. Drilling programs are speculative, illiquid, and can lose money at any price. Their deductions are generally taken in the year the program is funded, can be recaptured as ordinary income on a later sale, and are not the same as a return. Whether any category fits depends on the client's full financial picture and on how the interest is held.

You are not tax counsel, and nobody expects you to be. But you are in the room early, and a client who hears "bring your CPA into this now" is better served than one who hears it in January.

This is a conversation, not a recommendation, and none of this is tax or legal advice. Please review your specific situation with your CPA.

If you or your clients are facing a significant tax event from a sale, I am glad to be a resource. Reach out anytime, or schedule a conversation.

Earl Proeger
Grace Capital Management | Austin, TX | (512) 293-7731

#MergersAndAcquisitions #BusinessSale #TaxPlanning #AustinBusiness #TexasLawyers

Intangible drilling cost programs are speculative, illiquid private placements for accredited investors only, offered only by private placement memorandum. text:
Board Meeting of BundleCorp Inc.
======================
In the luxurious conference room on the 27th floor of a Manhattan skyscraper, with the New York skyline glowing at dusk through floor-to-ceiling windows, the animals of the Board of Directors and Management gathered around the long mahogany table.

Golden Tail the Fox, Chairman of the Board, tapped his paw on the polished surface.

“Gentlemen,” he began in a smooth, measured voice, “the minority sheep shareholders still hold a few percent. We need to gently squeeze them out. At a price we will deem fair market value.”

Gray Fang the Wolf smiled, baring his teeth.

“Fair? Meaning a price that works for us and isn’t worth fighting over?”

“Exactly,” the Fox confirmed. “We’ll deliver a valuation that looks respectable on paper. Not low enough to trigger immediate outrage, not high enough to leave real money on the table. Most importantly, it must appear independent and arm’s length.”

The Owl from Management adjusted her glasses.

“What if someone goes to the Delaware Court of Chancery?”

The Fox waved his tail.

“Let them. These cases drag on for three, four, five years. Expert witnesses, fairness opinions, motions, appeals. Lawyers charge a fortune. A sheep holding twenty shares will quickly realize the legal fees exceed any possible recovery. Most won’t even start. They’ll take the offer and move on.”

The Bear from the Board nodded slowly.

“What if they organize a class action?”

“Even better,” the Fox replied. “The more sheep in one lawsuit, the longer and more expensive it becomes. We have time and deep pockets. They have nerves and legal bills. After two years, half will drop out saying it’s no longer worth it. The rest will start arguing among themselves.”

The Hyena from Management laughed.

“And if the Wall Street Journal writes about it?”

“They will,” the Fox said calmly. “Then someone else will. In six months everyone will have moved on to the next scandal. By then the deal will be closed. Officially: voluntary tender offer, fair market price, full transparency.”

The Wolf added:

“The best part is that we get to define what market price means. Because we are the market. If we say it’s worth this much, then it is. Anyone who disagrees can prove otherwise… in court… over years.”

The Owl sighed.

“So the plan is simple: offer them a little, call it generous, then wait until they get tired of fighting.”

“Precisely,” Golden Tail confirmed. “Sheep like peace and quiet. We like control. If we play this right, most of them will even be grateful they got something at all. And those who complain will eventually give up on their own. Everyone will be satisfied. Well… almost everyone.”

The Hyena laughed again.

“Almost. But the ones who aren’t still won’t be able to do anything about it.”

The Fox smiled widely and closed his folder.

“Exactly. Let’s record the resolution. Fair value — whatever we decide is fair. And let the sheep be glad we even asked them.”

The meeting adjourned. Down the hall, the sheep still had no idea their value had just been decided for them.

text:
The propensity for AI systems to make mistakes and for humans to miss those mistakes has been on full display in the US legal system as of late. The follies began when lawyers—including some at prestigious firms—submitted documents citing cases that didn’t exist. Similar mistakes soon spread to other roles in the courts. In December, a Stanford professor submitted sworn testimony containing hallucinations and errors in a case about deepfakes, despite being an expert on AI and misinformation himself.

The buck stopped with judges, who—whether they or opposing counsel caught the mistakes—issued reprimands and fines, and likely left attorneys embarrassed enough to think twice before trusting AI again.

But now judges are experimenting with generative AI too. Some are confident that with the right precautions, the technology can expedite legal research, summarize cases, draft routine orders, and overall help speed up the court system, which is badly backlogged in many parts of the US. This summer, though, we’ve already seen AI-generated mistakes go undetected and cited by judges. A federal judge in New Jersey had to reissue an order riddled with errors that may have come from AI, and a judge in Mississippi refused to explain why his order too contained mistakes that seemed like AI hallucinations. 

The results of these early-adopter experiments make two things clear. One, the category of routine tasks—for which AI can assist without requiring human judgment—is slippery to define. Two, while lawyers face sharp scrutiny when their use of AI leads to mistakes, judges may not face the same accountability, and walking back their mistakes before they do damage is much harder.

Drawing boundaries

Xavier Rodriguez, a federal judge for the Western District of Texas, has good reason to be skeptical of AI. He started learning about artificial intelligence back in 2018, four years before the release of ChatGPT (thanks in part to the influence of his twin brother, who works in tech). But he’s also seen AI-generated mistakes in his own court. 

In a recent dispute about who was to receive an insurance payout, both the plaintiff and the defendant represented themselves, without lawyers (this is not uncommon—nearly a quarter of civil cases in federal court involve at least one unrepresented party). The two sides wrote their own filings and made their own arguments. 

“Both sides used AI tools,” Rodriguez says, and both submitted filings that referenced made-up cases. He had authority to reprimand them, but given that they were not lawyers, he opted not to. 

“I think there’s been an overreaction by a lot of judges on these sanctions. The running joke I tell when I’m on the speaking circuit is that lawyers have been hallucinating well before AI,” he says. Missing a mistake from an AI model is not wholly different, to Rodriguez, from failing to catch the error of a first-year lawyer. “I’m not as deeply offended as everybody else,” he says. 

In his court, Rodriguez has been using generative AI tools (he wouldn’t publicly name which ones, to avoid the appearance of an endorsement) to summarize cases. He’ll ask AI to identify key players involved and then have it generate a timeline of key events. Ahead of specific hearings, Rodriguez will also ask it to generate questions for attorneys based on the materials they submit.

These tasks, to him, don’t lean on human judgment. They also offer lots of opportunities for him to intervene and uncover any mistakes before they’re brought to the court. “It’s not any final decision being made, and so it’s relatively risk free,” he says. Using AI to predict whether someone should be eligible for bail, on the other hand, goes too far in the direction of judgment and discretion, in his view.

Erin Solovey, a professor and researcher on human-AI interaction at Worcester Polytechnic Institute in Massachusetts, recently studied how judges in the UK think about this distinction between rote, machine-friendly work that feels safe to delegate to AI and tasks that lean more heavily on human expertise. 

“The line between what is appropriate for a human judge to do versus what is appropriate for AI tools to do changes from judge to judge and from one scenario to the next,” she says.

Even so, according to Solovey, some of these tasks simply don’t match what AI is good at. Asking AI to summarize a large document, for example, might produce drastically different results depending on whether the model has been trained to summarize for a general audience or a legal one. AI also struggles with logic-based tasks like ordering the events of a case. “A very plausible-sounding timeline may be factually incorrect,” Solovey says. 

Rodriguez and a number of other judges crafted guidelines that were published in February by the Sedona Conference, an influential think tank that issues principles for particularly murky areas of the law. They outline a host of potentially “safe” uses of AI for judges, including conducting legal research, creating preliminary transcripts, and searching briefings, while warning that judges should verify outputs from AI and that “no known GenAI tools have fully resolved the hallucination problem.”

Dodging AI blunders

Judge Allison Goddard, a federal magistrate judge in California and a coauthor of the guidelines, first felt the impact that AI would have on the judiciary when she taught a class on the art of advocacy at her daughter’s high school. She was impressed by a student’s essay and mentioned it to her daughter. “She said, ‘Oh, Mom, that’s ChatGPT.’”

“What I realized very quickly was this is going to really transform the legal profession,” she says. In her court, Goddard has been experimenting with ChatGPT, Claude (which she keeps “open all day”), and a host of other AI models. If a case involves a particularly technical issue, she might ask AI to help her understand which questions to ask attorneys. She’ll summarize 60-page orders from the district judge and then ask the AI model follow-up questions about it, or ask it to organize information from documents that are a mess. 

“It’s kind of a thought partner, and it brings a perspective that you may not have considered,” she says.

Goddard also encourages her clerks to use AI, specifically Anthropic’s Claude, because by default it does not train on user conversations. But it has its limits. For anything that requires law-specific knowledge, she’ll use tools from Westlaw or Lexis, which have AI tools built specifically for lawyers, but she finds general-purpose AI models to be faster for lots of other tasks. And her concerns about bias have prevented her from using it for tasks in criminal cases, like determining if there was probable cause for an arrest.

In this, Goddard appears to be caught in the same predicament the AI boom has created for many of us. Three years in, companies have built tools that sound so fluent and humanlike they obscure the intractable problems lurking underneath—answers that read well but are wrong, models that are trained to be decent at everything but perfect for nothing, and the risk that your conversations with them will be leaked to the internet. Each time we use them, we bet that the time saved will outweigh the risks, and trust ourselves to catch the mistakes before they matter. For judges, the stakes are sky-high: If they lose that bet, they face very public consequences, and the impact of such mistakes on the people they serve can be lasting. 

“I’m not going to be the judge that cites hallucinated cases and orders,” Goddard says. “It’s really embarrassing, very professionally embarrassing.”

Still, some judges don’t want to get left behind in the AI age. With some in the AI sector suggesting that the supposed objectivity and rationality of AI models could make them better judges than fallible humans, it might lead some on the bench to think that falling behind poses a bigger risk than getting too far out ahead. 

A ‘crisis waiting to happen’

The risks of early adoption have raised alarm bells with Judge Scott Schlegel, who serves on the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeal in Louisiana. Schlegel has long blogged about the helpful role technology can play in modernizing the court system, but he has warned that AI-generated mistakes in judges’ rulings signal a “crisis waiting to happen,” one that would dwarf the problem of lawyers’ submitting filings with made-up cases. 

Attorneys who make mistakes can get sanctioned, have their motions dismissed, or lose cases when the opposing party finds out and flags the errors. “When the judge makes a mistake, that’s the law,” he says. “I can’t go a month or two later and go ‘Oops, so sorry,’ and reverse myself. It doesn’t work that way.”

Consider child custody cases or bail proceedings, Schlegel says: “There are pretty significant consequences when a judge relies upon artificial intelligence to make the decision,” especially if the citations that decision relies on are made-up or incorrect.

This is not theoretical. In June, a Georgia appellate court judge issued an order that relied partially on made-up cases submitted by one of the parties, a mistake that went uncaught. In July, a federal judge in New Jersey withdrew an opinion after lawyers complained it too contained hallucinations. 

Unlike lawyers, who can be ordered by the court to explain why there are mistakes in their filings, judges do not have to show much transparency, and there is little reason to think they’ll do so voluntarily. On August 4, a federal judge in Mississippi had to issue a new decision in a civil rights case after the original was found to contain incorrect names and serious errors. The judge did not fully explain what led to the errors even after the state asked him to do so. “No further explanation is warranted,” the judge wrote.

These mistakes could erode the public’s faith in the legitimacy of courts, Schlegel says. Certain narrow and monitored applications of AI—summarizing testimonies, getting quick writing feedback—can save time, and they can produce good results if judges treat the work like that of a first-year associate, checking it thoroughly for accuracy. But most of the job of being a judge is dealing with what he calls the white-page problem: You’re presiding over a complex case with a blank page in front of you, forced to make difficult decisions. Thinking through those decisions, he says, is indeed the work of being a judge. Getting help with a first draft from an AI undermines that purpose.

“If you’re making a decision on who gets the kids this weekend and somebody finds out you use Grok and you should have used Gemini or ChatGPT—you know, that’s not the justice system.”

The following is a fictionalized story inspired by public news accounts. Any dialogue, internal motivations, and personal background details beyond the reported charges are imagined for dramatic narrative purposes.

The Cross-Country Haul, From Baton Rouge to The Gulch

The highway stretches out from Louisiana like a ribbon of endless possibility, at least when you are looking at it through the windshield of a rented Kia loaded down with designer bags. For Satonya Maiden, 46, and Ebony Hammond, 33, both hailing from Baton Rouge, the open road was not about sightseeing. It was a business route, one mapped out by high-end retail zip codes and dressing room mirrors.

By the time they rolled into Nashville’s trendy Gulch neighborhood, their trunk was already a rolling department store. Inside sat a curated collection of retail desire: sleek athletic wear from Alo, prestige cosmetics from Sephora and Ulta, rugged gear from Carhartt, and stacks of Lululemon leggings. Altogether, the haul would later be valued at more than ten thousand dollars. To a casual observer, they were just two women traveling together, maybe sisters or longtime friends on a southern road trip. In reality, they were operating on borrowed time, trailing a string of theft warrants tied to retail stores scattered across the country.

Every heist relies on the quiet anonymity of a busy storefront, the assumption that faces blur together when shoppers are focused on price tags and fabric blends. When Maiden and Hammond stepped into the Lululemon in The Gulch, they moved with practiced ease, selecting items and slipping behind the heavy curtains of the fitting room. Inside that small, brightly lit space, the familiar routine began: the subtle snap of security tags being detached, the careful folding of merchandise meant to leave without passing a register.

What they did not account for was institutional memory. Retail loss prevention has a long reach, and photos circulate faster than interstate traffic. Behind the counter and on the sales floor, employees recognized the pair almost immediately. The whispers turned into a quiet call to local authorities, and the perimeter outside the boutique tightened before the dressing room door even swung open.

When Metro Nashville police arrived, the road trip hit a hard wall. Hammond, attempting to buy a few final minutes of freedom, offered up two different last names and a pair of fraudulent Social Security numbers. It was a last-ditch effort to outrun a paper trail that had already caught up to them. A search of her purse revealed a key fob, which led officers directly to the parked Kia nearby and the ten-thousand-dollar inventory waiting inside.

The arrests brought an abrupt end to their interstate run. Maiden faced charges of burglary, theft, drug possession, and being a fugitive from justice, while Hammond was booked on burglary, theft, criminal impersonation, and her own fugitive warrant. What began on the highways out of Baton Rouge ended under the fluorescent lights of a booking room, a reminder that even the longest road eventually runs out of miles.

text:
So let me get this straight. Canada's biggest potash company, a Canadian company selling a Canadian resource, is about to spend up to a billion dollars on its next export terminal. And it's building it in Washington state?

The Globe and Mail reports Nutrien and the Port of Longview just put a development plan and lease terms in front of the port board. The vote is later this month. The terminal would move 5 to 8 million tonnes a year.

Now remember what Ottawa told you. Faster approvals. Major projects. Build it here. The transport minister even said he'd change Nutrien's mind. How'd that go? It didn't. The rail jams through the B.C. mountains are still there. So is the Second Narrows bottleneck.

The potash is ours. The terminal, the construction money and the jobs are theirs. And nobody in Ottawa seems embarrassed by it. Why not?

text:
Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen | Jonathan M Gitlin, Ars Technica

The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US.

Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01.

What’s a Kei car?

In the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output.

A Kei car must fit within the following dimensions: 11.2 feet (3.4 m) long, 4.9 feet (1.5 m) wide, and 6.6 feet (2 m) tall, with an engine displacement of no more than 0.66 L and an output of 63 hp (47 kW) or less. That’s a far cry from the more than 16 feet (4.9 m) of a full-size pickup truck, but it makes sense for a country where you’re not allowed to buy a car unless you have somewhere to park it, with those spaces being at an absolute premium.

Being affordable to buy and economical to run sure doesn’t hurt either, and last year, Japan bought almost 1.7 million Kei cars, out of total sales of 4.6 million vehicles. Depending on where you live in the US, it can be varying degrees of difficult to import a Kei car, at least until now.

Scion is back?

Toyota killed off its Scion sub-brand more than a decade ago, ending the haggle-free approach and cars aimed at younger buyers in favor of selling more Toyotas. But now it’s back as “Scion by Toyota,” which the automaker will apparently use to experiment with less traditional ideas. But forget about a cool-but-boxy EV in the mold of the Honda N-One or Nissan Sakura.

“The future of mobility will not be defined by one vehicle, one technology, or one way of thinking,” said Simon Humphries, Toyota’s chief branding officer and head of design. “Scion by Toyota gives us a place to challenge conventional thinking, explore new possibilities, and create mobility in new ways. The KEI-01, SxS, and BKE concepts each represent a different possibility—and together, they show what can happen when curiosity leads the way.”

Before anyone gets too excited, the KEI-01 will be classified as a “ low-speed vehicle,” which means it can’t go any faster than 25 mph (40 km/h). So if you were hoping to use one of these but need to drive on anything but surface streets, be prepared to get honked at a lot, and not in a good way. In fact, unless you’re buying a fleet, Toyota won’t sell you a KEI-01 at all, at least not to begin with.

The bed can carry up to 600 lbs  (272 kg).

You probably wanted a kei car like the Honda N-One. But that’s not what we’re getting.

Not only will the KEI-01 be dwarfed by other cars and limited to 25 mph, but the steering wheel is on the wrong side.

Oh, and it’s only available as right-hand drive, since that’s the side of the road Japan drives on. But it does feature all-wheel drive, so if you own a ranch—or perhaps a whole load of golf courses—the utility becomes a little more obvious. Toyota says the KEI-01 is suited to small business owners in urban environments, farmers and ranchers, organizations that have campuses that need fleets of facility vehicles, delivery drivers, and outdoor enthusiasts. The trucks will be shipped to Toyota’s assembly plant in Indiana as knock-down kits, adding 50 jobs to the plant in mid-2027.

Low-speed vehicles have been street-legal in parts of the US for many years now. In my neighborhood in Washington, DC, Circuit operates a low-speed EV shuttle on demand, and gas-powered golf carts are very popular in retirement communities. Pricing for the KEI-01 hasn’t been announced, but speculation runs from as little as $10,000 to as much as $28,000.

text:
Pyth Network is now an approved distributor of real-time NYSE market data

On November 11, 2026, @PythNetwork added NYSE Best Quote and Trades (BQT) to its Data Marketplace. This brings live Level 1 data from all five NYSE Group equity exchanges: NYSE,NYSE American, NYSE Arca, NYSE National & NYSE Texas.

What Pyth Network offers:
• Best bid and offer with size (top-of-book)
• Real-time trades and last sale
• Official closing prices and consolidated volume
• Market status messages (trading halts, resumptions, and short-sale restrictions)

Clients still license the data directly with NYSE and receive it through Pyth, subject to NYSE's market data policies.

Anthony Zawadzki, NYSE's head of data and digital asset products, said the collaboration "gives builders and institutions a new way to access NYSE data".

This follows Pyth's earlier Nasdaq data integration and expands options for apps offering equity perps, tokenized stocks, and 24/7 pricing (combined with Pyth Indices).
